lessons.title: What Is a Computer?
lessons.content:
Imagine you have a helper who never gets tired, never forgets, can add a million numbers in less than a second and never makes a silly mistake. Sounds like a superhero, right? But there is a catch. This helper has zero common sense. If you tell it to do something stupid, it will do the stupid thing perfectly and super fast. That helper is a computer, and this whole course is about understanding how that helper works.

The word computer comes from "compute", which simply means to calculate. Long ago, a "computer" was actually a person, usually someone whose job was doing long calculations by hand for things like ship navigation tables. Today the word means a machine. A simple definition you can use in any exam is this: a computer is an electronic device that accepts data as input, processes it according to a set of instructions called a program, produces output, and can store data and programs for later use.

Let us break that definition down slowly, because every single word in it is important. "Electronic" means it works using electricity and tiny electronic parts, not gears and wheels like old machines. "Accepts data" means it can take something in from the outside world. "Processes according to instructions" means it does not decide by itself what to do; it follows a program. "Produces output" means it gives you a result. "Stores" means it can keep things to use again later.

The input-process-output model: Computer scientists like to describe every computer using a simple model called IPO, which stands for Input, Process and Output. Many books add a fourth part, Storage, so you will also see it called IPOS. This model is like a recipe for understanding any computer, from a tiny calculator to a giant supercomputer. Once you learn to see the IPO model, you will start noticing it everywhere.

Input: Input is anything that goes into the computer. When you type on a keyboard, touch a phone screen, speak to a voice assistant, scan a QR code or take a photo, you are giving input. Input can also come from sensors, like a thermometer inside an air conditioner, or from another computer over the internet. The parts that take input are called input devices, and we will study them in detail in a later lesson.

Process: Processing is the thinking part, except the computer is not really thinking. It is following steps. Processing can mean adding numbers, comparing two values to see which is bigger, sorting a list of names, changing the colours of a photo or checking whether your password is correct. All this work is done mainly by the CPU, the Central Processing Unit, which people often call the brain of the computer. Inside, it is really just doing millions of tiny simple steps very fast.

Output: Output is the result that comes out after processing. It could be text on the screen, a printed page, a sound from the speaker, a vibration in your phone or even a signal that tells a motor to start. The devices that show or deliver results, like monitors, printers and speakers, are called output devices.

Storage: Storage is where the computer keeps data and programs so they are not lost. There are two big kinds. Primary storage, mainly RAM, is fast but temporary, like a whiteboard you wipe clean when the power goes off. Secondary storage, like a hard disk, SSD or memory card, keeps things permanently, like a notebook in your bag. Your photos stay on your phone after you switch it off because they are in secondary storage.

A tiny worked example: Let us see IPO in action with a calculator. You press 12, then plus, then 30, then equals. The key presses are input. The calculator chip adds 12 and 30; that is processing. The screen shows 42; that is output. If you press the M+ button, the calculator saves 42 in its memory; that is storage. Four steps, and you have just watched a computer do its whole job.

Data and information: These two words sound similar, but in computer science they mean different things, and exam questions love this difference. Data means raw facts and figures that have not been organised yet, like a list of numbers: 65, 72, 80, 45, 90. On their own, those numbers do not tell you much. Information is data that has been processed so it has meaning for someone. If I tell you "the average mark in the class is 70.4, and one student failed", now you have information. A computer's main job is turning data into information.

Here is another way to remember it. Data is like raw rice, dal and vegetables. Information is the cooked khichuri. The cooking is the processing. Nobody wants to eat raw rice, and nobody wants to read a giant list of raw numbers. We want the useful, ready-to-use result.

Characteristics of a computer: Textbooks usually list the special qualities that make computers so useful. You should know each one with a simple example. The first is speed. A modern computer can do billions of simple operations every second. Speed is often measured in units like GHz for the clock, or in operations per second. A task that would take a person a whole year, like adding every number from one to one billion, takes a computer only moments.

The second is accuracy. If the program and the input are correct, the output will be correct every single time. Computers do not get confused or careless. When a computer makes a "mistake", the cause is almost always a wrong program or wrong input given by a human. The third is storage capacity. A small memory card can hold thousands of books' worth of text, and a computer can find any word in it in a moment.

The fourth is diligence, which means it never gets tired or bored. A computer can do the same calculation a million times, and the millionth answer will be as accurate as the first. A human would be exhausted after a hundred. The fifth is versatility, meaning the same computer can do many different jobs. Right now your laptop can play music, edit a photo, run a video call and calculate your monthly budget, just by switching programs.

The sixth is automation. Once a program starts, the computer can run all the steps by itself without anyone pressing a button for each step. Think of a bank computer that calculates interest for one million accounts overnight. Nobody sits there clicking a million times. The program runs automatically from start to end.

The big limitation: no IQ: Now comes the most important characteristic, and it is a weakness. A computer has no intelligence of its own. It cannot decide what is right or wrong, it has no feelings and no common sense. Even modern AI systems only work because people designed and trained them. If you write a program that says "add the price twice", the computer will happily charge every customer double, without ever thinking "hmm, that looks wrong".

GIGO: Because of this, programmers have a famous rule called GIGO, which stands for Garbage In, Garbage Out. If you put wrong data into a computer, you will get wrong results out, no matter how powerful the computer is. If a shopkeeper types the price of rice as 6,500 taka per kilo instead of 65, the billing software will print a crazy bill. The computer did its job perfectly; the human input was garbage.

What makes something a computer: A good test is to ask two questions. First, does it follow a stored set of instructions, a program? Second, does it handle input, processing and output? A simple light switch takes input and gives output, but it does not process anything or follow a program, so it is not a computer. A digital watch, a microwave and a car's engine control unit all follow programs, so they do contain small computers.

General-purpose and special-purpose computers: A general-purpose computer can run many different kinds of programs. Laptops, desktops and smartphones are like this; you can install new apps and make them do new jobs. A special-purpose computer is built to do only one job, again and again. The chip inside a washing machine, a digital weighing scale in a shop or a traffic light controller are special-purpose. They are often called embedded computers because they are hidden inside other machines.

Real-life example 1, the bKash transaction: Think about sending 500 taka using bKash. You type the receiver's number, the amount and your PIN. That is input. The bKash servers check your PIN, check that you have enough balance, take 500 taka from your account and add it to the other account. That is processing. You get a confirmation message on the screen and an SMS. That is output. The transaction record is saved in a huge database so both of you can see it in your history later. That is storage. One small action, and the whole IPO model is there.

Real-life example 2, the school result: Every year, boards in Bangladesh publish SSC and HSC results for millions of students. Teachers' marks for each subject go into the computer system as input. The system adds marks, calculates the GPA using fixed rules and checks for pass or fail. That is processing. Then results appear on websites and are sent by SMS. That is output. All marks stay stored for years, so you can get your certificate later. Without computers, calculating results for so many students by hand would take months and would be full of mistakes.

Common mistakes students make: Many students think the computer "understands" what we want. It does not; it only follows instructions. Another mistake is mixing up data and information; remember that information is processed and meaningful. Some students think the monitor is the computer; actually the monitor is only an output device, and the real processing happens inside the system unit or the main chip. Also, do not forget storage when you explain the IPO model in an exam, because many teachers expect four parts.

What exams usually ask: Typical questions are "Define a computer", "Draw and explain the IPO model", "Write the difference between data and information with examples", "Write five characteristics of a computer" and "What is GIGO?". For short questions, a neat definition plus a small example always gets better marks than a long paragraph with no example. Drawing a simple box diagram of Input, then Process, then Output, with Storage connected to Process, is a quick way to impress the examiner.

Quick recap: A computer is an electronic machine that takes input, processes it by following a program, gives output and stores data. The IPO model with storage describes every computer. Data is raw; information is processed and useful. Computers are fast, accurate, tireless, versatile and automatic, but they have no common sense, so wrong input gives wrong output. In the next lessons, we will open up this machine piece by piece and see how each part does its job.
key_points: A computer is an electronic machine that takes input, processes it by following instructions, gives output and can store data.
The IPO model: Input, Process, Output, plus Storage, describes every computer from a calculator to a supercomputer.
Data is raw facts; information is processed data that has meaning for someone.
Main characteristics: speed, accuracy, storage, automation, versatility, diligence and no IQ of its own.
A computer only follows a program. The famous rule is GIGO: garbage in, garbage out.
General-purpose computers run many programs; special-purpose computers do one job.
Limits: no common sense, no feelings, needs power and needs humans to give correct instructions.
lessons.tip: Every time you use a phone, an ATM or a calculator this week, stop for two seconds and name the input, the process, the output and the storage. After ten tries, the IPO model will feel like common sense.
lessons.task: Pick three machines at home (for example a phone, a microwave and a TV remote). For each one, write a small table with four rows: input, process, output, storage. Then decide: is it a general-purpose computer, a special-purpose computer, or not a computer at all? Write one line explaining why.

quiz.q: Which order shows the basic working cycle of a computer?
options: Input, Process, Output, with Storage alongside
quiz.explain: Data comes in (input), gets worked on (process), results come out (output), and storage keeps data and programs for later.

quiz.q: A teacher types 40 students' marks into a spreadsheet and gets the class average. What is the class average?
quiz.explain: The 40 raw marks are data. The average is processed, meaningful information that helps the teacher decide something.

quiz.q: A calculator shows a wrong total because a student typed 5 instead of 50. Which idea explains this?
options: The calculator is a special-purpose computer
quiz.explain: The machine processed exactly what it got. Wrong input gives wrong output, and that is GIGO.

quiz.q: Which of these is a special-purpose computer?
options: The chip inside a washing machine
quiz.explain: A washing machine's chip runs only its washing program. Laptops, PCs and phones can run many different programs, so they are general-purpose.

quiz.q: Why do we say a computer has "no IQ"?
options: It cannot think for itself and only follows the instructions it is given
quiz.explain: A computer is very fast and accurate, but it has no common sense. It only does what its program tells it to do.

lessons.title: The History of Computers
lessons.content:
Your phone can do things that would look like magic to someone from 100 years ago. But it did not appear suddenly. It is the result of thousands of years of people trying to count faster and make fewer mistakes. Every machine in this story solved one problem and gave the next inventor an idea. When you know this story, the parts of a modern computer suddenly make more sense, because you see why each one was invented.

Counting with fingers and stones: The very first "computing devices" were our own fingers. That is one reason we count in tens. Later people used pebbles, sticks and knots on ropes to keep track of things like how many sheep they had or how much grain was stored. The Latin word for pebble is calculus, and that is where our word "calculate" comes from. These methods worked, but they were slow and it was easy to lose count.

The abacus: The abacus is a frame with beads sliding on rods. It appeared in different forms in Mesopotamia, China, Japan and other places, thousands of years ago. Each rod stands for a place value: ones, tens, hundreds and so on. By sliding beads, a skilled user can add, subtract, multiply and even divide very quickly. The abacus is still used today to teach mental maths to children. It is often called the first calculating device, but notice that it has no automatic processing; the human does all the work.

Napier's bones and the slide rule: In 1617, a Scottish mathematician named John Napier published a set of numbered rods, later called Napier's bones, that made multiplication easier by turning it into addition of digits. Napier also invented logarithms, which turn multiplication into addition. Using this idea, William Oughtred created the slide rule around 1622. Engineers used slide rules for more than 300 years, until pocket calculators replaced them in the 1970s. Even the engineers of early space missions did many calculations with slide rules.

Pascal's calculator: In 1642, a 19-year-old French boy named Blaise Pascal built a mechanical adding machine to help his father, who was a tax officer and had to do endless sums. It was called the Pascaline. It used gears with ten teeth each. When one gear turned past nine, it automatically pushed the next gear by one step. This is exactly the "carry" you do when 9 plus 1 becomes 10. The Pascaline could add and subtract directly. A programming language named Pascal was later named in his honour.

Leibniz's stepped reckoner: About 30 years later, the German mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz improved on Pascal's idea and built the stepped reckoner, which could also multiply and divide by repeated addition and subtraction. Leibniz also wrote about the binary number system, using only 0 and 1. He did not build a binary computer, but more than 200 years later, binary became the language of every digital computer. Remember his name when we study number systems.

The Jacquard loom and punched cards: In 1804, Joseph Marie Jacquard in France made a weaving loom that was controlled by punched cards. Each card had holes in a pattern. Where there was a hole, a hook could go through and lift a thread; where there was no hole, it could not. By changing the cards, you changed the cloth's design without changing the machine. This is a very important idea: the machine stays the same, but the instructions can change. That is the heart of programming.

Charles Babbage, the father of the computer: In the 1820s, an English mathematician named Charles Babbage was frustrated that printed maths tables were full of human errors. He designed the Difference Engine, a giant mechanical machine to calculate tables automatically. Later he designed something much bigger, the Analytical Engine. It was never fully built in his lifetime because the engineering and money were too much. But its design had four parts that sound very familiar: a way to give input using punched cards, a "store" to keep numbers (memory), a "mill" to do calculations (processor) and a way to print output. It could even make decisions and repeat steps. That is why Babbage is called the father of the computer.

Ada Lovelace, the first programmer: Ada Lovelace was a mathematician who worked with Babbage. In 1843 she translated an article about the Analytical Engine and added her own long notes, which were longer than the article itself. In those notes she wrote a step-by-step method for the engine to calculate a series called Bernoulli numbers. This is considered the first published algorithm written for a machine, so she is called the first computer programmer. She also imagined that such machines might one day work with music and pictures, not just numbers. That was a hundred years ahead of her time.

Hollerith and the census: In 1890, the United States needed to count its population. The previous census had taken about seven years to process by hand. Herman Hollerith built a tabulating machine that read punched cards using electricity. Each card stored one person's details as holes. The machine counted the holes automatically, and the work finished in a fraction of the time. Hollerith's company later became part of IBM, one of the most famous computer companies in history. This was the first big use of machines to process data.

Alan Turing and the idea of computation: In 1936, a young English mathematician named Alan Turing wrote a paper describing an imaginary machine, now called the Turing machine. It had a long tape, a head that could read and write symbols, and a simple set of rules. Turing showed that this simple machine could carry out any calculation that can be described as a step-by-step method. This idea is the foundation of computer science. During World War II, Turing also helped break secret German codes. Today the biggest award in computer science is called the Turing Award.

The first electronic computers: During the 1940s, people started building computers with electronic parts called vacuum tubes instead of gears. In Germany, Konrad Zuse built the Z3 in 1941, a programmable machine that used electromechanical relays. In Britain, Colossus was built to help break codes. In the United States, ENIAC was finished in 1945 and shown to the public in 1946. ENIAC had about 18,000 vacuum tubes, weighed around 27 tonnes and filled a big room. It could do about 5,000 additions per second, which was amazing then, but reprogramming it meant rewiring cables by hand, which could take days.

Von Neumann and the stored program: John von Neumann, a brilliant mathematician, described an important idea in 1945: the computer should keep its program in memory, together with its data. Then you could change what the computer does just by loading a different program, instead of rewiring it. Computers built this way, like EDSAC in 1949, are called stored-program computers. Almost every computer today, including your phone, still follows this von Neumann architecture with a CPU, memory, input and output. We will study it properly in a later lesson.

From tubes to chips: Vacuum tubes were big, hot and broke often. In 1947, scientists at Bell Labs invented the transistor, a tiny switch made from a material called a semiconductor. Transistors were smaller, cooler and much more reliable. Then in 1958 and 1959, Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce created the integrated circuit, or IC, which put many transistors onto one small chip. In 1971, Intel released the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, which put a whole CPU on one chip. Each step made computers smaller, faster and cheaper.

Personal computers and the internet: Once the CPU fit on a chip, computers could fit on a desk. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, machines like the Apple II and the IBM PC brought computers into homes and offices. Graphical interfaces with windows and a mouse made them easier to use. In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web, and in the 1990s the internet reached ordinary people. In 2007, the iPhone, and soon Android phones, put a powerful internet computer into everyone's pocket.

Computers in Bangladesh: Bangladesh's computer story is part of this history too. The first computer in the country, an IBM 1620, was installed in 1964 at the Atomic Energy Centre in Dhaka, when the country was still East Pakistan. Universities and banks slowly started using computers in the following decades. In the 2000s and 2010s, mobile phones, mobile banking, online admission and e-government services spread quickly. Today millions of Bangladeshis use smartphones, and there is a growing software and freelancing industry.

Real-life example 1, from abacus to your phone calculator: Think about the simple sum 457 plus 386. On an abacus, you slide beads and carry by hand. On a Pascaline, a gear automatically carries the one. On ENIAC, vacuum tubes switch on and off to add in electronic form. On your phone, billions of transistors inside a tiny chip do the same sum in a few billionths of a second. The maths is the same; only the speed, size and price changed across history.

Real-life example 2, punched cards to QR codes: Jacquard's cards stored patterns as holes and no-holes, which is really just yes and no, or 1 and 0. Today, when you scan a QR code in a shop to pay, the black and white squares do the same job: they store information as two kinds of marks that a machine can read. An idea from a weaving factory more than 200 years ago is in your pocket every day.

Common mistakes: Students often say ENIAC was the first computer, full stop. It is safer to say it was one of the first general-purpose electronic digital computers, because there were earlier machines like the Z3, Colossus and the Atanasoff-Berry Computer. Another mistake is mixing up Babbage and Pascal. Pascal built an adding machine; Babbage designed a programmable general-purpose engine. Also, Ada Lovelace did not build machines; she wrote the program.

What exams usually ask: Expect questions like "Who is called the father of the computer and why?", "Write a short note on the Analytical Engine", "Why is Ada Lovelace called the first programmer?", "What is the contribution of Alan Turing?" and "What is the stored-program concept?". Writing a short timeline with dates in your answer shows you understand the order of events and usually earns extra marks.

Quick recap: Computing started with fingers, pebbles and the abacus. Mechanical calculators by Pascal and Leibniz did arithmetic with gears. Jacquard's punched cards showed that instructions can be separate from the machine. Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, and Ada Lovelace wrote its first program. Hollerith used punched cards for data processing, Turing gave the theory, ENIAC and others brought electronics, von Neumann gave the stored program, and transistors, ICs and microprocessors made computers small enough for every pocket. Next lesson, we will organise this story into the five generations of computers.
key_points: Computing started with counting tools like fingers, pebbles and the abacus.
Napier's bones, the slide rule, Pascal's Pascaline and Leibniz's stepped reckoner were early mechanical aids for calculation.
Jacquard's loom used punched cards to control a machine, an idea later used for programs and data.
Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine; he is called the father of the computer.
Ada Lovelace wrote the first published algorithm meant for a machine and is called the first programmer.
Alan Turing gave the theory of computation; ENIAC was an early general-purpose electronic computer.
Von Neumann's stored-program idea, then transistors, ICs and microprocessors, led to PCs and smartphones.
lessons.tip: Do not try to memorise every date. Learn the story in order: counting tools, mechanical calculators, Babbage's idea, electronic computers, the stored program, then chips. Hang each name and year on that storyline and you will remember far more.
lessons.task: Make a timeline on one page with at least eight points, from the abacus to your own phone. For each point write the year (roughly), the name and one line about what was new. Then ask an older family member what the first computer or mobile phone they used was, and add it to your timeline.

quiz.q: Who is known as the father of the computer?
quiz.explain: Babbage designed the Analytical Engine with input, a store (memory), a mill (processor) and output, the same plan modern computers follow.

quiz.q: Why is Ada Lovelace called the first programmer?
options: She wrote an algorithm meant to be run by Babbage's Analytical Engine
quiz.explain: In 1843 she published notes with a step-by-step method for the Analytical Engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, the first published algorithm written for a machine.

quiz.q: Which old invention used punched cards to control a pattern, an idea later used for computer input?
quiz.explain: Jacquard's loom read holes in cards to decide the weaving pattern. Babbage and later Hollerith used punched cards for instructions and data.

quiz.q: What was the key idea of the stored-program concept described by John von Neumann?
options: Programs should be printed on paper
Computers should use gears instead of electricity
Only data should be stored in memory, never programs
Both the program and the data are kept in the same memory
quiz.explain: Keeping instructions in memory like data means you can change the program just by loading a new one, instead of rewiring the machine.

quiz.q: Which invention made small, cheap personal computers possible in the 1970s?
quiz.explain: A microprocessor puts the whole CPU on one chip. The Intel 4004 in 1971 started this, and soon PCs could fit on a desk.

lessons.title: Generations of Computers
lessons.content:
Think about how your family's phones changed. Maybe your grandparents had a landline with a rotating dial. Your parents may have had a small Nokia phone with buttons and a tiny screen. You have a smartphone with a touchscreen, camera and internet. Each change was a jump to a new "generation" of phone. Computers went through jumps like this too. Computer scientists group the history of computers into five generations, and each generation starts when the main electronic technology inside the computer changes.

Why we use generations: Grouping history into generations helps us understand the big picture. Instead of remembering hundreds of machines, we remember five big steps. For each generation, we usually ask the same questions. What was the main electronic component? How big and fast were the computers? What language did programmers use? How did people give input and get output? What problems did these computers have? If you can answer these five questions for every generation, you are ready for almost any exam question on this topic.

A note about dates: Different books give slightly different years for each generation, because changes did not happen on one single day. Old technology kept running while new technology was arriving. So the years in this lesson are approximate. In exams, writing years close to these is fine, as long as the order and the main technology are correct.

First generation, roughly 1940s to 1956: The first generation of electronic computers used vacuum tubes. A vacuum tube looks a bit like a light bulb. It can act as a switch or an amplifier for electric signals. Computers needed thousands of them. ENIAC had about 18,000 tubes. Other famous first-generation machines include EDVAC, EDSAC, UNIVAC I, which was one of the first computers sold to businesses, and the IBM 701.

How first-generation computers worked: Programmers wrote instructions in machine language, which is pure binary, 0s and 1s, that the hardware understands directly. Input was usually given through punched cards or paper tape, and output came on printouts or more punched cards. Memory was very small and used technologies like magnetic drums, mercury delay lines or cathode ray tubes. These computers could only do one job at a time, and an operator had to set everything up by hand.

Problems of the first generation: These machines were enormous; a single computer could fill a large room. Vacuum tubes produced a lot of heat, so the rooms needed powerful air cooling. They used a huge amount of electricity. Tubes burned out often, like light bulbs, so the computers broke down regularly and engineers had to keep finding and replacing bad tubes. They were also extremely expensive, so only governments, the military, big universities and a few large companies could afford them.

Second generation, roughly 1956 to 1963: The second generation replaced vacuum tubes with transistors. A transistor does the same job as a tube, acting as a switch, but it is much smaller, uses far less power, produces less heat and lasts much longer. Computers became smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable. Examples include the IBM 1401, the IBM 1620, which was the first computer installed in Bangladesh, the IBM 7090 and the CDC 1604.

Languages and memory in the second generation: Programming became easier. Instead of writing only 0s and 1s, programmers could use assembly language, which uses short words like ADD and MOV. Even more importantly, the first high-level languages appeared: FORTRAN for scientists and engineers, and COBOL for business work. Memory moved to magnetic cores, small rings of magnetic material, and magnetic tapes and disks were used for storage. Computers were still mostly used by organisations, but more companies could now afford them.

Third generation, roughly 1964 to 1971: The third generation used integrated circuits, or ICs. An IC is a small chip of silicon that contains many transistors and other parts, all made together. Instead of wiring thousands of separate transistors, engineers could use a few chips. This made computers much smaller, more reliable and cheaper to build. A famous example is the IBM System/360 family, launched in 1964, which offered computers of different sizes that could run the same software. Other examples include the PDP-8 minicomputer and the Honeywell 6000 series.

What changed for users in the third generation: People started using keyboards to type and monitors to see results, instead of only punched cards and printouts. Operating systems became common. An operating system is software that manages the computer, so that several programs can share the machine. Ideas like multiprogramming, where the CPU switches between several programs, and time-sharing, where many users connect to one computer through terminals, became popular. High-level languages like BASIC and Pascal appeared, and programming spread to more people.

Fourth generation, roughly 1971 to present: The fourth generation started with the microprocessor. Using a technology called VLSI, Very Large Scale Integration, engineers could put thousands, then millions and now billions of transistors on a single chip. The Intel 4004 in 1971 had about 2,300 transistors and was the first commercial microprocessor. A modern phone chip has billions. With the whole CPU on one chip, computers could become personal computers that sit on a desk, then laptops, and later tablets and smartphones.

What the fourth generation brought: This generation gave us personal computers like the Apple II and IBM PC, the graphical user interface with windows, icons and a mouse, and operating systems like MS-DOS, Windows, macOS and Linux. Languages like C, C++, Java and Python became popular. Storage moved to hard disks, then flash memory and SSDs. Computers were connected into networks, and the internet and World Wide Web connected the whole world. Prices fell so much that ordinary families and small shops could own computers.

Fifth generation, present and future: The fifth generation is less about one single part and more about what computers can do. The goal is computers that can understand natural language, learn from data, recognise images and speech, and make decisions, in other words, artificial intelligence. This generation uses massive parallel processing, where many processors work together, ULSI chips with even more transistors, and new ideas like quantum computing and neural network chips. Voice assistants, face unlock, translation apps and chatbots are examples you already use.

Comparing the generations in one picture: Imagine lining up five machines in a row. The first fills a room, uses a lot of power and needs a team of engineers. The second fills a smaller room. The third is like a large cupboard. The fourth sits on your desk or fits in your pocket. The fifth is in your pocket too, but it can talk with you and recognise your face. Across these steps, speed went from thousands of operations per second to billions, size went down, price went down, reliability went up and programming became much easier.

A small worked comparison: Suppose you want to calculate the total salary for 1,000 workers. In the first generation, a programmer writes the program in binary, punches it on cards, waits for a time slot on the only computer in the city and gets a printout hours later. In the second generation, the program is written in COBOL, which is easier to read. In the third, an operator types it on a terminal while the computer runs other jobs too. In the fourth, an accountant uses a spreadsheet on a PC and gets the total instantly. In the fifth, you might simply ask, "What is the total salary this month?", and an AI assistant answers.

Levels of integration: Engineers describe how many parts fit on one chip using names. SSI, Small Scale Integration, means up to about 100 transistors on a chip. MSI, Medium Scale Integration, means hundreds. LSI, Large Scale Integration, means thousands. VLSI, Very Large Scale Integration, means hundreds of thousands to millions and beyond, and ULSI, Ultra Large Scale Integration, is sometimes used for the billions in today's chips. Roughly, third-generation computers used SSI and MSI chips, the early fourth generation used LSI, and later fourth-generation machines use VLSI. Knowing these names helps you answer "which integration technology was used in which generation" questions.

Moore's law: In 1965, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, noticed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly. In 1975 he revised this to about every two years. This observation became known as Moore's law. It is not a law of nature, more like a prediction that the industry worked hard to keep true. Because of it, computers kept getting faster and cheaper for decades. Today transistors are so tiny, only a few nanometres, that keeping this pace is very hard, which is one reason engineers now add more cores and special AI chips instead of only shrinking transistors.

Input and output across the generations: The way people talked to computers changed as much as the electronics. First and second generation users mostly worked with punched cards, paper tape and printouts, and usually never touched the machine. Third generation users typed on keyboards and saw results on screens. Fourth generation users clicked with a mouse in graphical windows and later touched screens directly. Fifth generation users can simply speak or show a picture. Each change made computers usable by more and more ordinary people.

Real-life example 1, Bangladesh's first computer: The IBM 1620 installed in Dhaka in 1964 was a second-generation, transistor-based machine. It was used for scientific calculations at the Atomic Energy Centre. Compare that with today, when a student in a village can do more powerful calculations on a cheap Android phone, which uses fourth-generation microprocessor technology and some fifth-generation AI features like voice typing in Bangla.

Real-life example 2, your phone's camera: When your phone camera automatically finds faces, blurs the background and makes a night photo brighter, that is a mix of fourth and fifth generation ideas. A microprocessor chip with billions of transistors, fourth generation, runs AI models that have learned what faces and backgrounds look like, which is fifth generation. One small device shows how the newest generation is built on top of the earlier ones.

Common mistakes: Students sometimes say the first generation used transistors; remember tubes first, then transistors. Another mix-up is between ICs and microprocessors: an IC can be any chip with many parts, but a microprocessor is an IC that holds a whole CPU. Also, do not say the fifth generation is only about AI software; it also includes parallel processing hardware and new chip technologies. And remember the years are approximate.

What exams usually ask: Common questions are "Describe the generations of computers", "Compare first and second generation computers", "What is an IC and which generation used it?", "Write the characteristics of fourth-generation computers" and "What is the fifth generation computer?". A neat comparison table with technology, language, size, speed and examples for each generation is the best way to answer these.

Quick recap: Generations are defined by the main electronic technology. First: vacuum tubes and machine language. Second: transistors, assembly, FORTRAN and COBOL. Third: integrated circuits, keyboards, monitors and operating systems. Fourth: microprocessors, PCs, GUIs, networks and the internet. Fifth: AI, parallel processing and new technologies. Each step made computers smaller, faster, cheaper, more reliable and easier to use. Next, we will look at the different types of computers that exist today.
key_points: A generation of computers is a period defined by a big change in the main electronic technology.
First generation (about 1940s-1956): vacuum tubes, machine language, punched cards; huge, hot and unreliable.
Second generation (about 1956-1963): transistors, assembly language, early high-level languages like FORTRAN and COBOL.
Third generation (about 1964-1971): integrated circuits, keyboards and monitors, operating systems and multiprogramming.
Fourth generation (about 1971-present): microprocessors with VLSI, personal computers, GUIs, networks and the internet.
Fifth generation (present and future): artificial intelligence, parallel processing, natural language and new technologies like quantum computing.
Each new generation made computers smaller, faster, cheaper, more reliable and easier to use.
lessons.tip: Make a five-column table with the same rows for every generation: years, main technology, speed, size, language, example machines, problems. Exams love "compare" questions, and a table you have drawn yourself is the fastest way to remember them all.
lessons.task: Draw a table of the five generations with six rows: period, main electronic component, programming language, input/output, example computers, and one problem of that generation. Then look at your phone's specifications (Settings, About phone) and write which generation's technology it uses and why.

quiz.q: What was the main electronic component of first-generation computers?
quiz.explain: First-generation machines like ENIAC used thousands of vacuum tubes, which made them huge, hot and power hungry.

quiz.q: Which generation first used integrated circuits (ICs)?
quiz.explain: Third-generation computers, from about 1964, placed many transistors on one IC chip, which made them smaller and more reliable.

quiz.q: Which languages appeared during the second generation?
options: Assembly language and early high-level languages like FORTRAN and COBOL
quiz.explain: With transistors came assembly language and the first high-level languages, so programmers no longer had to write only in 0s and 1s.

quiz.q: What made the fourth generation special?
options: The microprocessor, a whole CPU on a single chip
quiz.explain: From 1971, the microprocessor put a whole CPU on a single VLSI chip, which made personal computers, laptops and later phones possible.

quiz.q: Which feature is most connected with the fifth generation?
options: Artificial intelligence and natural language processing
quiz.explain: The fifth generation is about computers that can understand language, learn and reason, using AI and massive parallel processing.

lessons.title: Types of Computers
lessons.content:
If someone asks you, "What kind of vehicle is this?", you could answer in many ways. You could say "a bus" by its shape, "a diesel vehicle" by its fuel or "public transport" by its purpose. Each answer is correct; they are just different ways to group vehicles. Computers are the same. We can group them by how they handle data, by their size and power, or by the purpose they are built for. In this lesson, we will go through all three ways with clear examples.

The three ways to classify: First, by the type of data they work with: analog, digital and hybrid. Second, by size, speed and capacity: supercomputers, mainframes, minicomputers and microcomputers. Third, by purpose: general-purpose and special-purpose. Some books also add groups like servers, workstations and embedded systems. One computer can belong to several groups at once. Your smartphone, for example, is digital, a microcomputer and general-purpose.

Analog computers: An analog computer works with continuous data. Continuous means the value can be anything in a range, not just fixed steps. Think of temperature: it does not jump from 30 to 31 degrees; it passes through 30.1, 30.25, 30.333 and so on. Analog devices measure physical quantities like voltage, pressure, speed or temperature and represent them with another physical quantity. A classic mercury thermometer, an old speedometer with a needle and a pressure gauge on a gas cylinder are analog measuring devices.

More about analog computers: Real analog computers were used in the past to solve maths problems, especially differential equations, by building electrical circuits whose voltages behaved like the problem. They were used for things like aiming guns, flight simulation and studying how bridges vibrate. Their strength is that they work in real time and naturally match the physical world. Their weakness is accuracy. Small noise or a slightly changed component gives a slightly wrong answer, and they are hard to reprogram, because the "program" is the wiring.

Digital computers: A digital computer works with discrete values, which means separate, countable steps. Inside, everything is represented using binary digits, 0 and 1. Numbers, letters, photos, songs and videos are all turned into long patterns of 0s and 1s. Almost every computer you use is digital: laptops, phones, ATMs, calculators and smartwatches. A digital clock that shows 10:42 and then jumps to 10:43 is a simple example of the digital idea, because it shows steps, not a smooth movement.

Why digital won: Digital computers are very accurate, because a signal only needs to be recognised as "high" or "low", not measured exactly. Small noise does not change a 1 into a 0. They can store huge amounts of data, copy it perfectly and run any program you load. That flexibility is why digital computers took over almost everything. When we say "computer" in this course without any other word, we mean a digital computer.

Hybrid computers: A hybrid computer combines analog and digital parts. Usually it takes analog input from the real world, converts it into digital form using a device called an analog-to-digital converter, processes it digitally and may convert results back to analog to control something. Hospital ICU monitors that read a patient's heart signals and show numbers and graphs on a screen are a common example. Petrol pumps that measure flowing fuel and show the price digitally, and many scientific instruments, also work in a hybrid way.

Classification by size and power: The second way to classify computers is by size, speed, storage and how many users they serve. Here we have four classic groups. From largest to smallest, they are supercomputers, mainframe computers, minicomputers and microcomputers. Do not take the word "size" too literally today; it is more about computing power and how many people the machine serves than about how much space it occupies.

Supercomputers: Supercomputers are the fastest and most powerful computers in the world. They have thousands or even millions of processor cores working together in parallel. Their speed is measured in FLOPS, floating-point operations per second. The fastest supercomputers today perform more than a quintillion operations per second, which is called exascale. They are used for weather forecasting, climate research, nuclear research, simulating earthquakes, designing medicines and training very large AI models. They cost huge amounts of money, use as much electricity as a small town and need special cooling.

Mainframe computers: Mainframes are large, powerful computers built to handle a huge number of transactions and users at the same time, with extreme reliability. Banks, insurance companies, airlines and big government offices use them. When thousands of people withdraw money from ATMs at once, or an airline handles bookings from all over the world, a mainframe may be working in the background. Mainframes are designed to run for years without stopping, and many parts can be replaced while the machine keeps running. IBM's Z series is a well-known mainframe family.

Supercomputer versus mainframe: These two are often confused. A simple way to remember: a supercomputer is built to do one giant calculation as fast as possible, like a racing car built for speed. A mainframe is built to do millions of small jobs for many users reliably, like a big bus service that carries thousands of passengers safely every day without breaking down.

Minicomputers: Minicomputers, also called midrange computers, sit between mainframes and microcomputers. They were very popular from the 1960s to the 1980s; the PDP-8 and VAX machines are famous examples. They could serve dozens or hundreds of users through terminals, so smaller companies, universities and factories used them. Today the classic minicomputer has mostly been replaced by servers, but the idea of a "midrange" machine serving a department still exists.

Microcomputers: A microcomputer is a computer whose CPU is a microprocessor and that is usually used by one person at a time. This is the biggest group today. It includes desktop computers, laptops, tablets, smartphones and wearables like smartwatches and fitness bands. Microcomputers are cheap enough for ordinary people, small enough to carry and powerful enough for study, office work, games, design and programming. The phone in your pocket is more powerful than a supercomputer from the 1980s.

Desktops, laptops and mobile devices: A desktop computer stays on a table and usually has a separate monitor, keyboard and mouse. It is easy to upgrade and repair and often gives the most power for the money. A laptop combines everything in one portable unit with a battery. Tablets use a touchscreen instead of a keyboard. Smartphones combine a computer, a phone, a camera and many sensors in one small device. Wearables like smartwatches put a tiny computer on your body to track steps, heart rate and notifications.

Servers and workstations: A server is a computer that provides services to other computers over a network, like storing websites, files, emails or app data. When you open Facebook or Daraz, your phone talks to servers in data centres. A server can be a powerful microcomputer, a group of machines or even a mainframe. A workstation is a powerful single-user computer used for heavy work like 3D animation, engineering design, video editing or scientific analysis. It has a strong processor, lots of memory and a powerful graphics card.

Classification by purpose: The third way is by purpose. A general-purpose computer can do many kinds of jobs; you just install different programs. Laptops, desktops and phones are general-purpose. A special-purpose computer is designed for one particular job. It usually has its program fixed inside and cannot easily be changed. Examples include the computer inside an ATM machine, a traffic signal controller, a digital camera and a GPS device in a car.

Embedded computers: Most special-purpose computers are embedded computers, meaning they are built inside another machine as one part of it. A modern car has dozens of small computers controlling the engine, brakes, airbags and the entertainment system. Washing machines, microwave ovens, rice cookers with digital timers, air conditioners, smart TVs and even some toys contain embedded computers. In fact, there are far more embedded computers in the world than laptops and phones put together; you just do not notice them.

Thin clients and the cloud: Today the line between types is getting blurry because of cloud computing. A cheap laptop or phone can act as a "thin client", a simple device that mainly shows a screen and sends your clicks, while the real work happens on powerful servers in a data centre far away. When you edit a Google Doc or watch a YouTube video, much of the processing is done by those servers. So a small microcomputer in your hand can borrow the power of huge machines over the internet.

Quantum computers, a new type: Quantum computers are a new and very different type that is still mostly in research labs. Instead of normal bits that are either 0 or 1, they use qubits, which follow the strange rules of quantum physics. For some special problems, like simulating molecules or certain kinds of code breaking, they may one day be much faster than any normal computer. For everyday tasks like typing or browsing, normal digital computers will stay the better choice. You will meet them again in the MSc Quantum Computing course.

Real-life example 1, one day of computers: In the morning, the embedded computer in your rice cooker switches to "keep warm". You check the weather on your smartphone, a microcomputer, which gets data that was calculated by a supercomputer at the weather department. You pay for breakfast with a mobile wallet, and the transaction is recorded by servers and possibly a mainframe at the bank. At the hospital, a hybrid ICU monitor watches a patient's heartbeat. Every type in this lesson can show up in one ordinary day.

Real-life example 2, choosing the right computer: Imagine three people in Dhaka. A freelancer who designs logos needs a laptop or a strong desktop, maybe a workstation if they do 3D. A garment factory that wants a machine to cut cloth automatically needs an embedded controller. A mobile financial service with millions of customers needs powerful servers and reliable systems like mainframes. Choosing the right type means asking: how fast, how many users, how reliable, how big and how much money?

Common mistakes: Students often think "analog" means old and "digital" means new. The real difference is continuous versus discrete data. Another common mistake is confusing a supercomputer with a mainframe; remember speed for one big task versus many reliable transactions. Some students forget that smartphones are microcomputers. And many forget embedded computers entirely, even though they are the most common type of all.

What exams usually ask: Typical questions are "Classify computers with examples", "Differentiate between analog and digital computers", "What is a hybrid computer? Give an example", "Write the differences between supercomputers and mainframes" and "What is an embedded system?". A tree diagram showing the three ways of classification with examples under each branch makes your answer clear and easy to mark.

Quick recap: Computers can be grouped by data type, by size and power, and by purpose. Analog computers handle continuous values, digital computers handle discrete 0s and 1s, and hybrids combine both. By size and power we have supercomputers, mainframes, minicomputers and microcomputers. By purpose, there are general-purpose and special-purpose computers, and most special-purpose ones are embedded inside other machines. Next, we will open a computer system and look at the parts it is made of.
key_points: Computers can be classified by data type, by size and power, and by purpose.
Analog computers work with continuous values; digital computers work with discrete values like 0 and 1; hybrid computers combine both.
By size and power: supercomputers, mainframes, minicomputers (midrange servers) and microcomputers.
Microcomputers include desktops, laptops, tablets, smartphones and wearables.
Embedded computers are small special-purpose computers hidden inside other machines.
Servers provide services to many users; workstations are powerful single-user computers for heavy work.
The right computer depends on the job: speed needed, number of users, cost, size and power use.
lessons.tip: Remember that computers are classified in three different ways: by how they handle data (analog, digital, hybrid), by size and power (super to micro) and by purpose (general or special). In an exam, first say which way you are classifying, then list the types.
lessons.task: Walk around your home, school or a nearby market and list ten things that contain a computer. For each one, write three labels: analog, digital or hybrid; its size class (micro, embedded, and so on); and general-purpose or special-purpose. Circle the one that surprised you the most.

quiz.q: A traditional car speedometer needle moves smoothly as speed changes. What kind of device is this?
quiz.explain: Analog devices show continuous values, like a needle that can point anywhere on the dial, not just at fixed steps.

quiz.q: Which type of computer would a country use for weather forecasting with huge simulations?
quiz.explain: Weather prediction needs trillions of calculations, so it runs on supercomputers with thousands of processors working in parallel.

quiz.q: A bank needs one central computer to handle millions of transactions from thousands of users at the same time, very reliably. Which type fits best?
quiz.explain: Mainframes are built for huge numbers of transactions, many users at once and very high reliability, which is exactly what banks need.

quiz.q: An ICU machine measures a patient's heartbeat as a continuous signal and shows it as numbers on a screen. What is it?
quiz.explain: It takes analog input (the continuous body signal) and processes and shows it digitally, so it combines both, which is a hybrid.

quiz.q: Which of these is an embedded computer?
options: The controller inside a microwave oven
quiz.explain: The microwave's controller is a small special-purpose computer built into another machine and does just one job.

lessons.title: The Parts of a Computer System
lessons.content:
Think about a cricket team. You need players, of course. But players alone cannot win. You also need the rules of the game, a captain's plan, the ball and bat, and the fans and coaches who make decisions. Take away any one of these and the match falls apart. A computer is similar. People often point at a laptop and say "this is the computer", but a working computer system is much more than the box. It is a team of parts that only work when all of them work together.

The five parts of a computer system: Most textbooks say a computer system has five components: hardware, software, firmware, data and people. Some books say four and combine firmware with software, or call people "liveware" or "humanware". Whatever names your book uses, the idea is the same. Hardware is the body, software is the instructions, firmware is the built-in starter instructions, data is the material being worked on, and people are the ones who use, build and manage the whole thing.

Hardware: Hardware means all the physical parts of a computer, the parts you can touch. The keyboard, mouse, monitor, processor, RAM, motherboard, hard disk, SSD, power supply, printer and cables are all hardware. Inside a smartphone, the screen, battery, camera, chip and speaker are hardware too. Hardware on its own is like a bicycle with no rider; it has all the parts but nothing happens until someone gives instructions.

Ways to group hardware: We can group hardware by what it does. Input devices bring data in, like the keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, microphone and camera. Processing hardware works on the data, mainly the CPU. Memory and storage keep data and programs, like RAM, ROM, hard disks and SSDs. Output devices show results, like monitors, printers and speakers. Communication hardware connects computers, like network cards, Wi-Fi chips and routers. We will study each group in its own lesson.

Peripheral devices: Hardware that is connected to the main computer but is not part of the core processing unit is often called a peripheral. Keyboards, mice, printers, scanners, external hard disks and webcams are common peripherals. The word comes from "periphery", meaning the edge. They sit around the main system and help it talk to the outside world.

Software: Software is the set of programs that tells the hardware what to do. A program is a list of instructions written by programmers. You cannot touch software, but you can see what it does. Windows, Android, Microsoft Word, Chrome, games, bKash and WhatsApp are all software. Without software, a computer is just an expensive box of metal and plastic. With software, the same hardware can become a music player, a calculator, a camera or a bank.

System software: Software is divided into two big groups. System software helps run and manage the computer itself. The most important system software is the operating system, like Windows, Linux, macOS, Android or iOS. It manages memory, files, processes and devices. Device drivers are system software that let the operating system talk to a specific piece of hardware, like a printer or a graphics card. Utility programs, like antivirus software, disk cleaners, backup tools and file compressors, also belong here because they help maintain the system.

Application software: Application software, or apps, helps users do specific tasks. Word processors for writing, spreadsheets for calculations, browsers for the web, photo editors, games, school management software and mobile banking apps are all applications. A simple way to remember: system software works for the computer, application software works for you. If you remove the operating system, nothing runs. If you remove one app, only that one task is lost.

Firmware: Firmware is a special kind of software that is stored permanently in a hardware chip, usually some type of ROM or flash memory. It sits between hardware and software. The best-known example is the BIOS or its modern replacement UEFI on a PC's motherboard. When you press the power button, the firmware runs first. It checks that the main hardware is working, a process called POST, the Power-On Self-Test, and then finds and loads the operating system. Your router, TV remote, printer, washing machine and even your SSD have firmware too. Sometimes companies release firmware updates to fix bugs or add features.

Data: Data is the raw material that the computer system works on. It can be numbers, text, images, sound, video or sensor readings. A school's computer system, for example, has data like student names, roll numbers, marks and attendance. As we learned earlier, when data is processed and organised so it is useful, it becomes information. Data must be correct, safe and backed up, because a perfect computer with wrong or lost data is useless. Remember GIGO.

People: The last and most important part is people, sometimes called liveware. Users use the computer for their tasks, like a cashier at a shop or a student writing an assignment. Programmers and software engineers write the software. System administrators keep computers and networks running. Hardware engineers design and repair devices. Data entry operators enter data. Even the best hardware and software cannot do anything useful without people deciding what problem to solve and checking the results.

How the parts work together: Imagine you write a message in WhatsApp. You, the person, decide what to say. Your fingers press the touchscreen, which is hardware. The WhatsApp app, application software, takes your typing. Android, the system software, manages the screen, memory and network. Firmware in the phone's chips helped the phone start up in the morning and still controls low-level parts like the modem. Your message text is data. All five parts were needed for one simple message.

The von Neumann architecture: Now let us look at how the hardware itself is organised. In 1945, John von Neumann described a design that almost every computer still follows. It is called the von Neumann architecture or stored-program architecture. It has these main parts: a Central Processing Unit, a main memory, input and output devices, and buses that connect them. The most important idea is that the program instructions and the data are both stored in the same memory.

Inside the CPU: The CPU in this design has two main parts. The Arithmetic Logic Unit, ALU, does calculations like addition and subtraction and logical comparisons like "is A greater than B?". The Control Unit, CU, is the manager. It reads each instruction from memory, figures out what it means and sends signals to the ALU, memory and input/output devices to carry it out. The CPU also has a few tiny, super-fast storage spaces called registers, which hold the values it is working on right now.

Memory and buses: Main memory, mainly RAM, holds the program that is running and the data it is using. Each memory location has an address, like a house number on a street, so the CPU can say "give me what is at address 2048". Buses are groups of wires that carry signals between parts. The address bus carries the address the CPU wants. The data bus carries the actual data or instruction. The control bus carries signals like "read" or "write". Together they are called the system bus.

A tiny worked example: Suppose memory holds a program with three instructions: load the number at address 100 into a register, add the number at address 101, and store the result at address 102. Address 100 holds 7 and address 101 holds 5. The control unit fetches the first instruction from memory, decodes it and loads 7. It fetches the second, the ALU adds 5, and the register now holds 12. It fetches the third and writes 12 to address 102. Instructions and data came from the same memory, one after another. That is the von Neumann architecture in action. We will study this fetch-decode-execute cycle in detail in the CPU lesson.

The von Neumann bottleneck: Because instructions and data share one path to memory, the CPU can only fetch one thing at a time over that path. Modern CPUs are much faster than memory, so the CPU often waits for data to arrive. This waiting problem is called the von Neumann bottleneck. Engineers reduce it with cache memory, a small, fast memory near the CPU, with wider buses, and with clever tricks like fetching the next instructions early.

Harvard architecture: Another design, the Harvard architecture, uses separate memories and separate buses for instructions and data, so the CPU can read an instruction and data at the same time. Many small microcontrollers and digital signal processors use this design. Modern PC processors use a mix: separate caches for instructions and data close to the CPU, but one shared main memory, a style often called modified Harvard architecture.

Real-life example 1, a shop's billing system: In a superstore, the barcode scanner, cash drawer, monitor and receipt printer are hardware. The billing software is application software, running on an operating system. Firmware inside the scanner and printer controls their basic functions. Product codes, prices and each sale are data. The cashier, the store manager who checks reports and the technician who maintains the system are the people. If the scanner breaks, or the price data is wrong, or the cashier is not trained, the whole system suffers.

Real-life example 2, an online exam: When a university runs an online admission test, students use their phones or laptops (hardware) with a browser (application software) on Android or Windows (system software). The university's servers store questions and answers (data). Teachers set the questions, IT staff manage the servers and students take the exam (people). The servers' firmware starts the machines and keeps their hardware running. A failure in any one part, like a server crash, a bad question or a student's dead battery, can spoil the exam.

Common mistakes: Students sometimes say the monitor or the CPU box is "the computer". Remember that a computer system needs all five parts. Another common mistake is calling an operating system application software; it is system software. Some students think firmware is hardware because it lives in a chip; it is software stored in hardware. Also, do not confuse the ALU and control unit: the ALU calculates, the control unit controls.

What exams usually ask: Expect "What are the components of a computer system?", "Differentiate between hardware and software", "What is firmware? Give examples", "Differentiate between system software and application software", "Draw and explain the von Neumann architecture" and "What is the von Neumann bottleneck?". For architecture questions, always draw the diagram with labelled arrows; many teachers give half the marks for the diagram alone.

Quick recap: A computer system is made of hardware, software, firmware, data and people. Hardware is physical; software is programs; firmware is software stored in chips; data is the material; people use and manage the system. Software splits into system software and application software. The von Neumann architecture has a CPU with a control unit and ALU, a memory that holds both programs and data, input/output devices and buses. Its shared memory path causes the von Neumann bottleneck. Next, we will go inside the CPU and see how it actually runs instructions.
key_points: A computer system has five parts: hardware, software, firmware, data and people (users).
Hardware is the physical parts you can touch; software is the set of programs that tell the hardware what to do.
Firmware is software stored permanently in a chip, like the BIOS or UEFI that starts a PC.
Software is divided into system software (OS, drivers, utilities) and application software (apps for users).
Data is the raw material the system works on; people include users, programmers and administrators.
The von Neumann architecture has a CPU (control unit and ALU), memory holding both programs and data, input/output and buses.
The von Neumann bottleneck: one shared path between CPU and memory limits speed; caches and other designs help.
lessons.tip: Draw the von Neumann diagram from memory once a day for a week: input, output, memory, and the CPU with its control unit and ALU, joined by buses. When you can draw it in under a minute, you understand the core of every computer architecture course that comes later.
lessons.task: Choose a computer you use, like your phone or a school PC. Make a list under five headings: hardware, software, firmware, data and people. Write at least three items under each. Then draw the von Neumann architecture and mark where each hardware item from your list belongs.

quiz.q: Which of these is firmware?
options: The BIOS or UEFI stored on a chip on the motherboard
A photo saved on the disk
quiz.explain: Firmware is software stored permanently on a hardware chip. The BIOS or UEFI is the classic example because it starts the computer before the operating system loads.

quiz.q: In the von Neumann architecture, where are programs and data kept?
options: Programs in the CPU, data in the printer
Programs on punched cards, data in memory
Both in the same main memory
quiz.explain: The key idea of the stored-program design is that instructions and data share the same memory and travel over the same bus.

quiz.q: Which part of the CPU decides what to do next and sends control signals to other parts?
quiz.explain: The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and tells the ALU, memory and I/O what to do. The ALU only does arithmetic and logic.

quiz.q: A device driver for a printer is an example of...
quiz.explain: Drivers help the operating system talk to hardware. They work for the system, not directly for the user's task, so they are system software.

quiz.q: What is the von Neumann bottleneck?
options: The single shared path between CPU and memory limiting how fast data and instructions can move
A virus that slows the computer
quiz.explain: The CPU can work faster than data arrives over the one memory bus, so it often waits. Cache memory and wider buses are ways to reduce this.

lessons.title: The CPU: The Brain That Follows Orders
lessons.content:
Imagine a big restaurant kitchen in Dhaka during iftar time. Orders are flying in. There is one head chef who reads each order slip, decides what needs to happen, and shouts instructions. There are cooks who actually chop, fry and mix. And there is a small counter right next to the stove where the chef keeps the few things needed right now: a bowl of onions, the salt, the order slip in hand. A computer has its own kitchen like this, and its head chef is the CPU.

What it is: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit. It is the part of the computer that carries out the instructions of a program, one after another, extremely fast. When you tap an app, scroll Facebook, play a game or type in Word, every single action is turned into small instructions, and the CPU runs them. People often call it the brain of the computer, but it is a strange brain: it is not smart at all. It cannot guess or understand. It can only follow very simple instructions, but it follows them billions of times every second without getting tired.

Where it lives: In a desktop or laptop, the CPU is a small square chip, about the size of a matchbox or smaller, sitting in a socket on the motherboard with a metal heat sink and a fan on top. In a phone, the CPU is part of a bigger chip called an SoC (System on a Chip), which also holds the graphics processor, the modem and more. Inside that tiny chip there are billions of microscopic switches called transistors. A modern phone chip has more than 10 billion of them.

The three main parts: A classic CPU is explained as three parts working together. The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) does the calculations. The Control Unit (CU) directs the work. The registers hold the small pieces of data the CPU is working on right now. In our kitchen, the ALU is the cooks, the Control Unit is the head chef, and the registers are that small counter beside the stove.

The ALU: The Arithmetic Logic Unit is where the real work on numbers happens. "Arithmetic" means maths operations like add, subtract, and in most CPUs multiply and divide. "Logic" means operations like comparing two numbers (is A bigger than B? are they equal?) and bitwise operations like AND, OR, NOT and XOR, which you will meet properly in the logic gates lesson. For example, when a cricket app checks whether Bangladesh's score of 245 is bigger than the target of 244, the ALU does that comparison and says "yes". After every operation, the ALU also sets little flags, such as a zero flag (the result was zero) or a carry flag (the result was too big to fit). The Control Unit uses these flags to decide what to do next.

The Control Unit: The Control Unit does not calculate anything itself. Its job is management. It reads each instruction, figures out what it means, and then sends control signals to the right places: "ALU, add these two", "memory, give me the data at this address", "register, store this result". It also keeps everything in step with the clock. Without the Control Unit, the ALU would be like cooks standing in the kitchen with nobody telling them which dish to make.

Registers: Registers are the fastest storage in the whole computer, faster even than cache and RAM, because they sit right inside the CPU. But they are tiny: a CPU has only a few dozen of them, and each one holds just one value, for example 64 bits. Some registers have special jobs. The Program Counter (PC) holds the memory address of the next instruction. The Instruction Register (IR) holds the instruction being worked on right now. The Memory Address Register (MAR) holds the address the CPU wants to read or write, and the Memory Data Register (MDR, also called MBR) holds the data that just came from memory or is about to go there. The Accumulator (ACC) in simple CPU designs holds results of the ALU. Modern CPUs also have many general purpose registers that programs use freely.

The fetch, decode, execute cycle: Everything the CPU does is one simple loop repeated forever. It is called the instruction cycle or machine cycle. Step 1, fetch: the CPU looks at the Program Counter, copies that address into the MAR, reads the instruction from memory through the MDR, puts it into the Instruction Register, and adds one to the Program Counter so it points at the next instruction. Step 2, decode: the Control Unit looks at the instruction and works out what it means and what data it needs. Step 3, execute: the instruction is carried out, for example the ALU adds two numbers, or data is copied from memory into a register. Some books add a fourth step, store, where the result is written back to a register or memory. Then the cycle starts again with the next instruction.

A worked example: Suppose memory holds a tiny program that adds the price of a burger (150 taka) and a drink (40 taka). The instructions might look like this: LOAD 150 into register A; LOAD 40 into register B; ADD A and B, put the answer in A; STORE A into memory. The PC first points at instruction 1. Fetch brings in "LOAD 150", decode sees it is a load, execute puts 150 into A. The PC now points at instruction 2, and the cycle loads 40 into B. Instruction 3 makes the ALU add them, and A becomes 190. Instruction 4 writes 190 back to memory so the app can show "Total: 190 taka". Four instructions, four trips around the cycle. Your phone does billions of these per second.

Jumps and decisions: Programs are not always straight lines. An instruction like "if the result was zero, jump to address 500" changes the Program Counter to 500 instead of letting it simply move to the next instruction. This is how if-else and loops work deep inside the machine. The ALU's flags decide whether the jump happens. So a whole game of Ludo on your phone, with all its rules, is just millions of loads, adds, compares and jumps.

The clock: The CPU has a clock, a tiny crystal that ticks at a steady rate and keeps every part in step, like the beat of a drum for marching soldiers. Clock speed is measured in hertz (ticks per second). 1 MHz is one million ticks per second, and 1 GHz is one billion. A CPU running at 3 GHz gets about 3 billion ticks every second. Each step of the instruction cycle takes one or more ticks. A faster clock generally means more work per second, but it also means more heat and more battery use, which is why phones raise and lower their clock speed all the time.

Why GHz is not the whole story: A common mistake is to think that the CPU with the higher GHz is always faster. It is not. Speed depends on how many instructions the CPU completes per tick (often called IPC, instructions per clock), on how many cores it has, on how much cache it has, and on its design. A modern 2.5 GHz laptop CPU can easily beat a 3.5 GHz CPU from ten years ago, because it does much more work in each tick. It is like comparing two rickshaw pullers: one pedals faster, but the other has a better rickshaw with gears and carries more passengers per trip.

Cores: A core is a complete processing unit with its own ALU, Control Unit and registers. Old CPUs had one core. Today a phone may have 8 cores and a laptop 4 to 16. With several cores, the CPU can truly run several instruction streams at the same time. Many phone chips mix big fast cores for heavy work like games with small efficient cores for light work like checking messages, to save battery. Some CPUs also support hyper-threading (simultaneous multithreading), where one core handles two streams of instructions by filling idle gaps, so 8 cores can appear as 16 logical processors.

More cores is not magic: Cores only help if the work can be split. Exporting a video can be split into pieces, so all cores help. But a task where every step needs the previous step's answer must run on one core, so the rest sit idle. Think of eight people building one wall: they can each lay bricks on a different part at the same time, but eight people cannot boil one pot of rice eight times faster.

Word size, 32-bit and 64-bit: The word size is how many bits the CPU naturally works on at once. A 64-bit CPU has 64-bit registers and can handle 64-bit numbers in one go. It can also use a huge range of memory addresses. A 32-bit system can address only about 4 GB of RAM (2 to the power 32 bytes), which is why old 32-bit Windows could not use more than about 4 GB. Almost every new computer and phone today is 64-bit.

Cache, a sneak peek: RAM is much slower than the CPU, so the CPU keeps copies of recently used data in a small, very fast memory called cache, built into the chip in levels named L1, L2 and L3. L1 is the smallest and fastest. The next lesson on memory explains this properly, but remember that a CPU with a good cache wastes far less time waiting.

Instruction sets, CISC and RISC: Every CPU family understands a fixed list of instructions called its instruction set architecture (ISA). Intel and AMD laptop chips use the x86 family, which is called CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) because it has many, sometimes complicated, instructions. Most phones and Apple's newer Macs use ARM, which follows RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) ideas: fewer, simpler instructions that each finish quickly, which saves power. A program compiled for one ISA cannot run directly on another, which is why apps are built separately for different chips.

Heat and cooling: Billions of transistors switching billions of times a second produce heat. That is why desktop CPUs have heat sinks and fans, and why your phone gets warm while gaming. If the chip gets too hot, it slows itself down to protect itself. This is called thermal throttling, and it is why a phone may lag after a long PUBG or Free Fire session.
