Real life example 1, a bKash payment: You type 500 taka and your PIN and press send. The app's code becomes thousands of instructions. The CPU fetches each one: compare the PIN with what is expected, check that your balance is at least 500 plus charge, subtract, prepare the message to send over the network, update the screen. Each check is an ALU comparison; each "if balance too low, show error" is a conditional jump. All of it is done in a tiny fraction of a second, and you just see "Transaction successful".

Real life example 2, a traffic signal controller: A smart traffic light at a busy junction like Shahbag has a small embedded CPU. Its program loops forever: read the sensor counts, compare which road has the longer queue, decide the green time, switch the lights, wait, repeat. It is the same fetch, decode, execute cycle and the same ALU comparisons, just in a much smaller and slower chip than your phone's, because it does not need more.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up the ALU and the Control Unit, so remember: the ALU calculates, the CU commands. Another mix-up is between registers and RAM: registers are inside the CPU, tiny and fastest; RAM is outside, bigger and slower. Typical exam questions are: "Draw the block diagram of a CPU and explain each part", "Explain the fetch, decode, execute cycle with the roles of PC, MAR, MDR and IR", "What is clock speed? Why is a higher GHz not always faster?", "What is the difference between a single-core and a multi-core processor?", and "Differentiate between RISC and CISC". If you can draw the diagram and trace one instruction, you can answer all of them.

Quick recap: the CPU runs instructions; the ALU does maths and comparisons; the Control Unit directs; registers hold the few values being used right now; the CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute endlessly; GHz, cores, cache and design together decide speed. Next we will look at where the CPU gets its data from: memory.
key_points: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) runs every instruction of every program.
The ALU does the maths and the comparisons; the Control Unit directs everything else.
Registers are tiny, super fast storage boxes inside the CPU, like the program counter, instruction register and accumulator.
The CPU repeats the fetch, decode, execute cycle billions of times per second.
Clock speed (GHz) says how many ticks per second, but cores, cache and instructions per tick also decide real speed.
More cores help only when the work can be split into parts that run at the same time.
A 64-bit CPU works on 64-bit chunks of data at once and can address far more memory than a 32-bit one.
lessons.tip: Draw the fetch, decode, execute cycle as a circle and trace one simple instruction like ADD through it by hand. Once you can do that for two or three instructions, almost every exam question on the CPU becomes easy.
lessons.task: Find your phone's or computer's processor name (on a phone: Settings, About phone; on Windows: Settings, System, About). Search it online and write down its number of cores, its clock speed in GHz and whether it is 64-bit. Then explain in two lines why it does not work 2 times faster than a CPU with half its GHz.

quiz.q: Which part of the CPU actually adds two numbers or checks whether one is bigger than the other?
quiz.explain: The ALU does arithmetic (add, subtract) and logic (compare, AND, OR). The Control Unit only tells it what to do and when.

quiz.q: What does the Program Counter (PC) hold?
options: The address of the next instruction to fetch
The result of the last addition
quiz.explain: The PC points at the memory address of the next instruction. After each fetch it moves forward, unless a jump changes it.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the instruction cycle?
quiz.explain: The CPU first fetches the instruction from memory, then decodes it to understand it, then executes it. Then it starts again.

quiz.q: A CPU runs at 3 GHz. Roughly how many clock ticks does it get every second?
quiz.explain: Giga means billion, and hertz means per second. So 3 GHz is about 3,000,000,000 ticks every second.

quiz.q: Why does an 8-core CPU NOT always make a program 8 times faster?
options: Because cores turn off when the screen is on
Because many programs cannot split their work into 8 parts that run at the same time
Because only the first core has an ALU
Because more cores always slow down the clock
quiz.explain: Extra cores help only when work can run in parallel. A task whose every step depends on the previous step can only use one core at a time.

lessons.title: Primary Memory and the Memory Hierarchy
lessons.content:
Think about how you study for an exam. The book you are reading right now is open on your desk, within arm's reach. A few other books you need today are in your bag next to the chair. All your other books are on the shelf across the room, and your old class notes from previous years are packed in a trunk under the bed. The closer something is, the faster you can grab it, but the less space there is. Your desk fits one or two books; the trunk fits a hundred. A computer organises its memory in exactly this way, and that idea is called the memory hierarchy.

What memory means: In computers, memory is any place where data and instructions are kept so the CPU can use them. We split it into two big groups. Primary memory is memory the CPU can access directly, word by word, using addresses: registers, cache, RAM and ROM. Secondary storage, like hard disks, SSDs and pen drives, keeps data long term but the CPU cannot work on it directly; data must first be copied into RAM. This lesson is about primary memory. The next one covers storage.

Why the CPU needs memory: The CPU can only work on what is in front of it. A program like WhatsApp is stored on your phone's storage, but to run it, its instructions and data are loaded into RAM. The CPU then fetches from RAM, as you saw in the CPU lesson. If memory is slow, the super fast CPU just sits and waits, like a chef who must walk to the market for every onion. So computer designers spend huge effort to keep the CPU fed.

RAM, the main working memory: RAM stands for Random Access Memory. "Random access" means the CPU can jump to any address and read it in the same amount of time, whether it is address 5 or address 5 billion. Compare this to a cassette tape, where you must wind through everything before the song you want. RAM is where your open apps, the document you are typing and the web page you are viewing live while you use them. Phones today have about 4 to 16 GB of RAM, and laptops about 8 to 32 GB.

Volatile means it forgets: RAM is volatile: it holds data only while it has power. If the electricity goes during load-shedding and your desktop has no UPS, everything in RAM disappears instantly. That is why the unsaved Word file is gone and why we say "save often". When you turn the computer on again, everything has to be loaded from storage into RAM again, which is part of why booting takes time.

SRAM and DRAM: There are two main kinds of RAM. SRAM (Static RAM) stores each bit using a small circuit of about six transistors called a flip-flop. It keeps its value as long as power is on, without any help, and it is very fast. But six transistors per bit makes it big and costly, so it is used only for small, fast memories like cache. DRAM (Dynamic RAM) stores each bit as a tiny electric charge in a capacitor with one transistor. That makes it small and cheap, so we can have gigabytes of it. The catch: the charge leaks away, so the memory controller must refresh every bit thousands of times per second. Your computer's main RAM sticks are DRAM, usually DDR4 or DDR5 in laptops and LPDDR in phones. DDR means Double Data Rate: it moves data twice per clock tick.

ROM, the memory that remembers: ROM stands for Read Only Memory. It is non-volatile: it keeps its contents even with the power off. It holds things that must be there the moment the machine wakes up, like the firmware that starts the computer (BIOS or UEFI on PCs), or the program inside a microwave oven, a washing machine or a TV remote. Originally ROM could only be written once, at the factory, and never changed. Over time, more flexible types appeared.

Types of ROM: Mask ROM is written at the factory during chip making and can never be changed; it is cheap in huge quantities. PROM (Programmable ROM) is sold blank and can be written once by the buyer with a special device, after which it is fixed. EPROM (Erasable PROM) can be erased by shining strong ultraviolet light through a small glass window on the chip, then rewritten. EEPROM (Electrically Erasable PROM) can be erased and rewritten with electricity, even while it sits in the circuit, byte by byte. Flash memory is a fast, block-based kind of EEPROM, and it is what modern BIOS chips, pen drives, memory cards and phone storage use. So "read only" today often means "mostly read, rarely written".

The speed gap problem: A modern CPU can do something every fraction of a nanosecond, but fetching data from main RAM takes something like 50 to 100 nanoseconds. That means the CPU could waste hundreds of ticks waiting for a single piece of data. If nothing were done, a 3 GHz CPU would spend most of its life waiting. The fix is cache.

Cache memory: Cache is a small amount of very fast SRAM built inside the CPU chip that keeps copies of the data and instructions the CPU used recently or is likely to use soon. It comes in levels. L1 cache is the smallest (tens of kilobytes per core) and fastest, often split into one cache for instructions and one for data. L2 is bigger (hundreds of KB to a few MB per core) and a bit slower. L3 is bigger still (several MB to tens of MB), shared by all cores, and slower again, but still much faster than RAM. When the CPU needs something, it checks L1, then L2, then L3, and only then goes to RAM.

Hits and misses: If the data is found in the cache, that is a cache hit, and it is delivered very quickly. If not, it is a cache miss: the CPU must fetch it from the next level, and a copy is placed in the cache for next time. The hit ratio is hits divided by total accesses. For example, if out of 1000 memory accesses 950 are found in cache, the hit ratio is 950 / 1000 = 0.95, or 95 percent. Good programs and good hardware aim for very high hit ratios, often well above 90 percent.

Why cache works, locality: Cache is small, so why does it help so much? Because programs behave in predictable ways, called locality of reference. Temporal locality: if you used a piece of data just now, you will probably use it again soon, like the loop counter in a for loop. Spatial locality: if you used one address, you will probably use the addresses next to it soon, like walking through an array of student marks one by one. So the cache keeps recently used items and also brings in whole small blocks (cache lines, often 64 bytes) of neighbouring data at once.

Worked example, average access time: Suppose cache takes 2 ns, RAM takes 100 ns, and the hit ratio is 95 percent. On a hit, the access costs 2 ns. On a miss, it costs about 2 + 100 = 102 ns (check the cache, then go to RAM). Average = 0.95 x 2 + 0.05 x 102 = 1.9 + 5.1 = 7 ns. Without a cache, every access would be 100 ns. So a small cache makes memory look about 14 times faster here. This kind of calculation appears in exams quite often.

The memory hierarchy: Put it all together and you get a pyramid. At the top: registers, inside the CPU, tiny, fastest, most costly per byte. Next: cache L1, L2, L3. Then main memory, RAM. Then secondary storage: SSD, then hard disk. At the bottom: offline and backup storage like external drives, tapes and the cloud. Going down the pyramid, each level is bigger, cheaper per GB and slower. Going up, each level is smaller, costlier and faster. The trick of the hierarchy is to keep the most needed data in the fast top levels, so the whole system feels almost as fast as the top and almost as big as the bottom.

Memory size units and addresses: Memory is a long row of numbered boxes, each holding one byte (8 bits). The number of a box is its address. 1 KB is 1024 bytes, 1 MB is 1024 KB, 1 GB is 1024 MB. The number of address lines decides how many boxes a CPU can reach: with 16 address lines it can name 2 to the power 16 = 65,536 addresses, which is 64 KB. With 32 lines, 4 GB, which is why 32-bit systems are limited to about 4 GB of RAM.

Virtual memory, a first look: What happens if you open more apps than your RAM can hold? The operating system uses a trick called virtual memory. It sets aside part of the storage (a page file on Windows, swap space on Linux) and moves parts of programs you are not using right now out of RAM onto the disk. When you switch back, it moves them back in. Programs think they have more RAM than really exists. The price is speed: storage is far slower than RAM, so if the system keeps swapping back and forth (called thrashing), the computer becomes painfully slow. You will study this properly in Operating Systems.

Real life example 1, a slow office PC: An office in Motijheel has an old PC with 4 GB of RAM. Staff open Chrome with 20 tabs, Excel and Zoom. RAM fills up, Windows starts using virtual memory on the slow hard disk, and every click takes seconds. The IT person adds another 4 GB stick of DRAM, and suddenly the same PC feels much faster, even though the CPU did not change. Nothing magic happened: the work simply fits in RAM now, so the CPU stops waiting for the disk.

Real life example 2, a microwave oven and its ROM: When you press "Popcorn" on a microwave, a tiny processor runs a program stored in ROM or flash inside the oven. That program never changes during the oven's life and must survive power cuts, so it lives in non-volatile memory. The current timer value and power level, which change every second, live in a little bit of RAM. Unplug it, and the timer is forgotten, but the program in ROM is still there next time.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Many students write that ROM is "storage like a hard disk". It is not; ROM is primary memory the CPU reads directly. Another mistake is saying "more cache means more storage". Cache does not add space for files; it only speeds up access. And remember: SRAM is for cache, DRAM is for main memory, not the other way around. Typical exam questions: "Differentiate between RAM and ROM", "Compare SRAM and DRAM", "Explain the memory hierarchy with a diagram", "What is cache memory? Explain hit, miss and hit ratio", "Calculate the average access time given hit ratio and access times", and "Write short notes on PROM, EPROM and EEPROM".

Quick recap: primary memory is what the CPU reaches directly; RAM is fast and volatile, ROM is non-volatile; SRAM builds cache, DRAM builds main memory; cache works because of locality; the hierarchy trades speed against size and cost; and virtual memory stretches RAM using the disk at a cost in speed. Next lesson, we go down the pyramid to secondary storage.
key_points: Primary memory (RAM, ROM, cache) is what the CPU can reach directly; secondary storage (disk, SSD) is not.
RAM is volatile: it forgets everything when power goes off. ROM is non-volatile and keeps its contents.
SRAM is fast and costly and is used for cache; DRAM is cheaper, needs constant refreshing and is used for main RAM.
The memory hierarchy goes registers, cache (L1, L2, L3), RAM, then storage: each step is bigger, cheaper and slower.
Cache works because of locality: programs reuse the same data (temporal) and nearby data (spatial).
ROM types include mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM and flash; firmware like BIOS/UEFI lives in such memory.
Virtual memory lets the OS use part of the disk as pretend RAM, which keeps programs running but slows things down.
lessons.tip: Make one table with four rows (register, cache, RAM, SSD) and three columns (speed, size, cost per GB). Fill it from memory every few days. Almost every memory question in exams is a version of this table.
lessons.task: Open Task Manager on Windows (Ctrl+Shift+Esc, then Performance, then Memory) or Settings, About phone, RAM on a phone. Write down the total RAM, how much is in use, and, on Windows, the RAM speed. Then open five browser tabs or apps and see how much the usage goes up.

quiz.q: What happens to the data in RAM when the computer suddenly loses power?
options: It is saved automatically to ROM
It is lost, because RAM is volatile
It is kept for a week
quiz.explain: RAM needs power to hold its data. Without power the contents disappear, which is why unsaved work is lost in a load-shedding blackout.

quiz.q: Which memory is used to build CPU cache?
quiz.explain: Cache uses SRAM because it is very fast and needs no refreshing. It is too costly and too large per bit to use for all of main memory.

quiz.q: Arrange from fastest to slowest:
quiz.explain: Registers are inside the CPU and fastest, then cache, then main RAM, and storage like SSD is the slowest of these.

quiz.q: Which type of ROM can be erased electrically and rewritten many times, byte by byte?
quiz.explain: EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM) can be erased and rewritten with electricity. Flash memory is a faster block-based relative of it.

quiz.q: A program reads the same variable again and again inside a loop. Which idea explains why cache makes this fast?
quiz.explain: Temporal locality means data used recently will likely be used again soon. Keeping it in cache saves trips to slow RAM.

lessons.title: Secondary Storage: Where Data Lives Long Term
lessons.content:
Think of your RAM as a table in a busy restaurant kitchen and your storage as the store room in the back. The table is where cooking happens, and it gets cleared every night. The store room is where rice sacks, oil tins and spices are kept for weeks or months. You cannot cook inside the store room, you must first bring things to the table. In a computer, the store room is secondary storage: the place where your photos, apps, songs and the operating system itself stay, even when the device is switched off.

What it is: Secondary storage is storage that keeps data permanently (non-volatile), holds a lot of it, and costs much less per GB than RAM. The CPU cannot fetch instructions directly from it. When you open an app, the operating system copies the needed parts from storage into RAM first, and then the CPU works from RAM. When you press save, data goes the other way: from RAM to storage. So storage is the long-term home, and RAM is the short-term workspace.

Why we need both: Why not just make all memory permanent and fast? Because no technology is fast, huge, cheap and permanent all at once. RAM is fast but volatile and costly per GB. Storage is permanent and cheap per GB but much slower. Together, in the memory hierarchy you met in the last lesson, they give a system that is fast enough and big enough at a price people can pay.

How we measure storage: The smallest unit is the bit, a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte, which can store one English letter. Then: 1 kilobyte (KB) = 1024 bytes, 1 megabyte (MB) = 1024 KB, 1 gigabyte (GB) = 1024 MB, 1 terabyte (TB) = 1024 GB, and 1 petabyte (PB) = 1024 TB. For feel: a page of plain text is about 2 KB, a phone photo about 3 to 5 MB, a song in MP3 about 4 MB, a full HD movie about 2 to 4 GB, and a typical laptop SSD is 256 GB to 1 TB.

The 1000 versus 1024 puzzle: Drive makers usually use decimal units, where 1 GB = 1000 MB and 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. Windows counts in binary, 1024 at each step. So a "1 TB" hard disk has 10 to the power 12 bytes, and Windows divides by 1024 three times, showing about 931 GB. Nothing is stolen; it is just two different units. Officially, the binary units are called KiB, MiB, GiB and TiB, though most people still say KB, MB and GB.

Hard disk drive (HDD): A hard disk stores data magnetically. Inside the sealed box are one or more round metal or glass platters coated with a magnetic material, stacked on a spindle that spins very fast, commonly 5400 or 7200 revolutions per minute (rpm). An arm carrying tiny read/write heads floats a few nanometres above each surface, closer than the width of a fingerprint ridge, without touching it. To write, the head magnetises tiny areas in one direction or the other, meaning 0 or 1. To read, it senses those directions.

How data is organised on an HDD: Each platter surface is divided into circles called tracks, like the rings of a tree. Each track is divided into slices called sectors, traditionally 512 bytes and now usually 4096 bytes. The same track on all platters together is called a cylinder. To read data, the disk first moves the arm to the right track (this time is called seek time), then waits for the right sector to spin under the head (rotational latency), then reads the data (transfer time). Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time.

Worked example, rotational latency: At 7200 rpm, the disk spins 7200 / 60 = 120 times per second, so one full turn takes 1 / 120 second, about 8.33 milliseconds. On average, the sector we want is half a turn away, so the average rotational latency is about 4.17 ms. Add an average seek time of about 9 ms, and a single random read takes roughly 13 ms. That sounds small, but the CPU could do tens of millions of operations in that time. This is why HDDs are the slowest part of most old computers.

Pros and cons of HDDs: Hard disks give a lot of space for little money, which is why they are still used for big backups, CCTV recorders and data centres storing huge amounts of rarely used data. But they are slow at random access, noisy, use more power, and have moving parts that can be damaged if the laptop is dropped while running. A "head crash", where the head touches the spinning platter, can destroy data.

Solid state drive (SSD): An SSD stores data in NAND flash memory chips, the same family as pen drives, controlled by a small processor called the SSD controller. There are no moving parts at all. Data is read and written electronically, so random access is extremely fast: a read takes about 0.1 ms or less instead of around 10 ms. SATA SSDs reach about 550 MB per second. NVMe SSDs, which plug into an M.2 slot and talk directly over the fast PCIe bus, reach several thousand MB per second. Upgrading an old laptop from HDD to SSD is often the single biggest speed boost you can buy: boot time can drop from over a minute to about fifteen seconds.

How flash stores bits: Flash memory keeps electric charge trapped in tiny cells, and the charge stays even without power. Cells can store 1 bit (SLC), 2 bits (MLC), 3 bits (TLC) or 4 bits (QLC) by using different charge levels. More bits per cell means cheaper and bigger drives, but slower and less durable. Flash cells wear out after many write cycles, so the controller spreads writes evenly across all cells, a trick called wear levelling. In normal use, modern SSDs last many years.

SSD versus HDD in one picture: SSD is faster, silent, lighter, uses less power and survives drops better. HDD is cheaper per GB and available in bigger sizes. Many people use both: an SSD for the operating system and apps, an HDD for big files and backups. Phones use flash storage built directly into the board, often of a type called UFS or eMMC.

Optical discs: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs store data as tiny pits and flat areas called lands along a spiral track. A laser shines on the spinning disc; light bounces back differently from pits and lands, and those changes are read as 0s and 1s. A CD holds about 700 MB, a single layer DVD 4.7 GB, and a single layer Blu-ray 25 GB. Blu-ray holds more because its blue-violet laser has a shorter wavelength, so the pits can be smaller and closer together. Discs can be ROM (read only, like a movie disc), R (recordable once) or RW (rewritable). Today they are mostly used for films, game distribution and long-term archives.

Flash drives and memory cards: A pen drive (USB flash drive) is NAND flash plus a small controller inside a plastic case with a USB plug. Memory cards like SD and microSD do the same job in a tiny flat shape for cameras, phones and drones. They are cheap, small and portable, which also makes them easy to lose and a common way to spread viruses between computers in cyber cafes and offices. Always scan an unknown pen drive before opening files from it.

Magnetic tape: It sounds old, but tape is still alive in big companies and data centres. A tape cartridge can hold many terabytes at a very low cost per GB and lasts for decades on a shelf. The downside is sequential access: to reach data in the middle, the drive must wind the tape to that spot, which can take minutes. So tape is used for archives and backups that are rarely read, not for everyday work.

Cloud storage: Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox and iCloud keep your files on huge storage systems in the provider's data centres, which themselves use SSDs, HDDs and tape. You access them over the internet from any device. The good side: you do not lose files when your phone is stolen or your laptop dies, and sharing is easy. The other side: you need internet, big uploads use your data pack, free space is limited, and you must trust the provider with your data and protect your account with a strong password and two-step verification.

Comparing storage devices: When choosing storage, look at five things. Speed: how fast it reads and writes. Capacity: how much it holds. Cost per GB: how much each gigabyte costs. Durability: how well it survives drops, heat and time. Portability: how easy it is to carry. An SSD wins on speed, an HDD on capacity per taka, tape on archive cost, a pen drive on portability, and the cloud on access from anywhere.

Backups, the 3-2-1 rule: All storage can fail. Disks die, phones get stolen, pen drives get lost, and ransomware can lock files. The well known 3-2-1 rule says: keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy somewhere else (another building or the cloud). For a student, that could be your thesis on your laptop, on a pen drive, and in Google Drive.

Real life example 1, a wedding photographer: A photographer in Dhaka shoots 3000 RAW photos at a wedding, about 25 MB each, which is around 73 GB. During the shoot, photos go to fast SD cards in the camera. At home, they are copied to a laptop SSD for quick editing, then to a large external HDD for keeping, and the final edited album is uploaded to the cloud to share with the family. Each storage type is used for what it is best at.

Real life example 2, a national ID or bank data centre: Banks and government data centres store millions of records. Data that is used every second, like account balances, sits on fast SSD arrays. Older transaction history sits on cheaper HDD arrays. Records that must be kept for many years by law go to tape libraries, stored safely and checked regularly. This is the memory hierarchy at the size of a building.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often call RAM "storage" or say "my phone has 128 GB of RAM" when they mean storage. RAM is working memory; storage is long-term. Another common error is calculating rotational latency for a full turn instead of half a turn. Typical exam questions: "Differentiate between primary memory and secondary storage", "Explain the structure of a hard disk: tracks, sectors, cylinders", "Define seek time, rotational latency and access time and calculate them", "Compare HDD and SSD", "Why does a 1 TB drive show about 931 GB?" and "Write short notes on optical discs and cloud storage".

Quick recap: storage keeps data when the power is off; HDDs are magnetic, cheap and slow; SSDs are flash, fast and tough; optical discs use lasers; pen drives and cards are portable flash; tape is for archives; the cloud is someone else's storage over the internet; and good backups follow the 3-2-1 rule. Next, we look at the devices that put data into the computer: input devices.
key_points: Secondary storage is non-volatile, large and cheap per GB, but slower than RAM; the CPU cannot use it directly.
A hard disk (HDD) stores data magnetically on spinning platters read by a moving head; it is cheap but slow and fragile.
An SSD stores data in flash memory chips with no moving parts, so it is much faster, quieter and tougher.
Optical discs (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) are read by a laser; they hold less and are mostly used for distribution and archives now.
Pen drives and memory cards are small, removable flash storage; cloud storage keeps files on a provider's servers over the internet.
Units: 8 bits = 1 byte, then KB, MB, GB, TB, each 1024 times the previous in binary terms (makers often use 1000).
Choose storage by speed, capacity, cost, durability and portability, and always keep backups.
lessons.tip: When a question says "compare", make a table. For storage, use the same five columns every time: speed, capacity, cost per GB, durability and portability. Examiners love tables and they make sure you never forget a point.
lessons.task: Look at your phone's storage (Settings, Storage) or This PC on Windows. Write down the total capacity, the free space and the three biggest categories using space. Then calculate how many 4 MB photos would fit in the free space, using 1 GB = 1024 MB.

quiz.q: Why can a laptop with an SSD start up much faster than the same laptop with an HDD?
options: SSDs have no moving parts, so data can be read almost instantly
quiz.explain: An HDD must spin the platter and move the head to the right spot before reading. An SSD reads flash chips electronically, with no waiting for mechanical movement.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT secondary storage?
quiz.explain: Cache is primary memory inside the CPU. Pen drives, hard disks and Blu-ray discs keep data long term and are secondary storage.

quiz.q: How many bytes are in 1 KB in the binary convention?
quiz.explain: In binary terms, 1 KB = 2 to the power 10 = 1024 bytes. Disk makers often use 1 KB = 1000, which is why a "1 TB" drive shows less space in Windows.

quiz.q: In a hard disk, what are the concentric circles on a platter called?
quiz.explain: Each platter surface is divided into circular tracks, and each track is divided into sectors. A cylinder is the same track on all platters.

quiz.q: Which storage medium uses a laser to read pits and lands on its surface?
quiz.explain: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs are optical. A laser reflects differently from pits and lands, and that difference is read as 0s and 1s.

lessons.title: Input Devices: How Data Gets In
lessons.content:
Imagine a very clever person locked in a room with no windows, no doors and no telephone. However smart they are, they cannot help you, because nothing can reach them. A computer is like that. The CPU can calculate at amazing speed, but only on data it has. Input devices are the doors and windows: they bring the outside world, your typing, your touch, your voice, a photo, a fingerprint, the temperature of a room, into the computer as numbers.

What an input device is: An input device is any hardware that captures data or commands from the outside and turns them into digital form, 0s and 1s, that the computer can process. Remember the IPO model from the first lesson: Input, Process, Output. Input devices handle the first part. Some capture data typed or pointed by a person; others capture data directly from the world without any person, like a temperature sensor in a factory.

Analog and digital: Most of the real world is analog: sound waves, light, temperature and movement change smoothly, with endless values in between. Computers only understand digital data, separate numbers. So many input devices contain an analog-to-digital converter (ADC). It measures the signal many times a second (sampling) and turns each measurement into a number (quantisation). A microphone, a camera sensor and a thermometer chip all do this. The lesson on data representation will show this in detail.

The keyboard: The keyboard is still the main way to enter text. Under the keys is a grid of wires called a key matrix. When you press a key, it connects a row and a column, and a small controller chip in the keyboard detects which one. It sends a code called a scan code to the computer. The operating system then maps that scan code to a character according to the selected layout. This is why the same key can give "k" in English and "ক" when you switch to a Bangla layout like Avro or Bijoy. The keyboard does not know any language; the software decides.

Kinds of keys and keyboards: The common English layout is called QWERTY, after its first six letters. Keys are grouped into alphanumeric keys, function keys (F1 to F12), modifier keys (Shift, Ctrl, Alt), navigation keys (arrows, Home, End) and the numeric keypad. Membrane keyboards are cheap and quiet; mechanical keyboards use a separate switch under each key and are loved by gamers and programmers for their feel. Phones show an on-screen virtual keyboard, which is really a touchscreen pretending to be a keyboard.

The mouse: A mouse moves a pointer on the screen. Old mice had a rubber ball that turned two rollers. Modern optical mice have a small LED or laser that lights up the desk and a tiny camera that takes thousands of pictures per second; a chip compares the pictures to see how far and in which direction the surface moved. Mice have left and right buttons and a scroll wheel. Sensitivity is measured in DPI (dots per inch): higher DPI means the pointer moves farther for the same hand movement.

Other pointing devices: A touchpad on a laptop senses your finger's position and gestures like two finger scroll. A joystick or game controller measures how far a stick is pushed in each direction. A graphics tablet with a stylus lets designers draw with pressure sensitivity. A trackball is like an upside-down mouse. A light pen was an old device for pointing directly at screens.

Touchscreens: A touchscreen is both an input and an output device, because it shows images and also senses touch. Most phones use capacitive touchscreens: a grid of transparent conductors under the glass holds a small electric field, and your finger, which conducts electricity, changes it at the point you touch. The controller calculates the exact position many times a second and supports multi-touch, which is why pinch to zoom works. This is also why a normal plastic pen or a thick glove does not work on your phone. Older resistive touchscreens, found in some ATMs and cheap devices, work by pressure: two layers touch when pressed, so any object works, but multi-touch is hard.

Scanners: A flatbed scanner moves a bright light and a row of sensors under the glass, capturing the page line by line as a digital image. Resolution is measured in DPI; 300 DPI is fine for documents. Handheld scanners and sheet-fed scanners work similarly. Today, many people just use a phone camera with a scanning app, which also straightens and sharpens the page.

OCR, turning pictures of text into text: A scanned page is just a picture: the computer sees dots, not letters. OCR (Optical Character Recognition) software finds the shapes of letters in the image and converts them into real, editable text. Google Lens can do this on your phone. Bangla OCR is harder than English because of joined letters (juktakkhor) and marks above and below letters, but tools for it exist and keep improving.

OMR, reading bubbles: OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) only checks whether certain marked spots on a form are filled. It does not read letters. If you have ever filled in an MCQ answer sheet for SSC, HSC or a university admission test, you have used OMR. The machine shines light on the sheet; a filled circle reflects less light, so it is detected as a mark. Thousands of sheets can be checked in an hour, and that is why the instructions say to fill the circle completely with a black ball-point pen.

MICR, reading cheques: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) is used by banks. The numbers at the bottom of a cheque, the cheque number, routing number and account number, are printed in a special font with ink containing iron oxide. A MICR reader magnetises the ink and reads the characters even if someone has scribbled or stamped over them. This makes cheque processing fast and hard to forge.

Barcodes: A barcode stores a short number as a pattern of black bars and white spaces of different widths. A barcode reader shines a red light or uses a camera, measures the bars and decodes the number, which the shop's computer looks up in its database to get the product name and price. The common product barcode, EAN-13, has 13 digits; the last one is a check digit that lets the scanner catch most reading mistakes.

QR codes: A QR (Quick Response) code is a two-dimensional code made of black and white squares. Because it uses both directions, it stores much more data than a barcode, up to a few thousand characters, and the three big squares in its corners let a camera read it from any angle. It also has error correction, so it still works if part of it is dirty or torn. That is why QR codes are everywhere in Bangladesh: bKash and Nagad merchant payments, restaurant menus, Wi-Fi sharing, and the code on your NID or vaccination certificate.

Microphones and audio input: A microphone has a thin membrane that vibrates with sound waves. The vibration creates a small changing electric signal, which is sent to an ADC on the sound card or phone chip. For music quality, the signal is usually sampled 44,100 times per second. Microphones feed voice calls, voice messages, Zoom classes and voice assistants like Google Assistant, which then use speech recognition software to turn speech into text.

Cameras and webcams: A digital camera or webcam focuses light through a lens onto an image sensor made of millions of tiny light-sensitive cells, one per pixel. Each cell measures how much light hits it, through red, green or blue filters, and an ADC turns that into numbers. A 12 megapixel phone camera has about 12 million such cells. Cameras are input devices for photos, video calls, QR scanning and face recognition.

Sensors: Sensors capture physical quantities directly. A phone alone has many: an accelerometer (movement and tilt, used to rotate the screen), a gyroscope (rotation), a magnetometer (compass), GPS (location from satellites), a proximity sensor (turns off the screen near your ear), and an ambient light sensor (auto brightness). Outside phones, there are temperature, humidity, gas, smoke, motion (PIR) and water level sensors. Sensors are the input devices of the Internet of Things and of embedded systems like automatic doors and smart irrigation.

Biometric devices: Biometric devices identify people by their body features. Fingerprint scanners read the pattern of ridges on your finger. In Bangladesh, mobile SIM registration uses fingerprint verification against the national ID database, and many offices use fingerprint attendance machines. Face recognition uses a camera and software to match facial features; iris scanners read the coloured ring of your eye. Biometrics are convenient because you cannot forget your finger, but if biometric data leaks, you cannot change it like a password.

Choosing the right input device: The best input device depends on the task. For a lot of text: a keyboard. For drawing: a stylus and tablet. For checking a thousand MCQ sheets: OMR. For a shop with many products: a barcode scanner. For a payment between strangers: a QR code. For a blind user: a microphone and speech recognition, or a braille keyboard. Accessibility is an important part of computer science: input methods should let everyone use computers.

Real life example 1, a supershop checkout: At a Shwapno or Agora till, the cashier scans each item's barcode. The scanner reads the number, the store's computer looks it up and adds the price. You pay by tapping a card (an NFC reader is an input device too) or by scanning a QR code with your bKash app (your phone camera is the input device there). At the end, the cashier may type your phone number on a keypad for reward points. Four input devices in one minute.

Real life example 2, the admission test: For a public university admission test, over a hundred thousand students fill in OMR sheets. The sheets go through OMR machines that read roll numbers and answers, while the question set codes help match each sheet to the right answer key. Results come out in days instead of months. The roll number box is also filled as bubbles, because bubbles are far more reliable to read by machine than handwriting.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse OCR, OMR and MICR. Remember: OCR reads characters (any printed text), OMR reads marks (filled bubbles), and MICR reads magnetic ink (cheques). Another mistake: calling a touchscreen only an output device; it is both input and output. Typical exam questions: "What is an input device? Give five examples", "Explain how an optical mouse works", "Differentiate between OCR, OMR and MICR", "What is a barcode? How is it different from a QR code?", "Write short notes on biometric devices", and "Why is an ADC needed for a microphone?"

Quick recap: input devices bring the world into the computer; keyboards send scan codes, mice and touchscreens track position, scanners and cameras capture images, OCR, OMR and MICR read text, marks and magnetic ink, barcodes and QR codes carry data in patterns, microphones and sensors use ADCs, and biometric devices identify people. Next, we look at the other side: output devices.
key_points: An input device turns something from the real world (a key press, touch, sound, light, movement) into digital data the computer can process.
Keyboards send a scan code for each key; the OS turns it into a character using the chosen layout, like English or Bijoy/Avro for Bangla.
Pointing devices include the mouse, touchpad, touchscreen, stylus and joystick; capacitive touchscreens sense the electric charge of your finger.
Scanners and cameras capture images; OCR turns images of text into editable text, OMR reads filled bubbles, and MICR reads magnetic ink on cheques.
Barcodes and QR codes store data as patterns read by scanners or phone cameras; QR codes hold far more data and work in any direction.
Microphones and sensors turn analog signals into digital numbers using an analog-to-digital converter (ADC).
Biometric devices like fingerprint and face scanners use body features to identify people.
lessons.tip: Learn input devices in groups (typing, pointing, scanning, audio-video, sensors, biometrics) and for each one remember three things: what it captures, how it works in one line, and one real place you have seen it in Bangladesh.
lessons.task: Walk through your home and list every input device you can find, including in phones, TV remotes, cars, ATMs and doors. Try to reach 15. Next to each, write what it captures (key press, touch, light, sound, movement, temperature and so on).

quiz.q: Which technology is used to read the answer sheets of an MCQ admission test where students fill in circles?
quiz.explain: OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) detects whether marked bubbles are filled. It is used for MCQ answer sheets in board exams and admission tests.

quiz.q: How does a capacitive touchscreen on a smartphone detect your finger?
options: It senses the small change in electric charge your finger causes
It measures the weight of your finger
It uses a tiny camera behind each pixel
It hears the tap with a microphone
quiz.explain: Your body conducts electricity, so a finger changes the electric field at that spot. The phone measures where the change happens.

quiz.q: What does OCR software do?
options: Turns an image of printed text into editable text
quiz.explain: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) recognises letters in an image, so a scanned page or photo of text becomes text you can edit and search.

quiz.q: Why are QR codes used for payments like bKash and Nagad merchant QR instead of normal barcodes?
options: QR codes are always printed in colour
QR codes can only be read by banks
QR codes store much more data and can be read from any angle with a phone camera
quiz.explain: A QR code is a 2D pattern that holds hundreds or thousands of characters and has error correction, and any phone camera can read it from any direction.

quiz.q: A microphone produces a smooth analog signal. What converts it into numbers the computer can store?
quiz.explain: An ADC samples the analog signal many times per second and turns each sample into a number. A DAC does the opposite for speakers.

lessons.title: Output Devices: How Results Come Out
lessons.content:
Imagine you asked a brilliant friend to solve a very hard maths problem, and they solved it perfectly but never told you the answer. All that work would be useless to you. A computer is the same. Input brings data in, the CPU processes it, but unless the result comes out in a form you can use, nothing has really happened. Output devices are how the computer talks back to you: through light on a screen, ink on paper, sound in your ears, or even a vibration in your hand.

What an output device is: An output device takes digital data from the computer and turns it into a form people or other machines can understand: images, text, sound, printed pages, physical objects or movement. In the IPO model, it handles the last O, output. Output can be soft copy, which is temporary and lives on a screen or as a file you can see but not hold, or hard copy, which is permanent and physical, like a printed certificate.

Digital to analog again: In the input lesson, an ADC turned the analog world into numbers. Output often needs the opposite: a DAC (digital-to-analog converter) turns numbers back into smooth signals, for example to drive a speaker. Screens also turn numbers into light levels, and printers turn numbers into ink dots. So output devices are translators from the computer's language of 0s and 1s back into our world.

Screens and pixels: A monitor, laptop screen, phone screen or TV is a grid of tiny dots called pixels (picture elements). Each pixel is made of three even tinier subpixels: red, green and blue. By mixing these three colours of light at different brightnesses, a pixel can show millions of colours. If each colour has 256 levels (0 to 255, one byte), a pixel can show 256 x 256 x 256 = 16,777,216 colours, which we call 24-bit colour or "true colour". Pure white is all three at 255; black is all three at 0; yellow is red and green full with no blue.

Resolution: Resolution is the number of pixels across and down. HD is 1280 x 720, Full HD (1080p) is 1920 x 1080, QHD (1440p) is 2560 x 1440 and 4K UHD is 3840 x 2160. More pixels means a sharper image and more detail, but also more work for the graphics processor and more data. Full HD is about 2 million pixels; 4K is about 8.3 million, four times as many.

Screen size and pixel density: Screen size is measured diagonally in inches, so a 15.6 inch laptop is 15.6 inches from one corner to the opposite one. The same resolution on a smaller screen looks sharper, because the pixels are packed more tightly. This is measured in PPI (pixels per inch). A phone with 400 PPI or more looks perfectly smooth at reading distance, while a big TV can have low PPI because you sit far away.

Refresh rate and response time: A screen does not show one fixed picture; it redraws the picture many times a second. Refresh rate is how many times per second, measured in hertz. 60 Hz means 60 times a second, the common standard. Gaming monitors and many new phones offer 90, 120, 144 Hz or more, so scrolling and fast games look smoother. Response time, measured in milliseconds, is how fast a pixel can change colour; slow response causes blur behind moving objects.

LCD screens: LCD stands for Liquid Crystal Display. Liquid crystals do not make light. Instead, a backlight shines from behind, and each subpixel has a liquid crystal that twists to let more or less light through a colour filter, like a tiny window blind. Older LCDs used fluorescent tubes as backlight; modern ones use LEDs, which is why shops sell "LED TVs" and "LED monitors": they are really LED-backlit LCDs. Panel types include TN (fast but poor viewing angles), IPS (good colours and viewing angles) and VA (good contrast).

OLED screens: OLED stands for Organic Light Emitting Diode. Each subpixel is a tiny light that glows on its own, so no backlight is needed. When a pixel should be black, it turns off completely, giving perfect black and very high contrast. OLED screens can be very thin and even flexible, which is why foldable phones exist. They are used in many mid-range and flagship phones and in premium TVs. Downsides: they are costlier, and a picture shown in the same place for a very long time can leave a faint ghost image, called burn-in.

The graphics card: Behind every screen is a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit), either built into the CPU chip (integrated graphics) or on a separate graphics card (dedicated GPU). The GPU calculates the colour of every pixel for every frame and keeps the image in a memory area called the frame buffer. For a Full HD screen at 60 Hz, that is over 120 million pixel colours per second. Games and video editing need strong GPUs, which also turned out to be very good at AI work.

Projectors: A projector throws an enlarged image onto a wall or screen, used in classrooms, offices and cinema halls. It contains a bright lamp or LED or laser light source and a small imaging chip (DLP with millions of tiny mirrors, or LCD panels). Brightness is measured in lumens; a classroom projector usually needs around 3000 lumens or more so students can see clearly even with some light in the room.

Printers, impact and non-impact: Printers make hard copies. Impact printers create marks by physically striking an inked ribbon against the paper. The main example is the dot matrix printer, whose print head has a column of tiny pins that hit the ribbon to form letters from dots. It is noisy and low quality, but cheap to run and able to print through carbon paper to make several copies at once, so you still see it in some banks, shops and ticket counters. Non-impact printers do not strike the paper: inkjet, laser and thermal printers.

Inkjet printers: An inkjet printer sprays extremely small droplets of liquid ink through tiny nozzles in the print head, as the head moves back and forth across the paper. Colour inkjets usually use four inks, CMYK: cyan, magenta, yellow and black. Note this is different from screens: screens add light (RGB), while printers subtract light with ink (CMYK). Inkjets are cheap to buy, great for colour photos, but the ink cost per page can be high. Ink tank printers, popular in Bangladesh, solve this with large refillable ink bottles.

Laser printers: A laser printer uses a laser beam to draw an invisible electric charge pattern of the page on a rotating drum. Fine powder called toner sticks to the charged areas, is transferred onto the paper and then melted onto it by a hot roller called the fuser. That is why pages come out warm. Laser printers are fast, sharp and cheap per page for text, which is why offices and photocopy shops near universities use them. Speed is given in pages per minute (ppm), and print quality in DPI, often 600 or 1200.

Thermal and 3D printers: Thermal printers use heat on special heat-sensitive paper, and they need no ink. The receipt from a supershop, an ATM slip and many bus or parking tickets come from thermal printers; that is why they fade over time. 3D printers are quite different: they build physical objects layer by layer, usually by melting plastic filament and laying it down in thin lines, following a digital 3D model. Engineers use them to make prototypes, students for robotics parts, and doctors even for models of bones before surgery.

Plotters: A plotter is used for very large, precise drawings, like architectural plans, engineering designs and big banners. Old pen plotters moved actual pens across the paper; modern large-format plotters are basically wide inkjet printers that can print on rolls of paper or vinyl several feet wide.

Speakers and headphones: Digital audio is a long list of numbers. The sound card or phone chip uses a DAC to turn them back into a changing electric signal, which is amplified and sent to a speaker. Inside the speaker, an electromagnet attached to a cone (diaphragm) moves back and forth with the signal and pushes the air, creating sound waves. Headphones and earphones are tiny speakers placed close to your ears. Bluetooth earbuds receive the digital audio wirelessly and have their own small DAC and amplifier inside.

Other kinds of output: Phones vibrate using a tiny motor, which is haptic (touch) output. Braille displays raise small pins to form braille characters for blind users. Many devices use simple LED indicator lights, like the charging light on a power bank. Computers also send output to machines, called actuators: motors in robots, relays that switch lights, and valves in a factory. In the Internet of Things, a phone command that turns on an AC is computer output acting on the physical world.

Devices that are both input and output: Some devices do both jobs. A touchscreen shows images and senses touch. A headset has both earphones and a microphone. A multifunction printer prints (output) and also scans (input). Storage devices like pen drives are sometimes called input/output devices because data both goes in and comes out.

Real life example 1, an exam result day: On SSC or HSC result day, results are published on the education board website and through SMS. A student sees the GPA on a phone screen (soft copy, through an OLED or LCD display). The school then downloads the result sheet and prints the marksheets on a laser printer (hard copy). Later, the official certificate is printed with special security features. The same data moves through several kinds of output, each chosen for a purpose.

Real life example 2, a ride on the Dhaka Metro Rail: At a metro station, large LCD screens show train times; the ticket vending machine's touchscreen displays menus and then a printer or card writer gives you a ticket or tops up your card; speakers announce the next station in Bangla and English; and the gates show green or red lights. Output devices quietly guide thousands of passengers every hour.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Many students say "LED TV" is a completely different technology from LCD; it is usually an LCD with an LED backlight. Others mix up RGB and CMYK: screens use RGB light, printers use CMYK ink. And remember that a higher resolution on the same screen size means higher PPI. Typical exam questions: "What is an output device? Give examples", "Differentiate between soft copy and hard copy", "Compare LCD and OLED", "Differentiate between impact and non-impact printers", "Explain how a laser printer works", "What are resolution, refresh rate and DPI?" and "Calculate the number of pixels and memory needed for an image".

Quick recap: output devices bring results back to us; screens are grids of RGB pixels described by resolution, size, PPI and refresh rate; LCDs need a backlight while OLED pixels glow on their own; printers can be impact or non-impact, and 3D printers build objects; speakers use a DAC; some devices are both input and output. Next, we open up the case and look at the motherboard, buses, ports and power that connect all these parts together.
key_points: Output devices turn digital results into something people (or machines) can see, hear, hold or feel.
A screen is a grid of pixels; resolution is the number of pixels (like 1920 x 1080) and each pixel mixes red, green and blue light.
LCD screens need a backlight (LED-backlit LCDs are often sold as "LED"); OLED pixels make their own light, giving true black and thin screens.
Refresh rate (Hz) is how many times per second the picture is redrawn; higher means smoother motion.
Impact printers (dot matrix) strike a ribbon; non-impact printers (inkjet, laser, thermal) do not; 3D printers build objects layer by layer.
Speakers and headphones use a DAC to turn digital audio back into analog sound waves.
Soft copy is output on a screen; hard copy is output on paper or another physical form.
lessons.tip: For each output device, remember one key number: resolution for screens, refresh rate for gaming monitors, DPI and pages per minute for printers, and wattage or frequency range for speakers. Questions that ask "which device would you choose" are answered using these numbers.
lessons.task: Find the resolution and refresh rate of your phone or laptop screen (Settings, Display, or search your model online). Calculate the total number of pixels. Then estimate how many bytes one full screen image takes in raw form if each pixel uses 3 bytes (one for each of red, green and blue).

quiz.q: A Full HD screen has 1920 x 1080 pixels. About how many pixels is that in total?
quiz.explain: 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600, which is about 2.07 million pixels. Each one is a tiny dot of red, green and blue light.

quiz.q: Why can an OLED screen show deeper black than an LCD?
options: Each OLED pixel makes its own light and can switch fully off
quiz.explain: An LCD blocks a backlight that is always on, so some light leaks. An OLED pixel showing black simply turns off and gives no light.

quiz.q: Which printer is an impact printer?
quiz.explain: A dot matrix printer hits an inked ribbon with tiny pins, so it is an impact printer. It can print carbon copies, which is why some offices still use it.

quiz.q: What does a 120 Hz refresh rate mean?
options: The screen has 120 pixels per inch
The picture is redrawn 120 times every second
quiz.explain: Refresh rate is how many times per second the display updates. 120 Hz looks smoother than 60 Hz in games and scrolling.

quiz.q: Output on a monitor that disappears when you turn it off is called...
quiz.explain: Soft copy is temporary output on a screen or as a file. Hard copy is printed or physical output you can hold.

lessons.title: Motherboard, Buses, Ports and Power
lessons.content:
Imagine a big city like Dhaka. Houses, offices and markets are useless without roads between them, electricity wires and gates to come in and go out. A computer is the same. The CPU, RAM and storage are the important buildings, but something must connect them, feed them power and let the outside world plug in: the motherboard, its buses, its ports and the power supply. In this lesson we open the case and look at the city map.

What the motherboard is: The motherboard is the big main circuit board inside a computer. Everything important either sits on it or connects to it. If you open a desktop PC you will see a large green or black board covered with tiny lines, slots and chips. Those tiny lines are copper tracks printed on the board, and they carry signals between parts. In a laptop or a phone the motherboard is much smaller and more crowded, and many parts are soldered on permanently, but the idea is exactly the same.

What sits on a motherboard: Let's take a tour. There is a CPU socket, a special seat where the processor is placed and locked down. Next to it are the RAM slots, long thin slots where memory sticks click in. There are expansion slots for extra cards such as a graphics card. There are connectors for storage: SATA ports for hard disks and older SSDs, and M.2 slots for small, very fast NVMe SSDs. There is a small chip that stores the BIOS or UEFI firmware, a coin-shaped CMOS battery, power connectors, and along the back edge a row of ports where you plug in your keyboard, monitor and internet cable.

The chipset: The chipset is the traffic police of the motherboard. It manages how data moves between the CPU and the other parts, like USB ports, storage and network. Older motherboards had two chips called the northbridge and the southbridge. The northbridge handled fast things like RAM and graphics, and the southbridge handled slower things like USB and audio. In modern computers most of the northbridge's job has moved inside the CPU itself, so the RAM and the main graphics slot talk to the CPU directly, and one remaining chipset chip looks after the slower devices. When you buy a motherboard, the chipset name tells you which CPUs it supports and how many ports and slots it can offer.

Form factors: Desktop motherboards come in standard sizes, called form factors, so they fit standard cases: ATX is full size, Micro-ATX is smaller and Mini-ITX is tiny. Laptops and phones use custom boards made for one model, which is why a desktop board is easy to replace and a laptop board almost never is.

What a bus is: Now let's talk about the roads. A bus is a set of parallel wires that carries signals between parts of the computer. The word comes from the everyday bus, a vehicle that carries many passengers on a fixed route. A computer bus carries many bits at the same time along a fixed route. Inside the classic computer design there are three kinds of bus that work together: the data bus, the address bus and the control bus.

The data bus: The data bus carries the actual data, the numbers and instructions, between the CPU, memory and other devices. Its width is the number of bits it can carry at once. A 64-bit data bus can move 64 bits in one go, like a road with 64 lanes. A wider bus moves more data per trip, so the computer can be faster. The data bus is two-way, because data goes from memory to the CPU when reading and from the CPU to memory when writing.

The address bus: The address bus carries addresses, which tell the computer where in memory to read or write. Think of memory as a huge apartment building where every flat has a number. The CPU sends the flat number on the address bus, and the data travels on the data bus. The width of the address bus decides how many different addresses exist. With n wires you can make 2 to the power n addresses. A 32-bit address bus gives 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 addresses, and if each address holds one byte, that is 4 GB. This is exactly why old 32-bit Windows could not use more than about 4 GB of RAM. A 64-bit system can in theory address far more memory than any computer has today. The address bus is one-way: the CPU sends addresses out.

The control bus: The control bus carries command and timing signals, small messages like read, write, interrupt and clock. If the address bus says where and the data bus says what, the control bus says what to do and when. For example, to read memory the CPU puts the address on the address bus, sends a read signal on the control bus, and the memory answers by putting the data on the data bus. All three buses together are sometimes called the system bus.

Bus speed and modern links: Bandwidth is roughly the bus width multiplied by the number of transfers per second. Modern PCs also use fast point-to-point links instead of one shared road. The main one is PCI Express, PCIe, built from lanes: a slot is x1, x4, x8 or x16. A graphics card usually uses x16 and an NVMe SSD x4, and each new PCIe generation roughly doubles the speed per lane.

Ports: the gates of the city: A port is a socket on the outside of the computer where you plug in a cable or device. Ports let the computer talk to the outside world. Old computers had serial ports, which send bits one after another on a single line, and parallel ports, which send several bits side by side and were used for printers. Today most of these have been replaced by USB, because USB is fast, small and works with almost everything.

USB: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus. It is serial, so bits go one after another, but it is very fast. USB 2.0 runs at up to 480 megabits per second, USB 3.0 at up to 5 gigabits per second, and newer versions go higher. The plug shape is a separate thing from the speed. Type-A is the old flat rectangle, and Type-C is the small oval plug that goes in either way up, used on most new phones and laptops. USB can also carry power, which is why you can charge your phone from a laptop. USB devices are hot-swappable, which means you can plug them in and pull them out without switching the computer off.

Display, network and audio ports: HDMI carries digital video and sound to a monitor, TV or classroom projector. DisplayPort does a similar job on computer monitors. VGA is an old blue analog video port still found on some office projectors. The Ethernet port, RJ45, takes the network cable from a router. The 3.5 mm jack is for headphones, and Thunderbolt is a very fast port that now uses the USB Type-C shape.

The power supply: Every part of the computer needs electricity, but not the kind that comes out of the wall. In Bangladesh the wall socket gives alternating current, AC, at about 220 volts and 50 hertz. Computer chips need direct current, DC, at low voltages. Inside a desktop the box that does this job is the power supply unit, usually an SMPS, which stands for Switched Mode Power Supply. It converts 220 V AC into steady DC lines of 12 volts, 5 volts and 3.3 volts. The 12 V line powers hungry parts like the CPU and graphics card, and the motherboard then uses small circuits called voltage regulators to bring the voltage down further to around 1 volt for the CPU cores. A laptop does the first step in its charger brick.

Watts and UPS: A power supply is rated in watts. An office PC may need 300 to 400 watts, a gaming PC 650 or more. A cheap, weak SMPS is a common mistake: when it cannot keep up, the computer restarts randomly or parts get damaged. Many people in Bangladesh also use a UPS, an Uninterruptible Power Supply, whose battery keeps the computer running for a few minutes during load-shedding so you can save and shut down properly. It also absorbs sudden voltage spikes.

Booting: what happens when you press the power button: Now let's see everything work together. When you press the power button, the power supply sends power to the motherboard and the CPU starts running the firmware stored in the BIOS or UEFI chip. The word booting comes from the old saying about pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps, because the computer has to start itself from nothing.

Step 1, POST: The firmware first runs the Power-On Self-Test, called POST. It checks that the CPU, RAM, graphics and keyboard are present and working. If something important is missing, the computer may beep in a pattern, called beep codes, or show an error. For example, a desktop with no RAM inserted usually just beeps and shows nothing on the screen.

Step 2, find a boot device: Next the firmware looks at the boot order, a list such as SSD first, then USB drive, then network. It finds the first device that has a bootable operating system. This is why, when you install Windows or Linux from a pen drive, you go into the BIOS settings and put USB at the top of the boot order.

Step 3, load the operating system: The firmware hands control to a small program called the bootloader, which loads the operating system kernel into RAM. The operating system then starts its drivers and services, and finally you see the login screen. Turning a computer on from completely off is called a cold boot. Restarting it without switching off the power, like choosing Restart, is called a warm boot.

BIOS versus UEFI: BIOS, the Basic Input Output System, is the old firmware used since the early IBM PCs. UEFI, the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, is its modern replacement. UEFI can boot from disks larger than 2 TB using the GPT partition style, starts faster, often has a mouse-friendly settings screen, and supports Secure Boot, which checks that the bootloader has not been tampered with by malware. People still say BIOS out of habit even when the computer actually has UEFI.

The CMOS battery: Settings like boot order and the date and time live in a tiny memory that needs constant power. A coin cell on the motherboard, usually a CR2032, keeps it alive when the computer is unplugged. When it dies after some years, the computer shows the wrong date at every start, and a cheap new battery fixes it.

Real life example 1, a computer shop in Elephant Road or IDB Bhaban: You go to build a desktop for your studies. The seller asks which CPU you want, then shows motherboards whose socket and chipset match it. You pick RAM sticks of the type the board supports, such as DDR4 or DDR5, and an M.2 NVMe SSD for the M.2 slot. The seller adds up the watts and suggests a 450 watt SMPS with spare room, plus a UPS for load-shedding. Every choice was about the motherboard, its slots, its buses and its power.

Real life example 2, the classroom projector: Your teacher plugs a laptop into the projector and nothing appears. The laptop only has HDMI and USB-C, and the projector only has VGA. A cheap adapter that converts HDMI to VGA solves it, because it turns the digital HDMI signal into the analog VGA signal. Knowing which port carries what saves the whole class ten minutes of confusion.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often mix up the buses. Remember: the address bus is one-way and says where, the data bus is two-way and carries what, and the control bus carries commands like read and write. A very common exam question is: if the address bus is 16 bits wide, how much memory can be addressed? The answer is 2^16 = 65,536 locations, which is 64 KB if each location holds one byte. Another mistake is thinking USB Type-C means a certain speed. Type-C is only the shape of the plug, and the speed depends on the USB version behind it. Exams also ask you to list the steps of booting, explain POST, or name the parts of a motherboard from a diagram.

Recap: The motherboard is the main board that connects all parts of the computer. The chipset manages traffic between the CPU and other devices. Buses are the roads: the data bus carries data, the address bus carries memory addresses and decides how much memory can be used, and the control bus carries commands. Ports like USB, HDMI and Ethernet connect the outside world. The power supply turns 220 V AC from the wall into low-voltage DC, and a UPS keeps you safe during load-shedding. Booting goes power, POST, boot device, bootloader, operating system. Next, we learn how a computer stores numbers, starting with number systems.
key_points: The motherboard is the main circuit board that holds or connects the CPU, RAM, storage, expansion cards and ports.
The chipset manages data traffic between the CPU and slower devices; much of the old northbridge now lives inside the CPU.
The data bus carries data both ways, the address bus carries addresses one way, and the control bus carries commands and timing.
An n-bit address bus can address 2^n locations, so 32 bits gives 4 GB of byte-addressable memory.
USB is a fast serial, hot-swappable port; Type-C is only a plug shape, not a speed.
The SMPS converts 220 V AC to 12 V, 5 V and 3.3 V DC; a UPS keeps the PC running during power cuts.
Booting order: power on, POST, find boot device, bootloader, operating system. UEFI is the modern replacement for BIOS.
lessons.tip: Learn the motherboard with a real picture. Search for a labelled photo of any ATX motherboard and point at each part while saying its name and job out loud. Ten minutes of this beats an hour of reading.
lessons.task: Look at your own laptop, desktop or a family member's computer. Write down every port you can see on the outside, name each one (USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, Ethernet, audio and so on) and write one line about what you would plug into it. If you can safely see the BIOS/UEFI screen during startup, note which key opens it and what the boot order is.

quiz.q: Which bus carries the memory location that the CPU wants to read from or write to?
quiz.explain: The address bus carries the address, meaning where in memory. The data bus carries the actual data and the control bus carries read or write commands.

quiz.q: A computer has a 16-bit address bus and each address holds one byte. How much memory can it address?
quiz.explain: 16 address lines give 2^16 = 65,536 addresses. At one byte each that is 65,536 bytes, which is 64 KB.

quiz.q: What does the SMPS in a desktop computer do?
options: Connects the monitor to the computer
Converts 220 V AC from the wall into low-voltage DC for the parts
quiz.explain: The Switched Mode Power Supply turns wall AC into steady DC lines such as 12 V, 5 V and 3.3 V that the computer parts need.

quiz.q: What is POST?
options: A self-test the firmware runs at power-on to check the main hardware
The program that loads the operating system kernel
quiz.explain: The Power-On Self-Test checks that the CPU, RAM, graphics and other key parts are working before the computer looks for an operating system.

quiz.q: Your new phone has a USB Type-C port. What does Type-C tell you for sure?
options: It is an analog video port
Only the shape of the plug, which fits either way up
quiz.explain: Type-C is a connector shape. The speed depends on which USB or Thunderbolt version the device supports, and Type-C can carry power.

lessons.title: Number Systems: Binary, Octal, Decimal and Hexadecimal
lessons.content:
Why do we count in tens? Most likely because we have ten fingers. If humans had eight fingers, we would probably count in eights and think that was normal. A computer has no fingers. It has billions of tiny switches that can only be off or on. So a computer counts in twos. In this lesson you will learn the four number systems every CSE student must know, binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal, and how to convert numbers between them by hand.

The big idea, place value: All four systems work the same way. Each digit has a value that depends on its position. In decimal, the number 345 means 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 5 ones: 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 5 × 1. The positions from right to left are worth 1, 10, 100, 1000, which are 10^0, 10^1, 10^2, 10^3. The number 10 is called the base or radix. Change the base and you get a different number system, but the rule stays the same: digit times base to the power of its position, then add everything up.

How many digits a base has: A number system with base b uses exactly b different digits, from 0 up to b minus 1. Decimal, base 10, uses 0 to 9. Binary, base 2, uses only 0 and 1. Octal, base 8, uses 0 to 7. Hexadecimal, base 16, needs sixteen digits, so after 0 to 9 it borrows letters: A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15. To avoid confusion we often write the base as a small number after the value, like 1011 in base 2, or use prefixes as programmers do: 0b1011 for binary, 0o17 for octal and 0x1F for hex.

Why computers use binary: A transistor inside a chip works best as a switch: current flowing or not flowing, high voltage or low voltage. Two states are easy to tell apart even when there is electrical noise. If a chip tried to use ten different voltage levels for ten digits, a tiny wobble could turn a 6 into a 7. With just two levels, there is a large safe gap between 0 and 1. One binary digit is called a bit, short for binary digit.

Binary place values: In binary the positions from right to left are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and so on, each one double the last. Learn this row by heart, it makes everything else fast. To read the binary number 1011, write the place values under the digits: 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Another example: 110010 = 32 + 16 + 2 = 50. Just add the place values where there is a 1.

Counting in binary: Counting is the same game as an odometer, but each wheel only has 0 and 1. 0, 1, then we run out of digits, so we carry: 10 (two), 11 (three), 100 (four), 101 (five), 110 (six), 111 (seven), 1000 (eight). Notice that with 3 bits you can make 8 patterns, 000 to 111, which means 0 to 7. In general n bits give 2^n patterns, and the largest unsigned value is 2^n minus 1. With 8 bits, one byte, you get 256 patterns, from 0 to 255. That is why so many things in computing stop at 255.

Decimal to binary, the division method: To convert a decimal whole number to binary, divide it by 2 again and again and write down the remainders. Then read the remainders from bottom to top. Let's convert 13. 13 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 1. 6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0. 3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1. 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1. Reading the remainders from the last one up gives 1101. Check: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13. Correct. The same method works for any base: to go to octal, divide by 8; to go to hex, divide by 16.

Decimal to binary, the subtraction method: There is a quicker method for small numbers. Find the biggest power of two that fits, put a 1 there, subtract, and repeat. For 50: 32 fits, 50 − 32 = 18. 16 fits, 18 − 16 = 2. 8 does not fit, 4 does not fit, 2 fits, 2 − 2 = 0, 1 does not fit. So we have 1s in the 32, 16 and 2 places: 110010. Many students find this method easier to do in their head.

Octal, base 8: Octal uses digits 0 to 7, and its place values are 1, 8, 64, 512 and so on. For example, 157 in octal = 1 × 64 + 5 × 8 + 7 × 1 = 64 + 40 + 7 = 111 in decimal. Octal is useful because 8 = 2^3, so every octal digit matches exactly 3 bits. To convert binary to octal, group the bits in threes from the right, adding zeros on the left if needed, and replace each group with its value. Binary 110010 becomes 110 010, which is 6 and 2, so 62 in octal. Check: 6 × 8 + 2 = 50. Correct.

Where octal is still used: Octal was popular on older computers whose word sizes were multiples of 3 bits. Today the most common place you will meet it is Linux file permissions. When someone types chmod 755 file.sh, each digit is octal and each one stands for 3 bits: read, write and execute. 7 = 111 means read, write and execute for the owner, and 5 = 101 means read and execute for the group and for everyone else.

Hexadecimal, base 16: Hex uses 0 to 9 and A to F, with place values 1, 16, 256, 4096 and so on. For example, 2F in hex = 2 × 16 + 15 × 1 = 32 + 15 = 47. Hex is very popular because 16 = 2^4, so each hex digit matches exactly 4 bits, also called a nibble. One byte, 8 bits, is always exactly two hex digits. That makes hex a short, friendly way to write long binary numbers. Compare 11111111 with FF: same value, much easier to read and to say out loud.

Binary to hex and back: Group the bits in fours from the right and convert each group. Binary 1101 0110 becomes D and 6, so D6 in hex. Going back is just as easy: each hex digit becomes 4 bits. Hex 3A becomes 0011 1010. Keep a small table in your head: 0000 = 0, 0001 = 1, up to 1001 = 9, then 1010 = A, 1011 = B, 1100 = C, 1101 = D, 1110 = E, 1111 = F. After a few days of practice you will read hex like a second language.

Octal to hex: There is no direct short cut between octal and hex, so we go through binary. Convert each octal digit to 3 bits, join them, then regroup into 4 bits. Octal 754 becomes 111 101 100, which is 111101100. Regroup from the right in fours: 1 1110 1100, and pad the left group to 0001. That gives 1, E and C, so 1EC in hex. Check in decimal: 7 × 64 + 5 × 8 + 4 = 448 + 40 + 4 = 492, and 1 × 256 + 14 × 16 + 12 = 256 + 224 + 12 = 492. Same number.

One number, four costumes: Let's look at 255 in all four systems. Decimal 255, binary 11111111, octal 377 and hex FF. And 100 is binary 1100100, octal 144 and hex 64. A number is an idea, and the base is only the costume it wears. The value does not change when you convert it, only the way it is written.

Fractions in binary: Numbers after the point work the same way, but the place values go down: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, which are 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625. So binary 0.101 = 0.5 + 0 + 0.125 = 0.625. To convert a decimal fraction to binary, multiply by 2 again and again and take the whole part each time.
