For 0.625: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25, take 1, keep 0.25. 0.25 × 2 = 0.5, take 0, keep 0.5. 0.5 × 2 = 1.0, take 1, nothing left. Read the digits from top to bottom: 0.101.

A surprising fact about 0.1: Some simple decimal fractions never end in binary. Try 0.1: 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 (0), 0.4 (0), 0.8 (0), 1.6 (1, keep 0.6), 1.2 (1, keep 0.2), and then it repeats forever: 0.0001100110011 and so on. A computer has to cut it off somewhere, so 0.1 is stored as a tiny bit wrong. This is why in many programming languages 0.1 + 0.2 does not give exactly 0.3 but something like 0.30000000000000004. It is not a bug in the language. It is a property of binary fractions, and it is the reason banks store money in whole paisa instead of fractions of a taka.

Real life example 1, colours on a screen: Open any design app or website code and you will see colours like #FF0000 or #1E90FF. That is hex. The six digits are three pairs: red, green and blue, each from 00 to FF, which is 0 to 255. So #FF0000 means full red, no green, no blue, which is pure red. #FFFFFF is white and #000000 is black. If a designer at a Dhaka software company asks you to make a button a bit darker, you lower those hex numbers. Now you know what you are actually changing.

Real life example 2, addresses everywhere: Every Wi-Fi and network card has a MAC address that looks like 3C:52:82:1A:BF:07. That is six bytes written as hex pairs. IPv6 internet addresses, the new kind, are also written in hex. When a program crashes, the error often shows a memory address like 0x7ffe5a3c, again in hex. And the IPv4 address on your home router, 192.168.0.1, is really 32 bits written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255, one for each byte.

Common mistakes: The biggest one is reading remainders in the wrong order in the division method. The first remainder is the rightmost bit, so read from bottom to top. Another is forgetting to pad with zeros when grouping. Always group from the right side, never from the left. Students also write digits that do not exist in a base, like an 8 in octal or a 2 in binary, which instantly shows the answer is wrong. In hex, people forget that A means 10, not 1, and that 10 in hex means sixteen, not ten.

What exams ask: Expect questions like convert 156 to binary, octal and hexadecimal. Convert 3AF in hex to decimal. Convert 101101.11 in binary to decimal. Why is hexadecimal used in computing? How many different values can be stored in 10 bits? Answers to the last two: hex is a compact way to write binary because one hex digit equals exactly 4 bits, and 10 bits give 2^10 = 1024 values. Always show your working step by step. Teachers give marks for the method, and the method also helps you catch your own mistakes.

A quick way to check yourself: After any conversion, convert your answer back to decimal using place values. If you get the number you started with, you are right. On a phone or computer the built-in calculator also has a programmer mode that shows a number in binary, octal, decimal and hex at the same time. Use it to check your homework, but do the work by hand first, because exams do not allow calculators that do this for you.

Recap: Every number system uses place value with a base. Decimal is base 10, binary base 2, octal base 8 and hex base 16. Computers use binary because two states are reliable for electronic switches. Convert decimal to another base by repeated division and reading remainders from bottom to top, and convert back by multiplying each digit by its place value. Octal groups bits in threes and hex groups bits in fours, which is why hex is everywhere in computing. In the next lesson we will add, subtract and store negative numbers in binary.
key_points: Every number system uses place value: digit × base^position, then add.
Binary is base 2 (0, 1), octal base 8 (0-7), decimal base 10 (0-9), hexadecimal base 16 (0-9, A-F).
Computers use binary because transistors are reliable as two-state switches.
Decimal to base b: divide by b repeatedly and read the remainders from bottom to top.
One octal digit = 3 bits and one hex digit = 4 bits, so group bits from the right to convert.
n bits give 2^n patterns; 8 bits (one byte) give 0 to 255, written 00 to FF in hex.
Some decimal fractions like 0.1 never end in binary, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in many languages.
lessons.tip: Memorise the row 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 and the 16-line table from 0000 = 0 to 1111 = F. With those two in your head, almost every conversion becomes quick mental maths.
lessons.task: Take your birth year, for example 2007. Convert it to binary, octal and hexadecimal by hand, showing every step. Then check all three answers with the programmer mode of a calculator app. If any answer is wrong, find exactly which step went wrong.

quiz.q: What is binary 101101 in decimal?
quiz.explain: Place values 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. The 1s are at 32, 8, 4 and 1, so 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.

quiz.q: Using repeated division by 2, how should you read the remainders to get the binary answer?
options: From bottom to top, the last remainder is the leftmost bit
quiz.explain: The first remainder is the rightmost bit, so you read the remainders from the last one back to the first.

quiz.q: Why is hexadecimal so common in computing?
options: Each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so it is a short way to write binary
Computers calculate in base 16 inside the CPU
It was the first number system ever invented
quiz.explain: Computers work in binary, but long binary strings are hard to read. Since 16 = 2^4, one hex digit maps exactly to 4 bits and one byte is exactly two hex digits.

quiz.q: What is hex 2F in decimal?
quiz.explain: 2 × 16 + F × 1 = 32 + 15 = 47, because F means 15.

quiz.q: How many different values can be stored in 8 bits?
quiz.explain: n bits give 2^n patterns, so 8 bits give 2^8 = 256 values, from 0 to 255 for unsigned numbers.

lessons.title: Binary Arithmetic and Negative Numbers
lessons.content:
Every time you add marks on a result sheet, check your bKash balance or play a game, the CPU inside the device is adding and subtracting binary numbers billions of times a second. In the last lesson you learned how to write numbers in binary. Now we will do maths with them: addition, subtraction, a little multiplication, and the clever trick computers use to store negative numbers. By the end you will understand why a number can suddenly flip from a big positive value to a negative one, a bug that has crashed rockets and broken video games.

Binary addition rules: Binary addition works exactly like school addition, column by column from the right, carrying when a column gets too big. The only difference is that a column gets too big at 2 instead of 10. There are just four rules: 0 + 0 = 0. 0 + 1 = 1. 1 + 1 = 10, which means write 0 and carry 1. And when there is a carry too, 1 + 1 + 1 = 11, which means write 1 and carry 1. That is the whole table. Compare that with the decimal addition table you had to learn as a child.

A worked addition: Let's add 1011 (11) and 0110 (6). Rightmost column: 1 + 0 = 1. Next: 1 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1. Next: 0 + 1 + carry 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1. Leftmost: 1 + 0 + carry 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1. The final carry becomes a new digit on the left. Result: 10001. Check: 16 + 1 = 17, and 11 + 6 = 17. Correct. Always check by converting back to decimal while you are learning.

Binary subtraction with borrowing: Subtraction also works column by column, borrowing when the top digit is smaller. The rules: 0 − 0 = 0, 1 − 0 = 1, 1 − 1 = 0, and 0 − 1 needs a borrow. When you borrow in binary, the column receives 2, not 10, so 0 − 1 becomes 2 − 1 = 1, and the column on the left loses 1. Example: 1010 (10) minus 0011 (3). Rightmost column: 0 − 1 needs a borrow. The next column has a 1, so it lends and becomes 0, and the rightmost column gets 2: 2 − 1 = 1. Second column: now 0 − 1, so it needs a borrow too. The third column is 0 and has nothing to lend, so it first borrows from the leftmost 1, which becomes 0. The third column now holds 2, lends 1 to the second column and keeps 1. Second column: 2 − 1 = 1. Third column: 1 − 0 = 1. Leftmost column: 0 − 0 = 0. Result: 0111, which is 7. Correct, 10 − 3 = 7. Borrowing chains can get confusing, which is one reason computers use a smarter method you will see soon.

Binary multiplication: Multiplying in binary is surprisingly easy because you only ever multiply by 0 or 1. Multiply by 1 and you copy the number. Multiply by 0 and you get zero. Then shift and add, just like long multiplication. Example: 101 (5) × 11 (3). First row: 101 × 1 = 101. Second row: 101 × 1 shifted one place left = 1010. Add: 101 + 1010 = 1111, which is 15. Correct. Notice that shifting a binary number one place to the left doubles it, just as adding a zero in decimal multiplies by ten. CPUs use this trick all the time: shifting left is a very fast way to multiply by 2, 4 or 8.

Fixed size: computers have a fixed number of bits: On paper you can write as many digits as you like. Inside a computer, numbers live in boxes of a fixed size, such as 8 bits, 16 bits, 32 bits or 64 bits. An 8-bit box holds unsigned values from 0 to 255. This fixed size is what makes negative numbers and overflow interesting. For the rest of this lesson we will use 8-bit boxes, because they are small enough to write by hand.

The problem of the minus sign: A computer cannot write a little minus sign. It only has bits. So we need a rule that uses some of the bit patterns for negative numbers. Over the years three methods became famous: sign-magnitude, 1's complement and 2's complement. Almost every modern computer uses 2's complement, but exams love asking about all three, and seeing why the first two fall short helps you understand why the third one wins.

Method 1, sign-magnitude: Use the leftmost bit as the sign: 0 means positive, 1 means negative. The other 7 bits hold the size of the number. So +5 = 00000101 and −5 = 10000101. This is easy for humans to read. But it has two problems. First, there are two zeros: 00000000 is +0 and 10000000 is −0, which wastes a pattern and makes comparisons awkward. Second, the addition circuit must check the signs and decide whether to add or subtract, which makes the hardware more complex. The range with 8 bits is −127 to +127.

Method 2, 1's complement: To make a negative number, flip every bit of the positive number, turning 0s into 1s and 1s into 0s. +5 = 00000101, so −5 = 11111010. Positive numbers still start with 0 and negative ones with 1. Addition becomes simpler than sign-magnitude, but there are still two zeros: 00000000 and 11111111. Also, when adding, a carry out of the left end has to be added back in at the right, called the end-around carry, which is an extra step. The range with 8 bits is again −127 to +127.

Method 3, 2's complement: To make a negative number, flip every bit and then add 1. +5 = 00000101. Flip: 11111010. Add 1: 11111011. So −5 = 11111011. That's it. There is only one zero now, because if you take 00000000, flip it to 11111111 and add 1, you get 1 00000000, and the extra carry falls off the 8-bit box, leaving 00000000 again. The leftmost bit still tells you the sign: 0 for positive and zero, 1 for negative.

Why 2's complement is so clever: The leftmost bit in 2's complement has a negative place value. In 8 bits the place values are −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. So 11111011 = −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = −5. This means the same adding circuit works for positive and negative numbers with no special checks. The range in 8 bits is −128 to +127. There is one more negative number than positive, because zero takes one of the non-negative patterns. In general, n bits give a range of −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1.

A quick way to read a negative 2's complement number: If the leftmost bit is 1, you can find its size by doing the same trick again: flip all bits and add 1. Take 11110110. Flip: 00001001. Add 1: 00001010, which is 10. So 11110110 is −10. Another shortcut many students like: copy the bits from the right up to and including the first 1, then flip all the remaining bits on the left. For 00001010: copy the 10 on the right, then flip the remaining 000010 into 111101, giving 11110110. Same answer, fewer steps.

Subtraction by adding: Here is the real reason computers love 2's complement. To calculate A − B, the computer calculates A + (−B). There is no need for a separate subtraction circuit. Example: 7 − 5. +7 = 00000111. −5 = 11111011. Add them: 00000111 + 11111011 = 1 00000010. The 9th bit is a carry out of the box, so we drop it. The answer is 00000010, which is 2. Correct. Another: 3 − 8. +3 = 00000011, −8 = 11111000. Add: 11111011, no carry. The leftmost bit is 1, so it is negative; flip and add 1 to get 00000101, so the answer is −5. Correct.

Overflow, when the box is too small: Overflow happens when the true answer does not fit in the fixed number of bits. With signed 8-bit numbers the range is −128 to 127. Try 100 + 50. 01100100 + 00110010 = 10010110. The leftmost bit is 1, so the computer reads it as negative: −128 + 16 + 4 + 2 = −106. Two positive numbers gave a negative answer. That is overflow. The rule to detect it: if you add two numbers with the same sign and the result has the opposite sign, overflow happened. Adding a positive and a negative number can never overflow.

Carry is not the same as overflow: Students often mix these up. A carry out of the leftmost bit is normal in 2's complement subtraction, like the 7 − 5 example, and it is simply thrown away. Overflow is about the signed meaning of the result being wrong. For unsigned numbers the story is different: there, a carry out means the result is too big. For example, unsigned 8-bit 255 + 1 = 11111111 + 00000001 = 1 00000000, the carry drops and you get 0. The value wraps around like a car's odometer going from 999999 back to 000000.

Real life example 1, the Gangnam Style counter: YouTube once stored view counts as signed 32-bit integers. The largest value that fits is 2^31 − 1 = 2,147,483,647. In 2014 the music video Gangnam Style got close to that number of views, and YouTube upgraded the counter to 64 bits. If they had not, the next view would have overflowed and the count could have jumped to a huge negative number. Google even joked about it on the video page. A 64-bit signed counter goes up to about 9.2 quintillion, which no video will reach.

Real life example 2, rockets and games: In 1996 the European Ariane 5 rocket exploded about 40 seconds after launch. A piece of software converted a large 64-bit floating-point value into a 16-bit signed integer. The number was bigger than 32,767, the largest value 16 bits can hold, the conversion failed, and the guidance system shut down. A much happier example is the old arcade game Pac-Man: the level counter was stored in 8 bits, and on level 256 the game glitched and half the screen filled with garbage, so the game could not be finished. Same lesson in both: always know how big your box is.

Where this shows up in programming: In C, an int is usually 32 bits and a char is 8 bits. If you write a loop that keeps adding to a signed int, it may eventually overflow, and in C signed overflow is officially undefined behaviour, meaning anything can happen. Java and many other languages wrap around in 2's complement. Languages like Python use big integers that grow as needed, so they avoid this problem for whole numbers but pay for it in speed. When you write programs that count money, students or likes, pick a type big enough for the worst case.

Common mistakes: The most common is forgetting the +1 when making a 2's complement number, which gives you 1's complement instead. Another is forgetting the fixed width: −5 in 8-bit 2's complement is 11111011, but if you write only 1011 you have lost the meaning. Always pad positive numbers with zeros on the left to the full width before flipping. Students also mix up carry and overflow, and some try to detect overflow by looking only at the final carry, which is wrong for signed numbers.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: add 1101 and 1011 in binary. Subtract 0110 from 1100 using 2's complement. Represent −25 in 8-bit sign-magnitude, 1's complement and 2's complement. What is the range of an 8-bit 2's complement number? Explain overflow with an example. For −25: +25 = 00011001. Sign-magnitude: 10011001. 1's complement: 11100110. 2's complement: 11100111. Practise this exact question until you can do it in under two minutes.

Recap: Binary addition uses four simple rules, and carries happen at 2. Subtraction can be done with borrowing, but computers use 2's complement and turn subtraction into addition. Sign-magnitude and 1's complement both have two zeros; 2's complement has one zero, a range of −128 to 127 in 8 bits, and works with one simple adder. To make a 2's complement negative, flip all bits and add 1. Overflow happens when the answer does not fit in the box, and you can spot it when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the other sign. Next we will see how bits represent not just numbers but letters, pictures and sound.
key_points: Binary addition rules: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=10 (carry 1), 1+1+1=11 (carry 1).
Shifting a binary number one place left multiplies it by 2, and binary multiplication is just shift and add.
Sign-magnitude and 1's complement both have two zeros (+0 and −0); 2's complement has only one.
2's complement negative: flip every bit, then add 1. In 8 bits the range is −128 to +127.
Computers subtract by adding the 2's complement: A − B = A + (−B), dropping any carry out.
Overflow happens when two numbers with the same sign give a result with the opposite sign.
Real bugs from overflow: the Gangnam Style 32-bit view counter, Ariane 5 in 1996 and Pac-Man level 256.
lessons.tip: Do every 2's complement problem in a fixed width, usually 8 bits, and always check your answer by converting back to decimal with −128 as the leftmost place value. This one check catches almost every mistake.
lessons.task: Write the numbers −1, −8, −25, −100 and −128 in 8-bit 2's complement. Then use them to calculate 20 − 25 and 100 − 8 entirely in binary by adding, and check both answers in decimal. Finally, add 120 + 10 in 8-bit signed binary and explain in one sentence why the answer is wrong.

quiz.q: What is 1011 + 0110 in binary?
quiz.explain: 11 + 6 = 17, and 17 in binary is 10001. Column by column you get carries in three places.

quiz.q: How do you form the 2's complement of a binary number?
options: Flip every bit and then add 1
quiz.explain: 2's complement is the 1's complement (every bit flipped) plus 1. For example, +5 = 00000101 becomes 11111011 for −5.

quiz.q: What is the range of an 8-bit 2's complement number?
quiz.explain: n bits give −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1, so 8 bits give −128 to +127. There is only one zero, so there is one extra negative value.

quiz.q: In 8-bit signed arithmetic, 100 + 50 gives a negative result. What is this called?
quiz.explain: The true answer 150 does not fit in −128 to 127. Two positive numbers gave a negative result, which is the sign of overflow.

quiz.q: Which representation has two different patterns for zero?
quiz.explain: Sign-magnitude has 00000000 and 10000000, and 1's complement has 00000000 and 11111111. 2's complement fixes this and has only one zero.

lessons.title: Data Representation: Text, Pictures and Sound in Bits
lessons.content:
Here is a puzzle. Inside your phone there are only 0s and 1s. Yet the phone shows your friend's message in Bangla, a photo from Cox's Bazar, a song and an emoji. How can a pile of bits become a picture or a voice? The answer is agreement. People agree on a rule, called an encoding, that says which pattern of bits means which letter, colour or sound. In this lesson you will learn the most important of these rules, and you will be able to calculate how much space a photo or a song really needs.

Bits, nibbles and bytes: A bit is a single 0 or 1, the smallest piece of data. Four bits make a nibble, which is one hex digit. Eight bits make a byte, the basic unit that memory and files are measured in. One byte can hold 2^8 = 256 different patterns. A word is the natural size a CPU works with in one go, today usually 64 bits on computers and phones. When you see a file size, it is almost always counted in bytes.

Units, and the 1000 versus 1024 confusion: A kilobyte is about a thousand bytes, a megabyte about a million, a gigabyte about a billion and a terabyte about a trillion. But there are two ways to count. Storage makers use powers of 10: 1 KB = 1000 bytes, 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes. Many operating systems count in powers of 2: 1 KiB = 1024 bytes, 1 MiB = 1024 × 1024 bytes, 1 GiB = 1024^3 bytes. This is why a new 1 TB hard disk shows about 931 GB in Windows. Nobody stole your space, the two sides just count differently. Also remember that a small b means bits and a capital B means bytes: internet speed 40 Mbps means 40 megabits per second, which is only 5 megabytes per second.

Text, the idea of a character code: To store text, we give every character a number, and then store the number in binary. The letter A gets one number, B gets another, the space gets another, and so on. As long as the computer that writes the file and the computer that reads it use the same table, the text arrives correctly. When they use different tables, you get strange symbols, which you have probably seen in a badly opened file.

ASCII: The most famous early table is ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, from the 1960s. It uses 7 bits, so it has 128 codes, from 0 to 127. Codes 0 to 31 are invisible control codes like newline and tab. Then come the printable characters. Some useful ones to remember: space is 32, the digit 0 is 48, capital A is 65 and small a is 97. So the word Hi is stored as 72 and 105, which in binary is 01001000 01101001. Notice that small letters are exactly 32 more than capitals, so changing case is just flipping one bit.

Digits are not numbers in text: The character 5 in a text file is code 53, not the number 5. The text 2026 is four separate characters with codes 50, 48, 50 and 54. When a program reads your age from a form, it gets text and must convert it to a number before doing maths. Forgetting this is why some beginners' programs calculate 2 + 3 as 23: they joined two pieces of text instead of adding two numbers.

The limit of ASCII: 128 codes are fine for English letters, digits and a few symbols, but there is no room for Bangla, Arabic, Chinese, Hindi or even accented European letters. Different countries created their own 8-bit extended tables using codes 128 to 255, but each one used those codes differently. A file written with one table looked like garbage with another. The world needed one big table for every language.

Unicode: Unicode is that big table. It gives every character in every writing system a unique number called a code point, written like U+0041 for A. Today Unicode has well over a hundred thousand characters, including Bangla, maths symbols, music notes, old scripts and emoji. The Bangla block runs from U+0980 to U+09FF. For example, অ is U+0985 and ক is U+0995. Because of Unicode, you can type Bangla on your phone, send it to someone with a different phone, and it shows correctly.

How Bangla letters are built: Bangla text in Unicode is stored as a sequence of basic letters and signs, and the font draws the final shape. A joined letter like ক্ষ is stored as three code points: ক (U+0995), the hasant ্ (U+09CD) and ষ (U+09B7). The font sees the hasant between two consonants and draws them joined. A vowel sign like the ি in কি is stored after the consonant, even though it appears before it on screen. This is why the same Bangla text can look slightly different in different fonts, while the stored data stays the same.

The Bijoy problem: Before Unicode was common, most Bangla in Bangladesh was typed with Bijoy, which used special fonts that put Bangla shapes on top of the normal ASCII codes. The file actually stored English letter codes, and only the special font made them look like Bangla. Open that file on a computer without the font, or paste the text into a website, and you get nonsense English letters. Unicode Bangla, typed with keyboards like Avro or the phone's built-in Bangla keyboard, stores real Bangla code points, so it works everywhere and search engines can find it. Always use Unicode for anything that goes online.

UTF-8, storing Unicode in bytes: A code point is a number, but how many bytes should we use to store it? The most common answer today is UTF-8, used by almost every website. UTF-8 is variable length. Code points 0 to 127, which are exactly the old ASCII characters, take just 1 byte, so plain English text in UTF-8 is identical to ASCII. Most European letters take 2 bytes. Bangla, Hindi, Chinese and many others take 3 bytes per code point. Most emoji take 4 bytes. So the word বাংলা, which is 5 code points, takes 15 bytes in UTF-8, while the word Hello takes only 5.

Images, the pixel grid: A digital picture is a grid of tiny squares called pixels. Each pixel stores a colour as a number. The resolution is the size of the grid. A Full HD image is 1920 pixels wide and 1080 tall, which is 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, about 2 megapixels. A 12 megapixel phone camera takes photos with about 12 million pixels. Zoom in far enough on any photo and you will see the squares.

Colour depth: How many bits each pixel uses is called the colour depth. With 1 bit per pixel you get only black and white, like an old fax. With 8 bits you get 256 colours or 256 shades of grey. Most screens use 24-bit colour: 8 bits for red, 8 for green and 8 for blue, the RGB model. Each channel goes from 0 to 255, so there are 256 × 256 × 256 = 16,777,216 possible colours, which is more than the human eye can tell apart. That is the same RGB you saw written in hex as #FF0000 in the number systems lesson.

Calculating image size: Uncompressed size = width × height × bytes per pixel. A Full HD image at 24 bits, which is 3 bytes per pixel, needs 1920 × 1080 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes, about 6.2 MB. A 12 megapixel photo would need about 36 MB uncompressed. Yet the photo on your phone is usually only 2 to 5 MB. The difference is compression, which we will see in a moment.

Sound, sampling: Sound in the air is a smooth wave of pressure. A microphone turns it into a smooth electrical signal. To store it as bits, the computer measures the signal many times per second. Each measurement is a sample. The number of samples per second is the sampling rate, measured in hertz. Music CDs use 44,100 samples per second, which is enough to capture all the sounds humans can hear, because our hearing tops out at around 20,000 hertz and you need more than twice that rate to capture it. Phone calls use far fewer samples, which is why voices on a call sound thinner.

Bit depth and sound file size: Each sample is stored as a number with a certain number of bits, called the bit depth. CDs use 16 bits per sample, giving 65,536 possible levels. Stereo means two channels, left and right. So CD-quality audio needs 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second, which is about 176 KB per second, or about 10.6 MB per minute. A 4-minute song would be over 40 MB uncompressed. An MP3 at 128 kilobits per second uses about 1 MB per minute, roughly 11 times smaller.

Video is pictures plus sound: A video is a series of pictures shown quickly, usually 24, 30 or 60 frames per second, plus a sound track. Uncompressed Full HD video at 30 frames per second would need about 6.2 MB × 30 = 186 MB every second. Nobody could stream that on mobile data. Video formats like MP4 work only because of very strong compression.

Compression, lossless: Compression means storing the same data in fewer bits. Lossless compression gives back exactly the original when you open it. A simple example is run-length encoding: the text AAAABBBCC can be stored as 4A3B2C, from 9 characters down to 6. Real formats like ZIP and PNG use cleverer tricks, but the idea is the same: find patterns and repetition and describe them briefly. Lossless is a must for text, program files and anything where one wrong bit would break things.

Compression, lossy: Lossy compression throws away details that people are unlikely to notice, and you can never get them back exactly. JPEG photos remove fine colour detail, MP3 and AAC remove sounds hidden behind louder sounds, and MP4 video reuses parts of the previous frame instead of storing every frame fully. This is how a 36 MB photo becomes 3 MB. The trade-off is quality: save a JPEG again and again, or forward a picture many times on a messaging app that recompresses it, and it gets blurrier and blockier each time.

Real life example 1, the 'forwarded many times' photo: A cousin sends a family photo in a WhatsApp group, it gets forwarded from group to group, and when it reaches you it looks blurry and full of little squares. Each time the app recompressed it with lossy compression to save data, and each round threw away more detail. If you need the original quality, ask for the photo to be sent as a document, which skips the recompression.

Real life example 2, your mobile data pack: You buy a 1 GB internet pack. Should you watch one hour of video or listen to music all day? Music at 128 kbps uses about 1 MB per minute, so 1 GB gives roughly 16 hours of listening. Standard-quality video can easily use several hundred MB per hour, and HD much more. Now you can estimate it yourself instead of guessing, because you know how sound and pictures turn into bits.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students mix up bits and bytes, forget that Mbps means megabits, and think the character 7 is stored as binary 111. Another common mistake is thinking Unicode and UTF-8 are the same: Unicode is the table of code points, UTF-8 is one way to store those code points as bytes. Exam questions often ask: what is the ASCII code of A and a? Why was Unicode needed? Calculate the size of a 1024 × 768 image with 24-bit colour (1024 × 768 × 3 = 2,359,296 bytes, about 2.25 MiB). Calculate the size of a 1-minute mono recording at 8,000 samples per second and 8 bits per sample (8000 × 8 × 60 = 3,840,000 bits = 480,000 bytes). Explain lossy and lossless compression with examples.

Recap: Everything in a computer is bits, given meaning by an agreed encoding. Text uses character codes: ASCII for 128 basic characters, Unicode for every language including Bangla, and UTF-8 to store Unicode efficiently. Images are grids of pixels, each storing a colour, usually 24-bit RGB. Sound is sampled many times a second, with a set number of bits per sample. Size = how many items × bits per item, and compression, lossless or lossy, makes real files far smaller. In the next lesson we look at how computers actually make decisions with bits, using Boolean logic and logic gates.
key_points: 8 bits = 1 byte; a small b means bits and a capital B means bytes, so 40 Mbps is 5 MB per second.
Storage makers count 1 GB = 10^9 bytes while many operating systems count in 1024s, so a 1 TB disk shows about 931 GB.
ASCII uses 7 bits for 128 characters: A = 65, a = 97, the digit 0 = 48, space = 32.
Unicode gives every character in every language a code point; Bangla is U+0980 to U+09FF, and UTF-8 stores Bangla in 3 bytes per code point.
Bijoy text stores English codes under a special font, so it breaks without that font; Unicode Bangla works everywhere.
Image size = width × height × bytes per pixel; 24-bit RGB gives 16,777,216 colours.
Sound size = sampling rate × bit depth × channels × seconds; CD quality is about 10.6 MB per minute uncompressed.
Lossless compression (ZIP, PNG) restores the exact original; lossy compression (JPEG, MP3, MP4) removes detail for much smaller files.
lessons.tip: For every size question, write the formula in words first, such as pixels × bytes per pixel, put in the numbers, and only then calculate. Keep bits and bytes in separate columns until the very last step and divide by 8 once.
lessons.task: Take one photo with your phone and look at its resolution and file size in the photo details. Calculate its uncompressed size with width × height × 3 bytes, then work out how many times smaller the real file is. Next, type your name in Bangla and in English, and count how many bytes each takes in UTF-8 using the rule 1 byte for English letters and 3 bytes for each Bangla code point.

quiz.q: What is the ASCII code of the capital letter A?
quiz.explain: Capital A is 65. Small a is 97, the digit 0 is 48 and the space is 32.

quiz.q: Why was Unicode created?
options: Because ASCII's 128 characters could not cover Bangla and the world's other languages
quiz.explain: ASCII only covered basic English characters. Unicode gives every character in every writing system its own code point, so text in any language shows correctly everywhere.

quiz.q: How many bytes does an uncompressed 1920 × 1080 image with 24-bit colour need?
quiz.explain: 24 bits is 3 bytes per pixel. 1920 × 1080 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes, about 6.2 MB.

quiz.q: Which of these is lossy compression?
quiz.explain: JPEG throws away fine detail people are unlikely to notice. ZIP, PNG and run-length encoding are lossless and give back the exact original.

quiz.q: In UTF-8, how many bytes does one Bangla letter such as ক take?
quiz.explain: Bangla code points are between U+0800 and U+FFFF, and UTF-8 stores that range in 3 bytes each. English letters take 1 byte.

lessons.title: Boolean Logic and Logic Gates
lessons.content:
Your mother says: you can go out to play if you finish your homework AND it is not raining. Without knowing it, she just gave you a logic circuit. Two conditions go in, one decision comes out. Computers make billions of decisions like this every second, and they do it with tiny circuits called logic gates. In this lesson you will learn the maths behind those decisions, called Boolean logic, the basic gates, how to write truth tables, and how a few gates together can even add two numbers.

George Boole and Claude Shannon: In 1854 an English mathematician named George Boole published a book showing that logic, the kind of reasoning with true and false, could be written as algebra with symbols. For decades it was seen as pure maths with no practical use. Then in 1937 a young American student, Claude Shannon, showed in his master's thesis that Boole's algebra describes exactly how circuits of electrical switches behave. That idea is the foundation of every digital computer. When a CPU decides something, it is doing Boolean algebra in hardware.

True and false as 1 and 0: In Boolean logic a value can only be true or false. In computers we write true as 1 and false as 0, and in a circuit 1 is usually a higher voltage and 0 a lower voltage. A Boolean variable, like A, is a name for something that can be 1 or 0, such as 'the homework is finished'. Everything in this lesson works with just these two values.

Truth tables: A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs and the output for each one. With one input there are 2 rows, with two inputs 4 rows, with three inputs 8 rows. In general n inputs give 2^n rows. You write the inputs in binary counting order, 00, 01, 10, 11, so that you never miss a row. Truth tables are the most reliable way to understand or check any logic.

The AND gate: AND gives 1 only when all its inputs are 1. In words: A AND B is true only if A is true and B is true. The truth table for two inputs: 0 and 0 gives 0, 0 and 1 gives 0, 1 and 0 gives 0, 1 and 1 gives 1. In Boolean algebra AND is written like multiplication, A · B or just AB, and that works nicely because 1 × 1 = 1 and anything × 0 = 0. Think of two switches in series on one wire: the bulb lights only when both switches are on.

The OR gate: OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1. A OR B is false only if both are false. Truth table: 0 and 0 gives 0, 0 and 1 gives 1, 1 and 0 gives 1, 1 and 1 gives 1. It is written like addition, A + B, with the special rule that 1 + 1 = 1 in Boolean algebra, because true or true is simply true. Think of two switches in parallel: the bulb lights if either one or both are on. Notice that this OR includes the case where both are true, which is different from how we sometimes use 'or' in everyday talk.

The NOT gate: NOT has only one input and flips it: NOT 0 = 1 and NOT 1 = 0. It is also called an inverter. In algebra it is written with a bar over the letter, or as A' or ¬A. NOT is how a circuit says 'it is not raining' when the sensor reports 'raining'. In circuit diagrams the NOT gate is a triangle with a small circle at its tip, and that small circle, called a bubble, always means 'invert' wherever you see it.

NAND and NOR: NAND means NOT AND. It gives the opposite of AND: 0 only when all inputs are 1, and 1 otherwise. NOR means NOT OR: 1 only when all inputs are 0. They look like the AND and OR symbols with a bubble on the output. NAND and NOR are called universal gates because you can build every other gate, and so any digital circuit at all, using only NAND gates, or only NOR gates. For example, a NAND gate with both inputs tied together acts as a NOT gate. Chip makers love this, because building a chip from one repeated kind of gate is simpler and cheaper.

XOR and XNOR: XOR, exclusive OR, gives 1 when the inputs are different and 0 when they are the same. Truth table: 0 and 0 gives 0, 0 and 1 gives 1, 1 and 0 gives 1, 1 and 1 gives 0. It is the 'one or the other but not both' kind of or. It is written A ⊕ B. XNOR is the opposite: 1 when the inputs are the same. That makes XNOR an equality checker, and XOR a difference detector. XOR also has a neat trick: if you XOR a value with a key twice, you get the original back, which is why it appears in simple encryption and error checking.

Gate symbols: In diagrams each gate has a standard shape. AND has a flat back and a round front, like a letter D. OR has a curved back and a pointed front, like a shield. NOT is a triangle with a bubble. NAND and NOR are AND and OR with a bubble on the output. XOR is the OR shape with an extra curved line at the back. Practise drawing them, because exams ask you to draw circuits from expressions and to write expressions from circuits.

From a sentence to an expression: Real problems are written in words, and your first job is to turn the words into Boolean algebra. Let G mean 'you can go out', H mean 'homework is done' and R mean 'it is raining'. Your mother's rule becomes G = H · R', meaning H AND NOT R. Now a security light: it should turn on when it is night and someone moves, or when the manual switch is on. With N for night, M for motion and S for switch: L = N · M + S. The order of operations is like normal algebra: NOT first, then AND, then OR, unless brackets say otherwise.

From an expression to a truth table: To fill the table for L = N · M + S, list all 8 combinations of N, M and S. For each row, first work out N · M, then OR it with S. The light is on in every row where S = 1, which is 4 rows, plus the row where N = 1, M = 1 and S = 0. So the light is on in 5 of the 8 rows. Working column by column like this, with a separate column for each part of the expression, keeps you from making mistakes.

A few useful Boolean laws: Boolean algebra has rules that let you simplify expressions, so circuits need fewer gates. Some of the most used: A + 0 = A and A · 1 = A. A + 1 = 1 and A · 0 = 0. A + A = A and A · A = A. A + A' = 1, because something is always either true or not true, and A · A' = 0, because it cannot be both. And the double NOT: (A')' = A. You will study these in full in the Digital Logic Design course; for now, know they exist and check them with truth tables.

De Morgan's laws: Two laws are so important that they have a name. (A · B)' = A' + B', and (A + B)' = A' · B'. In words: NOT (A and B) is the same as (not A) or (not B), and NOT (A or B) is the same as (not A) and (not B). A daily-life check: 'It is not true that I have both a pen and a pencil' means 'I am missing the pen or I am missing the pencil'. To use De Morgan, break the bar, and change the operation: AND becomes OR, OR becomes AND. Programmers use this constantly when rewriting if-conditions.

How gates are built: Each gate is made of a handful of transistors acting as switches. In modern CMOS chips, for example, a NOT gate uses 2 transistors and a NAND gate uses 4. A processor contains billions of transistors, so it holds a huge number of gates. They are so small and fast that a gate can switch billions of times a second. You do not have to design transistors in this course; just know that the abstract gate in your notebook is a real tiny circuit in the chip.

Gates that add: the half adder: Remember the binary addition rules from earlier: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 10. Look at the two output digits. The right digit, the sum, is 1 when exactly one input is 1: that is XOR. The left digit, the carry, is 1 only when both inputs are 1: that is AND. So one XOR gate and one AND gate add two bits. This circuit is called a half adder. Join two half adders with an OR gate and you get a full adder, which can also add an incoming carry. Chain 64 full adders and you have the adding part of a 64-bit CPU. Arithmetic, at the bottom, is just logic.

Logic in programming: Every programming language has Boolean operators. In C, Java and JavaScript, AND is &&, OR is || and NOT is !. In Python they are the words and, or and not. An if statement like if (marks >= 40 && attendance >= 75) is an AND gate deciding whether a student may sit the exam. Bitwise operators &, |, ^ and ~ apply AND, OR, XOR and NOT to every bit of a number at once, which is how programmers pack many on and off settings into one byte.

Real life example 1, the staircase light: Many homes have a staircase light with one switch at the bottom and one at the top. Flip either switch and the light changes. This is the XOR idea: with the usual two-way wiring, the light is on when the two switches are in different positions, and off when they are the same, or the other way round depending on how the electrician wired it, which would make it XNOR. Either way, changing any one input flips the output, which is exactly the special property of XOR.

Real life example 2, the ATM and the lift: An ATM gives money only if the card is valid AND the PIN is correct AND the balance is enough. If any one fails, no cash: a three-input AND. A lift in an office building moves only if the door is closed AND the weight is under the limit; its alarm rings if the door is open for too long OR the weight is over the limit. Engineers write these rules as Boolean expressions first, check them with truth tables, and then build them in software or hardware.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: The most common mistake is mixing up OR and XOR: OR is 1 when both inputs are 1, XOR is 0. Another is forgetting rows in a truth table; always count to 2^n. Students also apply De Morgan without changing AND to OR, or they break the bar only over one variable. Typical exam questions: draw the truth table for NAND, NOR and XOR. Prove De Morgan's laws with truth tables. Draw the circuit for Y = A · B + C'. Why are NAND and NOR called universal gates? Show that a NAND gate can act as a NOT gate. Design a half adder.

Recap: Boolean logic works with only true and false, 1 and 0. AND needs all inputs 1, OR needs at least one, NOT flips, NAND and NOR are their opposites and are universal, XOR detects difference and XNOR detects equality. Truth tables list all 2^n input combinations and are the surest way to check logic. Boolean laws and De Morgan's laws simplify expressions so circuits use fewer gates. With just an XOR and an AND you can add two bits, which shows that all of computer arithmetic is built from logic. The Digital Logic Design course goes much deeper; next in this course we move from hardware to software.
key_points: Boolean logic uses only two values, true = 1 and false = 0; Shannon showed in 1937 that it describes switching circuits.
AND outputs 1 only if all inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 if at least one input is 1; NOT flips its single input.
NAND and NOR are the inverses of AND and OR, and are universal gates: any circuit can be built from only NANDs or only NORs.
XOR outputs 1 when the inputs differ; XNOR outputs 1 when they are the same.
A truth table with n inputs has 2^n rows; list them in binary counting order so none is missed.
De Morgan: (A·B)' = A' + B' and (A+B)' = A'·B'. Break the bar and swap AND with OR.
A half adder is an XOR for the sum and an AND for the carry; chained full adders make a CPU's adder.
lessons.tip: Never trust your head with logic, trust the truth table. Whenever you simplify an expression or apply De Morgan, quickly write the truth table of the old and new versions side by side. If every row matches, you are right.
lessons.task: Write the rule for your own phone's lock screen or a game as a Boolean expression, for example 'unlock if the fingerprint matches OR the PIN is correct'. Then make a 3-variable rule from daily life, such as when you can watch TV, write its expression and full 8-row truth table, and draw the gate circuit on paper.

quiz.q: Which gate gives 1 only when both of its two inputs are 1?
quiz.explain: AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR outputs 1 if any input is 1, and XOR outputs 0 when both are 1.

quiz.q: What does XOR output when both inputs are 1?
quiz.explain: XOR outputs 1 only when the inputs are different. When both are 1 they are the same, so the output is 0. This is the key difference from OR.

quiz.q: How many rows does a truth table with 3 inputs have?
quiz.explain: n inputs give 2^n combinations, so 3 inputs give 2^3 = 8 rows.

quiz.q: According to De Morgan's law, (A + B)' equals what?
quiz.explain: Break the bar and change OR to AND: NOT (A or B) is the same as (not A) and (not B).

quiz.q: A half adder uses which two gates for the sum and the carry?
options: OR for sum, NOT for carry
XOR for sum, AND for carry
AND for sum, XOR for carry
quiz.explain: 1 + 1 = 10: the sum bit is 1 when exactly one input is 1 (XOR), and the carry is 1 only when both are 1 (AND).

lessons.title: Software: Types and Licenses
lessons.content:
Imagine buying a brand new phone, turning it on, and finding nothing inside. No home screen, no camera app, no calls, nothing. The glass, the battery and the chips are all there, but the phone is basically a shiny brick. What makes it useful is software. Hardware is the body of a computer, and software is the set of instructions that tells that body what to do. In this lesson we will sort software into its main families and learn the rules, called licenses, that decide how you are allowed to use it.

What software is: software is a collection of programs, the data they need, and the documents that explain them. A program is a list of instructions written for a computer. You cannot touch software the way you can touch a keyboard. It lives as patterns of 0s and 1s stored on a disk or in memory. That is why you can copy software in seconds and send it across the world, but you cannot copy a monitor that way.

A quick reminder about firmware: in an earlier lesson you met hardware, software and firmware. Firmware is software that is stored permanently inside a hardware device, like the BIOS chip on a motherboard or the program inside a washing machine. It sits between hardware and normal software. In this lesson our focus is the normal software that you install, update and remove.

The two big families: almost every textbook divides software into system software and application software. Here is an easy picture. Think of Dhaka's roads, traffic signals and traffic police as system software. They do not take you anywhere by themselves, but without them nothing moves safely. The cars, buses, rickshaws and CNGs are application software. They are what you actually use to reach your goal, like going to school or the bazar.

System software: system software manages the computer itself and gives other programs a platform to run on. The user often does not notice it, but it is always working in the background. The main members of this family are the operating system, device drivers, firmware, language translators such as compilers and interpreters, and utility programs. The operating system is so important that it gets its own lesson next, and translators get a lesson after that.

Device drivers: a device driver is a small program that teaches the operating system how to talk to one particular piece of hardware. Windows does not automatically know every printer ever made. When you plug in a new Canon or HP printer, the operating system loads the printer's driver, and only then can it send pages to print. Graphics cards, Wi-Fi cards, sound cards and webcams all need drivers. Modern systems support plug and play, which means the right driver is found and installed automatically when you connect the device. When a driver is missing or broken, you see problems like no sound or a yellow warning sign in Device Manager.

Utility software: utility programs are helpers that keep the computer healthy, safe and tidy. Antivirus software scans files for malware. Disk cleanup removes junk files. A disk defragmenter rearranges pieces of files on a hard disk so they can be read faster. Backup tools copy your important files to another place. Compression tools like 7-Zip or WinRAR squeeze many files into one smaller zip or rar file. File managers help you browse folders. Most textbooks place utilities inside system software, because they look after the system rather than doing a user's main job.

Application software: application software, often just called an app, is built to help a user do a specific task. Writing a letter, watching a video, editing a photo, chatting with friends, paying a bill, playing a game: each of these needs an application. Applications cannot run alone. They always run on top of an operating system, and they ask the operating system to use the hardware for them.

General purpose applications: some applications are useful for millions of different people, so they are called general purpose or off-the-shelf software. A word processor such as Microsoft Word or LibreOffice Writer is for writing documents. A spreadsheet such as Excel or Google Sheets is for tables and calculations. Presentation software such as PowerPoint is for slides. Web browsers such as Chrome and Firefox open websites. Media players such as VLC play music and videos. Graphics software such as Photoshop, GIMP or Canva edits images.

Special purpose and custom software: some applications are built for one specific job or one specific organisation. A hospital management system that tracks patients, doctors and beds in one hospital is an example. A university result processing system is another. Software written specially for one client is called custom-made or bespoke software. The good side is that it fits the client's needs perfectly. The bad side is that it costs much more and takes longer to build. Off-the-shelf software is cheaper and ready immediately, but the client may need to change their way of working to fit it.

Web apps, mobile apps and cloud software: today many applications do not even need installing. A web app runs inside the browser, like Gmail or Google Docs. A mobile app is installed from the Play Store or App Store. Cloud software delivered over the internet with a monthly fee is called Software as a Service, or SaaS. With Google Docs, for example, the program and your file both live on Google's servers, and you just use them through the browser.

Versions and updates: software keeps changing. Developers fix bugs, close security holes and add features, and they release these changes as updates. A common way to number versions is major.minor.patch. In version 4.2.7, the 4 is the major version, which changes when there are big changes. The 2 is the minor version for new features, and the 7 is the patch number for small bug fixes. A patch that fixes a security problem is very important to install quickly.

Why licenses exist: software is creative work, just like a book or a song, so it is protected by copyright law. The person or company who made it decides the rules for using it. Those rules are written in a software license. When you click I agree during installation, you are accepting a license agreement, often called an End User License Agreement or EULA. Usually you are not buying the software itself, only the right to use it under those rules.

Proprietary software: proprietary or closed source software is owned by a company that keeps the source code secret. You get only the ready-to-run program. Examples are Microsoft Windows, Microsoft Office, Adobe Photoshop and macOS. You usually pay for a license, and the license may say you can install it on only one computer, cannot copy it to friends, and cannot change it. The company gives support and updates.

Open source software: in open source software, the source code is public. Anyone can read it, learn from it, change it and share it, as long as they follow the license. Linux, Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, Python and the core of Android are all open source. Thousands of volunteers and companies around the world improve these programs together. Two common types of open source license exist. Copyleft licenses such as the GPL say that if you share a changed version, you must also share your source code under the same license. Permissive licenses such as MIT and Apache let you use the code even inside closed products, as long as you keep the original credit.

Free is not always free: here people get confused. Freeware is software you can use without paying, but its source code is still secret, so you cannot change it. Adobe Acrobat Reader is a good example. Open source is about freedom to see and change the code, not just about price. People say free as in free speech versus free as in free tea. Most open source software is also free of cost, but freeware is not open source.

Shareware, trial and freemium: shareware lets you try software for a limited time or with limited features, and then asks you to pay. WinRAR is a famous example, with its never-ending reminder to buy a license. Freemium software gives a basic version for free and charges for extra features. Canva, Spotify and many mobile games work like this. Public domain software is a rare case where the creator gives up all rights, so anyone can do anything with it.

The problem with pirated software: in many places, people install cracked versions of paid software. Apart from being illegal, this is risky. Cracked installers are a popular way to spread viruses and password stealers. Pirated software often cannot receive security updates, and if your company is caught using it, you can face heavy fines. A smart alternative is to use open source tools, such as LibreOffice instead of Office or GIMP instead of Photoshop, or use the free student licenses that many companies offer.

Real life example 1: Rafi, a first year CSE student, gets a new laptop. It comes with Windows 11, which is system software and proprietary. Windows installs the Wi-Fi and touchpad drivers, which are also system software. Rafi installs Windows Security and 7-Zip, which are utilities. Then he installs VLC, Firefox and LibreOffice, which are general purpose applications, and all three are open source. He uses Canva in the browser, which is a freemium web app. For his C programming class he installs a compiler, which is a language translator. In one evening Rafi has touched almost every category from this lesson.

Real life example 2: a pharmacy in Mirpur wants to track medicine stock and sales. The owner can buy an off-the-shelf point of sale program for a fixed price and start the same day, or hire a software firm to build custom software that also tracks expiry dates and doctor prescriptions. Meanwhile, the owner accepts payments through a mobile banking app on an Android phone. That app is application software, and Android is the system software it runs on. The phone's camera driver lets the app scan the customer's QR code.

Common mistakes and exam questions: many students call the operating system an application. It is not, it is system software. Another mistake is thinking freeware means open source. Some students also forget that applications cannot run without an operating system. In exams you will often see questions like: differentiate between system software and application software with examples, define utility software and give three examples, what is a device driver, compare proprietary and open source software, and explain freeware and shareware. Always give at least one real example for each type, because examiners love examples.

Recap: software is the set of instructions that brings hardware to life. System software, including the operating system, drivers, translators and utilities, runs and protects the machine. Application software helps people do their tasks, either general purpose or custom-made. Licenses decide how you can use software, from closed proprietary programs to open source projects that anyone can study and improve. Next, we zoom into the most important system software of all: the operating system.
key_points: Software is programs plus data and documentation; it tells hardware what to do.
System software (OS, drivers, translators, utilities) runs and maintains the computer.
Application software helps users do tasks; it always runs on top of an operating system.
Device drivers let the OS talk to a specific piece of hardware.
Off-the-shelf software is ready-made and cheaper; custom (bespoke) software fits one client exactly.
Proprietary software keeps source code secret; open source shares it under licenses like GPL or MIT.
Freeware is free of cost but closed; shareware is try-then-pay; freemium charges for extra features.
lessons.tip: Make a two-column table on paper: system software on one side, application software on the other. Every time you open something on your phone or laptop this week, write it in the right column.
lessons.task: Open the list of installed programs on a computer (or the apps list on a phone). Pick 10 of them and label each one: system or application, and proprietary, open source, freeware or freemium. Look up any you are unsure about.

quiz.q: Which of these is system software?
quiz.explain: A device driver helps the operating system control hardware, so it belongs to system software. The others are applications.

quiz.q: Software whose source code anyone can read, change and share under its license is called...
quiz.explain: Open source means the source code is public and can be studied, changed and shared under the license rules.

quiz.q: Adobe Acrobat Reader costs nothing but its code is secret. It is...
quiz.explain: Freeware is free to use but closed source. Free of cost does not mean open source.

quiz.q: Software written specially for one hospital's needs is called...
quiz.explain: Custom or bespoke software is built for one client. Off-the-shelf software is made for many users.

quiz.q: In version 4.2.7, what does the 7 usually mean?
quiz.explain: With major.minor.patch numbering, the last number counts small bug-fix releases.

lessons.title: Operating Systems
lessons.content:
Think about a big school. There are hundreds of students, dozens of teachers, a limited number of classrooms, one playground and one library. Someone has to decide which class uses which room at which time, make sure two classes do not crash into the same room, keep records safe and let only the right people into the office. That someone is the headmaster's office. A computer has the same problem, and its headmaster is the operating system.

What an operating system is: an operating system, or OS, is the system software that manages all the hardware and software of a computer. It does three big things. It controls the hardware so that nobody fights over it. It gives programs a set of ready-made services, so an app does not need to know how to talk to every type of disk or screen. And it gives you, the user, a way to talk to the computer. Without an operating system, every app would have to control the hardware by itself, which would be slow, messy and unsafe.

Where the OS sits: picture the computer as layers. At the bottom is the hardware: CPU, memory, disks and devices. Just above it is the operating system. Above that sit the applications, like your browser and games. At the very top is you. When you press print in a word processor, the app asks the OS, the OS uses the printer driver, and the driver talks to the printer. Each layer only talks to the layer next to it.

Starting the OS: when you press the power button, firmware such as BIOS or UEFI checks the hardware and then loads a small program called the bootloader. The bootloader finds the operating system on the disk and loads its core into RAM. From then on, the OS is in charge. You learned the details of booting in an earlier lesson, so here just remember that the OS is the first big program that runs, and it stays running until you shut down.

Kernel and shell: the kernel is the heart of the operating system. It stays in memory the whole time and directly controls the CPU, memory and devices. The shell is the outer layer that lets the user give commands to the kernel. A shell can be a text window where you type commands, or the graphical desktop you click on. A useful picture is a coconut: the hard kernel inside, and the shell around it that you touch.

Job one, process management: a program sitting on the disk is just a file. When you run it, the OS loads it into memory and it becomes a process, which means a program in action. Your computer may have one CPU with a few cores, but you might be playing music, downloading a file and browsing Facebook at once. The OS gives each process a tiny slice of CPU time, a few milliseconds, then switches to the next one. This switching happens so fast that everything seems to run at the same time. This is called multitasking.

How the OS chooses who runs next: the part of the OS that decides is called the scheduler. In First Come First Served scheduling, processes run in the order they arrive, like a queue at a bank counter. In Round Robin scheduling, each process gets a fixed time slice in turns. Suppose processes A, B and C each need 6 milliseconds and the slice is 2 milliseconds. The CPU runs A for 2, then B for 2, then C for 2, then back to A, and so on, until all three finish after 18 milliseconds. In Priority scheduling, more important processes run first, like an ambulance getting the road before regular cars.

Job two, memory management: RAM is limited, and many processes want it. The OS decides which process gets which part of memory, and it keeps track of free space. It also protects processes from each other, so a buggy game cannot overwrite your unsaved document. When RAM is full, the OS uses virtual memory: it moves parts of memory that are not being used right now onto the disk and brings them back when needed. The common method is paging, where memory is cut into equal blocks called pages. If you open fifty browser tabs and the computer becomes slow, you are watching virtual memory work hard.

Job three, file management: the OS organises data on storage into files and folders. It creates, opens, saves, renames and deletes files, keeps track of where each file lives on the disk, and checks who is allowed to read or change it. Without this, a disk would just be a huge sea of 0s and 1s with no labels. We will study files and file systems properly in a later lesson.

Job four, device management: every keyboard, mouse, printer, speaker and camera is controlled through the OS, which uses drivers to talk to them. The OS also handles input and output in an orderly way. For example, if three people in an office send pages to one printer at the same time, the OS puts the jobs in a queue and prints them one after another. This waiting line is called spooling. That is why you can keep working while your printout is still waiting.

Job five, security and user management: the OS asks for a password, PIN, fingerprint or face before letting you in. It keeps separate accounts so your files stay private from your brother's account on the same computer. It gives normal users limited power and gives the administrator full power, so a random app cannot change important system settings without asking. On phones, the OS asks you before an app can use your camera, microphone or location.

Job six, the user interface: the OS gives you a way to talk to the machine. In a command line interface, or CLI, you type commands. On Windows, typing dir lists the files in a folder, and on Linux the same job is done by ls. A graphical user interface, or GUI, uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer, often shortened to WIMP. Phones use touch interfaces with taps and swipes, and newer systems also accept voice commands. A CLI is powerful and fast for experts, while a GUI is easier for beginners.

Batch operating systems: in the early days of the 1950s and 1960s, people prepared jobs on punch cards and handed them to an operator. The operator grouped similar jobs into batches and ran them one after another without any user sitting at the machine. Monthly salary processing for a big company is a classic batch job even today. The weakness was that you might wait hours just to find out your program had a small mistake.

Multiprogramming and time-sharing: later systems kept several programs in memory at once. When one program waited for slow input or output, the CPU switched to another, so the CPU was not wasted. Time-sharing went further, letting many users sit at terminals and use one big computer at the same time, each getting small slices of CPU time. Unix, born in the early 1970s, was a famous time-sharing system, and many modern systems, including Linux and macOS, follow its ideas.

Real-time operating systems: some systems must respond within a strict time limit, every single time. A car's airbag must open within milliseconds of a crash. A heart pacemaker cannot be late. These use a real-time operating system, or RTOS. In a hard real-time system, missing a deadline is a disaster. In a soft real-time system, like video streaming, missing a deadline only lowers quality, such as a small glitch in the video.

Other types: a network operating system lets computers share files and printers over a network, managed from a server. A distributed operating system makes many computers work together so they look like one big computer to the user. Mobile operating systems such as Android and iOS are designed for touch screens, small batteries and wireless connections, and they control app permissions carefully. Embedded operating systems run inside devices like routers, smart TVs and washing machines.

Single-user and multi-user, single-tasking and multitasking: old MS-DOS could run only one program at a time for one user, so it was single-user and single-tasking. Windows on a personal laptop is usually single-user but multitasking. A Linux server at a university can be multi-user and multitasking, with hundreds of students logged in at once.

The popular operating systems: Microsoft Windows is proprietary and runs on most desktop and laptop computers in the world. Apple's macOS runs on Mac computers and is built on Unix ideas. Linux was started in 1991 by a Finnish student named Linus Torvalds; it is open source and comes in many versions called distributions, such as Ubuntu and Fedora. Linux runs most web servers, and every one of the world's top 500 supercomputers. Android, made by Google, uses the Linux kernel and runs on most smartphones in Bangladesh. Apple's iOS runs on iPhones.

Real life example 1: you are on your Android phone. You open YouTube and start a song, then switch to Facebook while the music keeps playing. A notification pops up from WhatsApp. Behind the scenes, Android's scheduler is giving CPU time to the music, Facebook and WhatsApp in turns. Its memory manager decides to close an old game you opened yesterday because RAM is getting full. When Facebook asks for the camera to post a story, Android stops and asks you for permission first. All of this is the operating system doing its jobs.

Real life example 2: at a Dhaka metro rail station, the gate must read your card and open within a fraction of a second, or a long queue will form behind you. Systems like this need quick, predictable responses, which is the world of real-time and embedded systems. Meanwhile, the bank's central computer that processes all ATM withdrawals at night runs big batch jobs to update records, and its servers are multi-user systems with strict security so that only authorised staff can log in.

Common mistakes and exam questions: an operating system is not the computer itself, and it is not an application. Android is an operating system, not an app. The kernel is only the core of the OS, not the whole OS. The GUI is a part of the OS, not a separate operating system. In exams you will often see: define an operating system and list its functions, differentiate batch, time-sharing and real-time systems, explain process and memory management, compare CLI and GUI, and explain the difference between a program and a process.

Recap: the operating system is the manager of the computer. It runs processes and shares CPU time, manages memory, organises files, controls devices, protects users and gives us an interface. Different jobs need different kinds of operating systems, from batch and time-sharing to real-time, mobile and embedded. Next, we will see how humans write the programs that the operating system runs: programming languages and their translators.
key_points: An operating system manages hardware, gives services to apps and provides a user interface.
The kernel is the core that controls CPU, memory and devices; the shell is how users give commands.
A process is a program in action; the scheduler shares CPU time using methods like FCFS, Round Robin and Priority.
Memory management allocates and protects RAM and uses virtual memory (paging) when RAM is full.
The OS also manages files, devices (with drivers and spooling) and security (accounts, permissions).
Types include batch, time-sharing, real-time (hard and soft), network, distributed, mobile and embedded.
Popular OS: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android (Linux kernel) and iOS.
lessons.tip: Learn the OS functions with one story: a school headmaster who schedules classes (processes), assigns rooms (memory), keeps records (files), manages equipment (devices), checks ID cards (security) and talks to parents (interface).
lessons.task: On a computer, open Task Manager (Windows: Ctrl+Shift+Esc) or Activity Monitor (Mac), or on Android open Settings > Apps. Write down 5 running processes or apps and how much memory each uses. Then close one heavy app and see the change.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a main job of an operating system?
quiz.explain: The OS manages processes, memory, files, devices and security. Writing your content is the job of you and an application.

quiz.q: A car airbag controller needs which type of operating system?
quiz.explain: An airbag must react within a strict deadline every time, so it needs a (hard) real-time operating system.

quiz.q: Which part of the OS stays in memory and directly controls the hardware?
quiz.explain: The kernel is the core of the OS that controls CPU, memory and devices. The shell is the user-facing layer.

quiz.q: In Round Robin scheduling, each process gets...
options: A small fixed time slice, in turns
The CPU until it finishes completely
CPU time based on its file size
quiz.explain: Round Robin gives every process a fixed time slice in turn, then moves to the next process.

quiz.q: Android is built on which kernel?
quiz.explain: Android uses the Linux kernel, with Google's software layers on top.

lessons.title: Programming Languages and Translators
lessons.content:
Imagine you speak only Bangla and you need to give instructions to a worker who understands only Chinese. You have two choices: learn Chinese yourself, which is very hard, or hire a translator. Humans and computers have exactly this problem. The CPU understands only patterns of 0s and 1s. Humans think in words. Programming languages and translators are the bridge between the two. In this lesson you will see the different levels of programming languages and the three kinds of translators that turn them into something a CPU can run.

What a programming language is: a programming language is a formal language for writing instructions that a computer can follow. Like any language, it has grammar and meaning. The grammar is called syntax: the exact rules about which words, symbols and punctuation are allowed and in which order. The meaning is called semantics: what the instruction actually does. In Bangla, a sentence can have perfect grammar and still make no sense. Code is the same. It can have correct syntax but the wrong semantics, and then the program runs but does the wrong thing.

The language ladder: programming languages are usually arranged from low-level to high-level. Low-level languages are close to the hardware, fast and powerful, but hard for humans. High-level languages are close to human thinking, easy to read and write, but they need more translation. People also talk about generations of languages, from the first generation in the 1940s up to the fifth. Let us climb the ladder one step at a time.

Machine language, the first generation: machine language is the CPU's own language, written in binary. For example, on Intel-type processors the bytes 10110000 01100001 mean put the number 97 into a small storage place called the AL register. The CPU can run this directly with no translation, so it is the fastest possible. But imagine writing a whole game like this. One wrong 0 or 1 breaks everything, and finding the mistake is a nightmare. Also, machine code for an Intel chip will not run on an ARM chip in your phone, so it is not portable.

Assembly language, the second generation: assembly language replaces binary with short memory-friendly words called mnemonics. Instead of 10110000 01100001 you write MOV AL, 97. Other common mnemonics are ADD for addition, SUB for subtraction and JMP for jump. Each assembly instruction usually matches one machine instruction. A translator called an assembler converts assembly into machine code. Assembly is still used today where speed and tight control matter, such as small parts of operating systems, device drivers and tiny microcontrollers. You will study it in depth in the Microprocessors course.

High-level languages, the third generation: high-level languages look much more like English and maths. In Python, adding two numbers is just total = a + b. In C, printing a message is printf("Hello"). One line of high-level code may become dozens of machine instructions. Famous examples are C, C++, Java, Python, JavaScript, C#, Go, Kotlin, Swift and Dart. Their biggest advantages are that they are easy to learn, easy to read and fix, and portable: the same Python program can run on Windows, Linux or Mac with very small changes.

Fourth and fifth generation: fourth generation languages let you say what you want instead of how to do it step by step. The most famous is SQL, the language of databases. Writing SELECT name FROM students WHERE gpa > 3.5 asks the database to find every student with GPA above 3.5, without telling it how to search. Report generators and some spreadsheet formula systems are also called 4GL tools. Fifth generation languages, like Prolog, are based on logic: you describe facts and rules, and the computer works out the answer. They were linked with early artificial intelligence research.

Programming styles, or paradigms: languages also differ in how they organise thinking. Procedural programming, as in C, writes a program as a sequence of steps and functions. Object-oriented programming, as in Java and C++, builds programs from objects that hold both data and actions, like a Student object with a name and a calculateGPA action. Functional programming, as in Haskell, builds programs from mathematical functions without changing data. Scripting languages, such as Python and JavaScript, are quick to write and often used to glue things together or run inside a web page. Many modern languages mix several styles.

Why translators are needed: no matter how beautiful your high-level code is, the CPU cannot read it. Every program must be turned into machine code before it runs. The program you write is called source code. The translated result that the CPU runs is called object code or machine code. There are three main kinds of translators: assemblers, compilers and interpreters.

The assembler: an assembler translates assembly language into machine code. Because each assembly instruction maps to about one machine instruction, the assembler's job is fairly direct: it looks up each mnemonic, converts numbers to binary and works out memory addresses for labels.

The compiler: a compiler reads the whole high-level program, checks it for errors, and translates all of it into machine code before running anything. The result is usually saved as an executable file, such as hello.exe on Windows. For example, when you type gcc hello.c -o hello, the GCC compiler turns your C file into a program called hello that you can run again and again without compiling each time. If there are syntax errors, the compiler lists them and refuses to build the program until you fix them. C, C++, Go and Rust are normally compiled.

The interpreter: an interpreter translates and runs the program one line or one statement at a time. It reads line 1, runs it, reads line 2, runs it, and so on. If it finds an error on line 20, the first 19 lines have already run, and it stops at line 20. No separate executable file is produced, so you need the interpreter every time you run the program. Python and JavaScript are usually run this way. Interpreters are great for learning and testing because you see results immediately.

Compiler versus interpreter: a compiled program usually runs faster, because the translation is done once in advance. An interpreted program runs slower because translation happens again during every run. A compiler shows all its errors together after reading the whole program, while an interpreter stops at the first error it meets. A compiler creates an executable you can share without sharing your source code, while an interpreted program usually needs its source code and the interpreter on the user's computer. Compilers need more memory and time during compilation, while interpreters need less upfront.

The hybrid way: many modern languages mix both ideas. Java source code is compiled into bytecode, a middle language that is not tied to any real CPU. Then the Java Virtual Machine, or JVM, on each device runs that bytecode, often using a Just-In-Time or JIT compiler that turns frequently used parts into fast machine code while the program runs. That is how Java achieved its famous promise: write once, run anywhere. Python also quietly compiles your code into bytecode, the .pyc files, before its interpreter runs it.

What happens during compiling: compiling a C program actually involves several steps. The preprocessor handles lines starting with #, such as #include. The compiler turns C into assembly. The assembler turns assembly into object code. Then the linker joins your object code with library code, such as the code behind printf, to make one executable.
