Finally, when you run it, the loader copies it into memory. You will study these phases in detail in the Compiler Design course.

Three kinds of errors: a syntax error breaks the grammar, like forgetting a semicolon in C or misspelling print as prnt in Python. The translator catches it. A runtime error happens while the program runs, like dividing by zero or opening a file that does not exist; the program crashes or shows an error. A logic error is the sneakiest. The program runs without complaining but gives the wrong answer. For example, writing avg = a + b / 2 instead of avg = (a + b) / 2. With a = 10 and b = 20 you get 20 instead of 15, because division happens before addition. No translator can catch this; only careful testing can.

Choosing a language: there is no single best language. For websites, JavaScript runs in every browser. For Android apps, Kotlin and Java are common, for iPhone apps Swift, and Dart with Flutter builds apps for both. For data science and AI, Python is the favourite. For operating systems, games and devices, C, C++ and Rust are popular. Most universities in Bangladesh start CSE students with C, because it teaches how memory and the machine really work.

Libraries and IDEs: programmers rarely write everything from scratch. A library is a collection of ready-made code that you can reuse, such as the C standard library that gives you printf, or Python's math library that gives you sqrt. A framework is a bigger set of libraries with its own structure, such as Flutter for apps or Django for websites. Most programmers write code inside an IDE, an Integrated Development Environment, such as VS Code, Code::Blocks or Android Studio. An IDE combines an editor, the translator, a debugger to run code step by step, and helpful features like colouring keywords and pointing out errors as you type.

Real life example 1: think of an international conference in Dhaka. A live interpreter sits in a booth and translates each sentence into English as the speaker talks. If the speaker says something unclear, the interpreter stops right there. That is an interpreter. Now think of a translator who takes a whole Bangla novel, translates the complete book into English, checks it, and publishes it. Readers just read the finished English book, and they never need the translator again. That is a compiler.

Real life example 2: this very app is built with Flutter, using the Dart language. While the developers are working, Dart runs with a JIT compiler, so a code change appears on the phone in about a second, a feature called hot reload. When the app is released, Dart is compiled ahead of time into ARM machine code, so it starts fast and runs smoothly on your phone. The same language uses both ways of translation for different moments.

Common mistakes and exam questions: HTML and CSS are not programming languages; they are markup and style languages that describe content and design. A compiler does not run your program; it only translates it. An interpreter does not create an exe file. An assembler translates assembly, not C. And a compiler cannot find logic errors. Exam favourites include: differentiate low-level and high-level languages, explain the generations of programming languages, compare a compiler and an interpreter, define assembler, linker and loader, and give examples of syntax, runtime and logic errors.

Recap: computers only understand machine language. Assembly makes it a bit friendlier, and high-level languages make programming human-friendly and portable. Assemblers, compilers and interpreters translate code into machine language, each in its own way, and modern systems often combine them. Next, we step back from code and learn how to plan a solution before writing any code: algorithms, flowcharts and pseudocode.
key_points: Syntax is a language's grammar; semantics is what the code actually means and does.
Machine language (binary) runs directly but is hard and not portable; assembly uses mnemonics like MOV and ADD.
High-level languages (C, Java, Python) are readable and portable; SQL is a 4GL that says what, not how.
An assembler translates assembly; a compiler translates the whole program into an executable first.
An interpreter translates and runs line by line, stopping at the first error and making no executable.
Java compiles to bytecode run by the JVM (with JIT); compiling C involves preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker and loader.
Syntax errors are caught by translators; runtime errors crash during a run; logic errors give wrong answers silently.
lessons.tip: Compare compiler and interpreter with a table of five rows: when translation happens, speed, how errors are shown, output file, and examples. Exams ask this table almost every year.
lessons.task: Open an online Python editor (search 'online python') and type: a = 10, b = 20, print(a + b / 2), then print((a + b) / 2). Notice the logic error. Then remove a bracket to cause a syntax error and read the message the interpreter shows.

quiz.q: Which translator converts the whole program at once and produces an executable file?
quiz.explain: A compiler translates the complete program before running and usually saves an executable.

quiz.q: Mnemonics like MOV and ADD belong to...
quiz.explain: Assembly language uses short words (mnemonics) in place of binary machine instructions.

quiz.q: avg = a + b / 2 runs but gives the wrong average. This is a...
quiz.explain: The program runs without complaint but the formula is wrong (division happens first). That is a logic error.

quiz.q: Java source code is first compiled into...
options: Bytecode that runs on the Java Virtual Machine
quiz.explain: Java compiles to bytecode, which the JVM on each device runs, often with a JIT compiler.

quiz.q: What is a main advantage of high-level languages?
options: They run only on one type of CPU
They are easier to read and write, and portable
quiz.explain: High-level languages are close to human language and can run on different machines after translation.

lessons.title: Problem Solving: Algorithms, Flowcharts and Pseudocode
lessons.content:
Before a builder lays a single brick, an engineer draws a plan. Before a cook starts a new dish, they read the recipe. Programming works the same way. Good programmers do not jump straight into typing code. They first think about the problem and plan the steps on paper. This lesson teaches the three classic planning tools of computer science: algorithms, flowcharts and pseudocode. Once you are good at these, learning any programming language becomes much easier, because you will already know what you want the code to do.

The steps of problem solving: solving a problem with a computer usually follows a path. First, understand the problem: what exactly is being asked? Second, analyse it: what are the inputs, what output is expected, and what rules connect them? Third, design a solution as an algorithm. Fourth, write the code in a programming language. Fifth, test it with different inputs, including tricky ones, and fix bugs. Sixth, document it so others, and your future self, can understand it. Beginners often skip steps one to three, and that is exactly why their code gets stuck.

What an algorithm is: an algorithm is a finite, ordered list of clear steps that solves a problem. The word comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a ninth century Persian mathematician whose books taught step-by-step methods for calculation. A recipe for cha, directions to a friend's house and the method you learned for long division are all algorithms. A computer program is simply an algorithm written in a language the computer can translate.

The five properties of a good algorithm: textbooks list five properties. Input: it takes zero or more inputs. Output: it produces at least one result. Definiteness: every step is clear and has only one meaning; add some sugar is not definite, add two spoons of sugar is. Finiteness: it must finish after a limited number of steps; it cannot run forever. Effectiveness: every step must be simple enough to actually be done, by a person with pen and paper if needed. If you can remember IODFE, you can remember these properties.

A first algorithm, the largest of three numbers: Step 1, start. Step 2, read three numbers A, B and C. Step 3, if A is greater than B and A is greater than C, then the largest is A. Step 4, otherwise, if B is greater than C, the largest is B. Step 5, otherwise, the largest is C. Step 6, print the largest. Step 7, stop. Notice that every step is clear, the steps are in order, and the algorithm always ends.

Three ways to write an algorithm: you can describe an algorithm in plain language, like the numbered steps above. You can draw it as a flowchart, a picture made of shapes and arrows. Or you can write it as pseudocode, which looks like simple code but does not follow any real language's strict rules. Each has its uses, and exams often ask you to write the same algorithm in two of these forms.

Flowchart symbols: a flowchart uses a small set of standard shapes. An oval, also called a terminal, marks start and end. A parallelogram shows input or output, such as read a number or print the result. A rectangle shows a process, such as sum = a + b. A diamond shows a decision with a yes-or-no question, such as is marks at least 40, with two arrows leaving it, one for yes and one for no. Arrows, called flow lines, show the direction the steps follow. A small circle, called a connector, joins parts of a flowchart that continue elsewhere on the page or on another page.

A simple sequence flowchart: to add two numbers, the flowchart goes like this. An oval saying Start. An arrow down to a parallelogram saying Read A, B. An arrow down to a rectangle saying Sum = A + B. An arrow down to a parallelogram saying Print Sum. An arrow down to an oval saying End. This straight line of steps, one after another, is called a sequence. Try drawing it yourself; it takes less than a minute.

The three control structures: in 1966, Corrado Böhm and Giuseppe Jacopini showed that every algorithm can be built from just three building blocks. Sequence means doing steps one after another. Selection means choosing between paths based on a condition, the if-else. Repetition, also called a loop or iteration, means repeating steps while a condition is true. Every program you will ever write, from a calculator to Facebook, is a big combination of these three structures.

Selection example, pass or fail: suppose the pass mark is 40. Start, read marks, then a diamond asks: is marks at least 40? If yes, the arrow goes to a parallelogram saying Print Pass. If no, it goes to one saying Print Fail. Both paths then join and go to End. You can also chain decisions. For a grade, first check marks at least 80 for A+, otherwise check at least 70 for A, otherwise at least 60 for A minus, and so on. In a flowchart this looks like a staircase of diamonds.

Repetition example, sum from 1 to N: we want 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + N. Start, read N, set sum = 0 and i = 1. A diamond asks: is i less than or equal to N? If yes, do sum = sum + i, then i = i + 1, and the arrow goes back up to the diamond. If no, print sum and end. Let us trace it with N = 5. After each round, sum becomes 1, then 3, then 6, then 10, then 15. Now i is 6, which is greater than 5, so the loop stops and prints 15. The arrow going back up is what makes it a loop.

What pseudocode is: pseudocode means fake code. It is a way of writing an algorithm with programming-style structure but in plain words, without worrying about semicolons or exact syntax. There is no single official pseudocode, but common keywords are READ or INPUT, PRINT or OUTPUT, SET, IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF, WHILE ... DO ... ENDWHILE and FOR ... TO ... ENDFOR. Indentation, the empty space at the start of lines, shows which steps belong inside an IF or a loop.

Pseudocode for the largest of three: READ A, B, C. IF A > B AND A > C THEN SET largest = A. ELSE IF B > C THEN SET largest = B. ELSE SET largest = C. ENDIF. PRINT largest. In a notebook, each of those would be on its own line with indentation. Compare it with the plain language version from earlier: same logic, but closer to how code will look, so translating it into C or Python later is almost mechanical.

Dry run with a trace table: a dry run means running an algorithm by hand to check it. Make a small table with one column for each variable. For the largest of three, try A = 7, B = 12, C = 5. Is A greater than B? 7 is not greater than 12, so no. Go to the next check: is B greater than C? 12 is greater than 5, yes. So largest = 12. Print 12. Correct. Now try a tricky case, A = 9, B = 9, C = 3. A is not greater than B, so we check B greater than C, yes, largest = 9. Still correct. Trace tables catch mistakes before you write any code.

More classic examples: to check even or odd, read N; if N mod 2 equals 0, print Even, otherwise print Odd. Mod gives the remainder after division, so 14 mod 2 is 0 and 15 mod 2 is 1. To find the factorial of N, which is 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x N, set fact = 1 and i = 1, and while i is at most N, do fact = fact x i and i = i + 1. Tracing with N = 4 gives fact = 1, 2, 6, 24, so 4 factorial is 24. To search for a name in a list, check each name from the first to the last, and stop when you find it or reach the end. This is called linear search, and you will meet many smarter searches later.

What makes an algorithm good: first, it must be correct for every valid input, not just the easy ones. Second, it should be efficient, meaning it should not waste time or memory. Imagine counting the rice in a 50 kg sack grain by grain, versus weighing it. Both give an answer, but one is far smarter. Third, it should be simple and clear, so others can understand and maintain it. In later courses, you will learn to measure efficiency with something called Big O notation.

Flowchart or pseudocode: flowcharts are visual and great for showing the flow of small algorithms and for explaining logic to non-programmers. But a big program becomes a huge messy web of arrows, and changing it means redrawing. Pseudocode is quicker to write, easier to change, and closer to real code, but less friendly for beginners who think in pictures. Most professionals sketch pseudocode, and use flowcharts for documentation and teaching.

Real life example 1: when you request a ride on Pathao, the app follows an algorithm. Read your pickup location. Find drivers within a certain distance. Sort them by distance. Send the request to the nearest driver. If the driver accepts, show their details to you. If they decline or do not reply in a few seconds, send the request to the next nearest driver. Repeat until someone accepts or the list ends, and if the list ends, tell you no driver is available. Can you see sequence, selection and repetition in that?

Real life example 2: an ATM withdrawal is a perfect flowchart. Start. Insert card. Enter PIN. Decision: is the PIN correct? If no, add 1 to the wrong attempts; if attempts reach 3, keep the card and end, otherwise ask for the PIN again, which is a loop. If yes, enter the amount. Decision: is the balance enough? If no, print insufficient balance. If yes, give the cash, update the balance and print the receipt. End. Bank programmers draw exactly this kind of diagram before writing code.

Common mistakes and exam questions: students often forget the Start and End ovals, use a rectangle for a decision instead of a diamond, or leave a diamond with only one exit arrow. A very common bug is the infinite loop, where the counter is never updated, so i stays 1 forever and the condition never becomes false. Another is writing vague steps like process the data. Exams love to ask: define algorithm and list its properties, draw a flowchart to find the largest of three numbers, draw a flowchart for the sum of a series, write pseudocode for factorial or even-odd checking, and explain the differences between a flowchart and pseudocode.

Recap: problem solving starts with understanding, then planning. An algorithm is a finite list of clear steps, and it can be written in plain language, drawn as a flowchart or written as pseudocode. Every algorithm is built from sequence, selection and repetition. Dry runs with trace tables catch mistakes early. Next, we will look at how computers store all these programs and your data in an organised way: files and file systems.
key_points: Problem solving steps: understand, analyse inputs and outputs, design an algorithm, code, test, document.
An algorithm is a finite, ordered list of clear steps; its properties are input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness.
Flowchart symbols: oval for start/end, parallelogram for input/output, rectangle for process, diamond for decision, arrows for flow.
Every algorithm is built from three control structures: sequence, selection and repetition (Böhm and Jacopini).
Pseudocode uses plain words with code-like structure (IF, WHILE, FOR) and no strict syntax.
A dry run with a trace table checks an algorithm by hand before coding.
A loop whose counter is never updated becomes an infinite loop.
lessons.tip: Practise the five classic exam algorithms until you can draw them without looking: largest of three, sum of 1 to N, factorial, even or odd, and pass or fail grading. Most first-year exams pick from these.
lessons.task: On paper, draw a flowchart and write pseudocode for this: read a student's marks and print A+ for 80 or more, A for 70 to 79, B for 50 to 69, and F below 50. Then do a dry run with marks 85, 72, 50 and 30.

quiz.q: Which flowchart symbol is used for a decision?
quiz.explain: A diamond asks a yes-or-no question and has two exits. Ovals are for start/end, rectangles for processes, parallelograms for input/output.

quiz.q: An algorithm must stop after a limited number of steps. This property is called...
quiz.explain: Finiteness means the algorithm always ends. Definiteness means each step is clear.

quiz.q: Using the loop sum = sum + i for i from 1 to N, what is the sum when N = 4?
quiz.explain: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. (24 would be 4 factorial, which multiplies instead of adds.)

quiz.q: What are the three basic control structures?
quiz.explain: Böhm and Jacopini showed any algorithm can be built from sequence, selection and repetition.

quiz.q: An infinite loop is most often caused by...
options: A counter that is never updated, so the condition never becomes false
Using an oval at the start
quiz.explain: If the loop variable never changes, the loop condition stays true forever.

lessons.title: Files and File Systems
lessons.content:
Walk into an old government office and you might see stacks of paper files tied with red string, piled to the ceiling. When someone asks for a five-year-old land record, a clerk might search for days. Now walk into a well-run library: every book has a number, every shelf has a label, and the catalogue tells you exactly where to go. A computer's storage can be like either of these places. What makes it a library instead of a pile is the idea of files, folders and the file system. That is what this lesson is about.

What a file is: a file is a named collection of related data stored on a storage device. Your CV, a selfie, a song, a video, a C program and even the apps themselves are all files. To the disk, everything is just 0s and 1s. The file gives those bits a name and a boundary, so the computer knows where one piece of data starts and ends and what it is called. When you save something, you are asking the operating system to create or update a file.

File names and extensions: a file name usually has two parts, the name and the extension, separated by a dot. In report.docx, report is the name and docx is the extension. The extension tells the operating system what type of file it is and which program should open it. Common ones are .txt for plain text, .docx for Word documents, .pdf for PDF documents, .jpg and .png for images, .mp3 for music, .mp4 for video, .zip for compressed archives, .c and .py for C and Python source code, .exe for Windows programs and .apk for Android apps.

A warning about hidden extensions: Windows often hides extensions by default. Attackers use this trick by naming a virus photo.jpg.exe. If extensions are hidden, you only see photo.jpg and think it is a picture, but double-clicking it runs a program. That is why many security experts recommend turning on show file extensions in File Explorer. On a phone, an unexpected .apk file sent over chat is a similar red flag.

File attributes and metadata: besides its content, every file carries information about itself, called metadata or attributes. These include its size, the date it was created, the date it was last modified and last opened, its owner, and its permissions. Some files have special flags: read-only means it cannot be changed, and hidden means it does not show up in normal folder views. A photo also stores extra metadata, such as the camera model and sometimes the GPS location where it was taken, which is worth remembering before you post photos online.

Text files and binary files: a text file stores characters only, using a code like ASCII or Unicode, so you can open it in Notepad and read it. Source code, .txt and .csv files are text. A binary file stores data in a format meant for a specific program, such as images, videos, Word documents and executables. If you open a .jpg in Notepad, you will see strange symbols, because those bytes describe pixels, not letters. Neither type is better; they are just made for different jobs.

Folders and the directory tree: a folder, also called a directory, is a container that holds files and other folders. Folders inside folders create a tree shape, upside down. At the top is the root. Below it are branches like Users, Program Files or home. Each folder that contains another is the parent, and the one inside is the child or subfolder. This tree lets millions of files live on one disk without becoming the red-string pile.

Paths: a path is the address of a file in the tree. On Windows a full path looks like C:\Users\Rahim\Documents\cv.docx, with backslashes and a drive letter. On Linux and Mac it looks like /home/rahim/Documents/cv.docx, with forward slashes and a single root written as /. A path that starts from the root is called an absolute path; it works from anywhere. A relative path starts from the folder you are currently in. If you are in Documents, the relative path to cv.docx is just cv.docx. Two dots, .., mean go up one level to the parent, so ../Pictures/photo.jpg means go up, then into Pictures.

Drives and partitions: one physical disk can be divided into separate sections called partitions, each acting like its own disk. Windows gives each one a letter, usually C: for the system and D: for data. Linux and Mac do not use letters; every partition and device, even a USB stick, is attached, or mounted, somewhere inside the single tree that starts at /. A USB drive on Linux might appear at /media/rahim/USB.

What a file system is: a file system is the method and set of rules an operating system uses to store, organise and find files on a storage device. The disk is divided into small fixed-size blocks, often 4 KB each. A file is stored in one or more blocks. The file system keeps a table, like a library catalogue, that records each file's name, its attributes and which blocks hold its data. When you open a file, the OS looks it up in this table and reads those blocks. Formatting a drive means creating a fresh, empty file system on it.

Common file systems: FAT32 is old and simple, and almost every device can read it, but it cannot store a single file bigger than 4 GB. exFAT is the modern choice for pen drives and memory cards, because it handles big files and still works on Windows, Mac, TVs and cameras. NTFS is the main file system for Windows; it supports file permissions, encryption and journaling, which means it keeps a log of changes so it can recover after a power cut. ext4 is the common Linux file system, and APFS is used on modern Apple devices, optimised for SSDs.

How a file is stored: a big file rarely fits in one neat row of blocks. Over time, as files are created, grown and deleted, free space gets scattered, and a new file may be split into pieces in different places. This is called fragmentation. On a hard disk with a moving head, reading scattered pieces is slower, so a defragmenter rearranges them side by side. SSDs have no moving parts, so fragmentation hardly matters and defragmenting only causes extra wear. Instead, SSDs use a command called TRIM to keep themselves fast.

Deleting a file: when you delete a file on Windows or Mac, it first moves to the Recycle Bin or Trash, so you can get it back. Even after you empty the bin, the data is usually not wiped immediately. The file system only marks those blocks as free and removes the entry from its table. Until new data overwrites those blocks, recovery software can often bring the file back. That is great news when you delete something by mistake, but bad news if you sell an old laptop without securely erasing it.

Everyday file operations: the operating system lets you create, open, read, write, save, close, rename, copy, move and delete files. Copy makes a second identical file and keeps the original. Move, or cut and paste, changes where the file lives; within the same drive the data does not even move, only the table entry changes, which is why moving a huge file on one drive is instant. Save As creates a new file with a new name, leaving the old one unchanged.

Permissions: the file system also stores who may do what with each file. The three basic permissions are read, write and execute. On Linux they are shown for three groups, the owner, the group and everyone else. For example, rwxr-xr-- means the owner can read, write and execute, the group can read and execute, and others can only read. Windows uses a similar idea with users and administrators, and Android asks you before an app may read your photos and files.

Organising your own files: good file habits will save you in every semester. Use clear names: CSE101_Assignment2_Rahim.pdf is far better than final_final_really_final2.docx. Put dates in the year-month-day form, like 2026-10-03, so files sort in order. Make a folder for each semester, and inside it one folder for each course. Do not keep everything on the Desktop or in Downloads. When you need to send many files, compress them into one .zip file.

Backups: storage fails. Hard disks crash, phones get stolen and laptops fall. The well-known 3-2-1 backup rule says: keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy somewhere else, off-site, such as in the cloud. For a student, that could mean the original on your laptop, a copy on an external drive, and a copy on Google Drive. Many cloud services also keep older versions, so you can go back to yesterday's draft.

Cloud storage and syncing: services such as Google Drive, OneDrive and Dropbox store your files on their servers. A sync app keeps a folder on your computer matched with the cloud copy, so a change on your laptop appears on your phone. If you edit the same file on two devices while offline, the service may create a conflicted copy, because it cannot decide which version wins. Cloud storage is convenient, but remember that it depends on internet access and on the security of your account.

Real life example 1: Nusrat keeps a folder called University, with subfolders for each semester and inside them one per course. The night before an assignment deadline, her laptop refuses to boot. She panics for a minute, then remembers that her course folders sync to Google Drive. She logs in from her friend's laptop, downloads CSE101_Assignment3_Nusrat.pdf and submits it on Google Classroom on time. Good file organisation and backups turned a disaster into a small story.

Real life example 2: your phone says storage is full. You open the file manager and find the DCIM folder full of camera photos, a WhatsApp folder full of forwarded videos, and old .apk files in Download. You delete duplicates, back up photos to the cloud and move videos to a memory card. When you put a new memory card in, the phone formats it as exFAT, so it can store videos bigger than 4 GB, which an old FAT32 card could not.

Common mistakes and exam questions: renaming a file's extension, such as changing report.docx to report.pdf, does not convert it; the content is still a Word file, and it may stop opening. Deleting does not truly erase data. Copy and move are not the same. A 5 GB file cannot go onto a FAT32 drive no matter how much free space it has. Exams often ask: define file and file system, explain file attributes, differentiate absolute and relative paths, compare FAT32 and NTFS, explain fragmentation, and describe file permissions.

Recap: a file is named data, and its extension hints at its type. Folders form a tree, and paths are addresses in that tree. The file system is the catalogue that maps names to blocks on the disk, and different file systems such as FAT32, exFAT, NTFS, ext4 and APFS make different trade-offs. Deleting only frees space, permissions protect files, and smart naming plus the 3-2-1 backup rule protect your work. Next, we leave the single computer behind and see how computers talk to each other through networks.
key_points: A file is a named collection of data; its extension (.pdf, .jpg, .exe) tells the OS its type and which program opens it.
Folders form a tree from the root; a path is a file's address, absolute from the root or relative from the current folder.
A file system stores files in blocks and keeps a table mapping each file name to its blocks and attributes.
FAT32 cannot hold files over 4 GB; exFAT suits pen drives; NTFS (Windows) adds permissions and journaling; ext4 is Linux; APFS is Apple.
Fragmentation slows hard disks (defragment them); SSDs do not need defragmenting.
Deleting usually only marks space as free, so data can be recovered until it is overwritten.
Permissions (read, write, execute) control access; the 3-2-1 rule keeps backups safe.
lessons.tip: Practise paths by writing the absolute and relative path to five real files on your own computer or phone. Once you can do it without thinking, path questions in exams and later in programming become easy.
lessons.task: On a computer, turn on 'show file extensions' and look at 10 files: write each name, extension and size. Then plug in a pen drive, check its file system (Windows: right-click > Properties) and note whether it could hold a 5 GB file.

quiz.q: What happens if you rename report.docx to report.pdf?
options: Only the name changes; the content is still a Word document
quiz.explain: Changing the extension does not convert the data. Use 'Save as PDF' or a converter to make a real PDF.

quiz.q: A 5 GB movie will not copy to a pen drive that has 16 GB free. The pen drive is most likely formatted as...
quiz.explain: FAT32 cannot store a single file bigger than 4 GB, no matter how much free space there is.

quiz.q: Which of these is an absolute path?
quiz.explain: An absolute path starts from the root or drive (C:\). The others are relative to the current folder.

quiz.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule means...
options: 3 copies, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 off-site
Back up every 3 days, 2 hours, 1 minute
quiz.explain: Keep three copies on two kinds of storage, with one copy somewhere else such as the cloud.

quiz.q: In Linux permissions like rwxr-xr--, what does x mean?
quiz.explain: r is read, w is write and x is execute, meaning the file can be run as a program.

lessons.title: Computer Networks: Connecting Computers Together
lessons.content:
Imagine your whole class had to sit in silence, and nobody could pass a note, share a pen or borrow a book. Everyone would have to buy everything for themselves, and nobody could help anyone. A computer that is not connected to anything is a bit like that student. It can do a lot on its own, but the moment you connect it to other computers, it can share, talk and work together. That connection is what we call a computer network.

What a network is: a computer network is two or more devices connected so they can exchange data and share resources. Each device on the network is called a node. A node can be a laptop, a phone, a printer, a smart TV or even a CCTV camera. The connection between two nodes is called a link, and it can be a cable or a wireless signal. Your home Wi-Fi is a network: your phone, your father's laptop and the smart TV are all nodes talking through the same router.

Why we build networks: the first big reason is resource sharing. An office with 30 computers does not need 30 printers; one shared network printer is enough. The second reason is communication: email, chat and video calls all need a network. Third, data can be kept in one central place, so everyone sees the same up-to-date file instead of 30 different copies. Fourth, networks save money and make backup easier, because important data can be copied to another machine automatically.

The five parts of any communication: every time data moves on a network, five things are involved. There is a sender (the device sending data), a receiver (the device getting it), the message (the data itself, like a photo), the medium (the path it travels on, like a cable or radio waves) and a protocol. A protocol is a set of rules both sides agree on. Think of a phone call: both people must speak the same language and take turns. If one speaks Bangla and the other only Japanese, nothing useful happens. Computers are the same; without shared rules they cannot understand each other.

PAN, the pocket network: networks are often grouped by how much area they cover. The smallest is a Personal Area Network, or PAN. It covers just a few metres around one person. When your Bluetooth earbuds connect to your phone, or your smartwatch syncs with it, that is a PAN.

LAN, the building network: a Local Area Network, or LAN, covers one building or a small group of buildings, like a school computer lab, an office floor or a university campus. LANs are fast, often 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps or more, because the distances are short. Usually one organization owns and manages the whole LAN. Most LANs use Ethernet cables, Wi-Fi or both.

MAN, the city network: a Metropolitan Area Network, or MAN, covers a city or a large town. It usually connects many LANs together. For example, an internet service provider may run fiber cables across Dhaka to link its customers, or a university with campuses in different parts of a city may join them with a MAN. A MAN is bigger and more expensive than a LAN, and it is often run by a company or a city authority.

WAN, the world network: a Wide Area Network, or WAN, covers a country, a continent or the whole world. The Internet itself is the biggest WAN. WANs use long-distance links like fiber lines, microwave towers, satellites and undersea cables. Bangladesh connects to the rest of the world partly through submarine cables: SEA-ME-WE 4 lands at Cox's Bazar and SEA-ME-WE 5 lands at Kuakata. WANs are slower per link than a LAN and much more expensive, and many different organizations share them.

An easy way to remember: PAN is your pocket, LAN is your building, MAN is your city and WAN is the world. As you go from PAN to WAN, the area grows, the cost grows, and usually the speed per connection drops, while the number of owners grows from one person to many companies and countries.

Client-server and peer-to-peer: networks can also be grouped by who serves whom. In a client-server network, some powerful computers called servers store data and provide services, and the other computers, called clients, ask for those services. It is like a restaurant: you, the client, order food, and the kitchen, the server, prepares it. Your university's result website works this way. In a peer-to-peer (P2P) network, every computer is equal and can both give and take. Two friends sharing files directly between their phones is peer-to-peer. P2P is cheap and simple for small groups, but client-server is easier to secure and manage when there are many users.

Topology, the shape of a network: topology means how the nodes are arranged and linked. Physical topology is how the cables or signals actually run, and logical topology is how data actually flows. Different shapes have different strengths, and exam questions love to ask about them, so let us go one by one.

Bus topology: all devices connect to one main cable called the backbone or bus, with a terminator at each end. Data sent by one device travels along the bus and every device sees it, but only the device it is addressed to keeps it. It is cheap and easy for a few computers, like houses along a single road. The problem is that if the main cable breaks, the whole network stops, and when two devices send at once, their signals collide.

Star topology: every device connects with its own cable to a central device, usually a switch. This is the most common layout in modern LANs, including your school lab. If one cable breaks, only that one computer goes offline, and it is easy to add new computers. The weak point is the centre: if the switch fails, everyone loses the network. Think of a class where every student only talks through the teacher. If the teacher leaves, nobody can talk.

Ring topology: each device connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a circle. Data travels around the ring from one node to the next until it reaches its destination. Some rings use a special message called a token: only the node holding the token can send, so there are no collisions. The weakness is that one broken link can stop the whole ring, unless a second ring is added as a backup, which is called a dual ring.

Mesh topology: in a full mesh, every device has a direct link to every other device. It is very reliable, because if one link breaks, data can take another path. But it needs a lot of cable. The number of links in a full mesh of n devices is n(n-1)/2. With 5 devices that is 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 links. With 10 devices it becomes 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 links. That is why full mesh is used only where reliability matters a lot, like the backbone links between big routers. A partial mesh, where only some nodes are interlinked, is more common.

Tree and hybrid topologies: a tree topology is like several stars joined in a hierarchy. A main switch connects to switches on each floor, and each floor switch connects to the computers on that floor. A hybrid topology mixes two or more types. Most real networks are hybrids. A university might use a star in every building and connect the buildings in a tree or a partial mesh.

Network devices, part one: every device that joins a network needs a Network Interface Card (NIC), either a separate card or a chip built into the motherboard. Each NIC has a unique hardware address called a MAC address, 48 bits long and written in hexadecimal like 3C:52:82:1A:9F:07. A hub is an old, simple device that receives data on one port and blindly repeats it to every other port. A switch is smarter: it learns which MAC address is on which port and sends data only to the right one, so the network stays faster and more private.

Network devices, part two: a router connects different networks together, for example your home LAN to your internet provider's network. It reads IP addresses and chooses the best path for each piece of data. A modem (modulator-demodulator) converts the computer's digital signals into a form that can travel over a phone line, cable or fiber, and back again. A repeater boosts a weak signal so it can travel further, and an access point lets wireless devices join a wired network. The box most homes call a "Wi-Fi router" is actually a router, a switch and an access point combined, and sometimes a modem too.

Wired media: the most common cable in a LAN is twisted pair, the Ethernet cable with an RJ45 plug, in categories like Cat5e and Cat6. The wires are twisted to reduce interference. Coaxial cable, with a thick copper core and a metal shield, is the cable that brings cable TV to many homes. Fiber optic cable carries data as pulses of light through thin glass threads. Fiber is extremely fast, works over long distances and is not disturbed by electrical noise or lightning, which is why internet providers in Bangladesh now run fiber (FTTH, fiber to the home) right into apartments.

Wireless media: wireless networks send data through the air using radio waves, microwaves or infrared. Wi-Fi uses radio waves, usually in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands; 2.4 GHz reaches further through walls, while 5 GHz is faster but shorter range. Bluetooth is for short-range devices. Mobile networks like 4G and 5G cover whole countries using towers. Microwave links connect towers in a straight line of sight, satellites cover remote areas, and infrared is used in your TV remote. Wired links are usually faster, more stable and more secure; wireless links give freedom to move and are easier to set up.

Bandwidth and speed: network speed is measured in bits per second. 1 Mbps means one million bits per second. Be careful: internet speeds use small b (bits), but file sizes use capital B (bytes), and 1 byte = 8 bits. So a 100 Mbps connection can move about 100 / 8 = 12.5 megabytes per second at best. Worked example: how long does a 500 MB file take on a 20 Mbps line? 500 MB x 8 = 4000 megabits, and 4000 / 20 = 200 seconds, so about 3 minutes and 20 seconds, if nothing else slows it down.

Transmission modes: simplex means data flows in only one direction, like a TV broadcast or a keyboard sending keys to the computer. Half duplex means both sides can send, but only one at a time, like a walkie-talkie where you say "over". Full duplex means both sides send and receive at the same time, like a normal phone call where both people can talk together.

A peek at layers: real networks split the job into layers, each with its own task. Sending a letter is a good picture: you write the letter, put it in an envelope with an address, the post office sorts it, and a truck carries it. Network models like OSI, with 7 layers, and TCP/IP, with 4 layers, work the same way. You will study them in detail in the Computer Networks course; for now, just remember that each layer does one part of the job and passes the data to the next.

Real-life example 1, your home internet in Dhaka: your internet provider runs a fiber cable to your building. In your flat, the fiber goes into a small box that converts light to electrical signals, and then into your Wi-Fi router. Your phone, laptop and TV connect to the router, forming a small star-shaped LAN. When you open YouTube, your phone sends a request to the router, the router forwards it to the provider's network, which is part of the city's MAN, and from there it goes out over the WAN, maybe through the undersea cable, to a server. The video comes back the same way, all in a fraction of a second.

Real-life example 2, a bank across Bangladesh: a bank has branches and ATMs in Sylhet, Khulna, Rajshahi and Dhaka. Each branch has its own LAN. All branches connect to the bank's central data centre through a secure WAN. When you withdraw money from an ATM in Sylhet, the ATM sends your card details over the WAN to the central server, the server checks your balance, approves the withdrawal and updates your account. That is why your balance is correct in every branch at the same time.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: students often mix up the hub, the switch and the router. Remember: a hub shouts to everyone, a switch whispers to the right person inside one network, and a router connects different networks. Another classic mistake is confusing Mbps with MBps. Exams often ask you to compare LAN, MAN and WAN, to draw bus, star, ring and mesh topologies with their advantages and disadvantages, to calculate the links in a mesh, to name transmission media, and to explain simplex, half duplex and full duplex with examples.

Quick recap: a network connects devices so they can share data and resources, following protocols. By size we have PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN. By role we have client-server and peer-to-peer. Topologies such as bus, star, ring, mesh, tree and hybrid describe the layout. NICs, switches, routers and modems are the building blocks, and cables or wireless signals are the roads. In the next lesson, we will ride these roads all the way to the biggest network of all, the Internet.
key_points: A computer network connects two or more devices so they can share data and resources using agreed rules called protocols.
By size: PAN (pocket), LAN (building), MAN (city) and WAN (world); the Internet is the biggest WAN.
Client-server networks have servers that provide services to clients; in peer-to-peer every computer is equal.
Topologies: bus, star, ring, mesh, tree and hybrid; star is the most common in modern LANs.
A full mesh of n devices needs n(n-1)/2 links.
A hub repeats data to all ports, a switch sends it to the right device, and a router connects different networks.
Media can be wired (twisted pair, coaxial, fiber) or wireless (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile, satellite).
Speed is in bits per second; divide by 8 to get bytes per second.
lessons.tip: Draw every topology yourself with small circles and lines, then imagine cutting one line or removing the centre. Seeing what breaks is the fastest way to remember the advantages and disadvantages.
lessons.task: Look at the network at your home, school or office. List every device connected to it, find the router, and decide which topology it uses. Then check one device's MAC address in its Wi-Fi or "About" settings and write it down.

quiz.q: Which type of network usually covers a single building, like a school computer lab?
quiz.explain: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers one building or a small campus and is usually owned by one organization.

quiz.q: In a star topology, what happens if the central switch stops working?
options: Data starts travelling around a ring
quiz.explain: Every device in a star connects through the centre, so if the switch fails, no device can reach any other.

quiz.q: How many links does a full mesh of 5 devices need?
quiz.explain: A full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links, so 5 x 4 / 2 = 10.

quiz.q: Which device connects different networks and chooses paths using IP addresses?
quiz.explain: A router joins different networks, like your home LAN and your provider's network, and picks a path for each packet.

quiz.q: A walkie-talkie, where only one person can talk at a time, is an example of which mode?
quiz.explain: In half duplex both sides can send, but only one at a time. Full duplex, like a phone call, lets both talk together.

lessons.title: The Internet and the Web
lessons.content:
Type "Bangladesh cricket score" into your phone, and in less than a second the answer appears. The data might have come from a server in Singapore, in the USA, or in a data centre just outside Dhaka. It crossed cables, towers and maybe the seabed, and came back to your hand before you could blink. That everyday magic is the Internet, and in this lesson we will open the box and see how it works.

What the Internet is: the Internet is a global network of networks. Millions of separate networks, belonging to homes, universities, companies, mobile operators and governments, are joined together so that any device can reach any other device. No single person or company owns the Internet. Each part is run by its owner, and they all agree to follow the same rules, called the TCP/IP protocols. Companies that connect you to the Internet are called Internet Service Providers, or ISPs. Your mobile operator and your home broadband company are both ISPs.

A short history: in 1969 the US built ARPANET, a research network that first linked four university computers. On 1 January 1983 ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, and that common language let many networks join into one big Internet. In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN in Switzerland, invented the World Wide Web, which made the Internet easy for ordinary people with clickable pages and links. Bangladesh got online in 1996 through satellite (VSAT) links, which were slow and costly. In 2006 the country joined the SEA-ME-WE 4 submarine cable, and speeds and prices got much better.

The Internet is not the Web: this is the most common confusion of all. The Internet is the infrastructure, like a country's road network. The World Wide Web is one service that runs on top of it, like the shops you can reach by those roads. Web pages travel on the Internet, but so do many things that are not the Web: email, WhatsApp and IMO calls, online games, and file transfers. So every web page uses the Internet, but not everything on the Internet is the Web.

Packets, the Internet's parcels: the Internet does not send a big file in one piece. It breaks the data into small chunks called packets. Each packet carries a piece of the data plus a header with the sender's address, the receiver's address and a sequence number. Packets may take different paths through different routers, and they can arrive out of order. The receiving computer uses the numbers to put them back together. Imagine posting a big book to a friend one chapter at a time, each chapter in its own numbered envelope. Even if chapter 7 arrives before chapter 3, your friend can sort them into the right order.

TCP and IP, the two partners: IP, the Internet Protocol, is responsible for addressing and moving packets from one computer to another, hop by hop through routers. IP does its best, but it does not promise that every packet arrives. TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, works on top of IP. It numbers the packets, checks that every one arrived, asks for missing ones to be sent again and delivers them in the right order. For things where speed matters more than perfection, like live video calls or online games, a lighter protocol called UDP is used. It sends packets without checking, because an old packet that arrives late is useless anyway.

IP addresses: every device on the Internet needs an address, just like every house needs one for the postman. An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, written as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, like 192.168.0.1. With 32 bits there are 2^32, about 4.3 billion, possible addresses, and the world has more devices than that. So a newer version, IPv6, uses 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal, like 2001:db8::1, which gives an almost endless supply. Your home router usually gives your devices private addresses such as 192.168.0.x, and they all share one public address on the Internet using a trick called NAT (Network Address Translation).

Domain names and DNS: numbers are hard for people to remember, so websites have names like www.example.com. The Domain Name System (DNS) works like a phonebook that turns names into IP addresses. When you type a web address, your device first asks a DNS server, "What is the IP address of this name?" The DNS server answers, and only then does your browser connect to that address. Domain names are read from right to left: in www.example.com, ".com" is the top-level domain, "example" is the name the owner registered, and "www" is a part inside it. Common top-level domains are .com, .org, .edu, .gov and country codes like .bd. Bangladeshi sites often end in .com.bd, .gov.bd or .edu.bd.

Reading a URL: a URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the full address of something on the web. Take https://www.example.com/books/page.html?id=5. The part "https" is the protocol, "www.example.com" is the domain, "/books/page.html" is the path to the exact page on that server, and "?id=5" is a query that passes extra information, like which book to show.

The client-server model: on the web, your browser is the client and the computer that stores the website is the web server. The client sends a request and the server sends a response. It is like ordering at a restaurant: you ask the waiter for kacchi biryani (request), and the kitchen sends the plate (response). One web server can serve thousands of clients at the same time.

HTTP, the language of the web: browsers and web servers talk using HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol. The most common requests are GET, which asks for a page or file, and POST, which sends data to the server, like a filled-in form. Every response comes with a status code. 200 means OK, everything worked. 301 means the page has moved to a new address. 404 means the page was not found. 500 means something went wrong on the server. Next time you see "404", you will know exactly what the server is saying.

HTTPS and the padlock: plain HTTP sends everything as readable text, so someone on the same public Wi-Fi could read it. HTTPS adds encryption using TLS, so the data is scrambled for anyone except you and the server. Browsers show a padlock for HTTPS sites. Always check for HTTPS before typing a password, a card number or a bKash PIN. But remember: HTTPS only means the connection is private. It does not prove that the website itself is honest. A fake site can have a padlock too.

What a web page is made of: a web page is built with three languages. HTML gives the structure: headings, paragraphs, images and links. CSS gives the look: colours, fonts and layout. JavaScript gives the behaviour: buttons that react, menus that open and live updates. Static pages show the same content to everyone, like a simple school notice page. Dynamic pages are built on the fly for each user, like your Facebook feed, which is different from your friend's.

Browsers: a web browser such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari or Edge is the program that fetches web pages and draws them on your screen. It sends the HTTP request, receives HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and then renders the page. Browsers keep a cache, a store of recently used files, so pages load faster the second time. Websites can also store small pieces of data in your browser called cookies, for example to remember that you are logged in or what is in your cart.

Email: an email address has two parts, a user name and a domain, joined by @, like rahim@example.com. When you send an email, your email program uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) to pass it to your mail server, which passes it on to the receiver's mail server. The receiver reads it using IMAP or POP3. IMAP keeps mail on the server, so your phone and laptop stay in sync; POP3 usually downloads mail to one device. "To" is the main receiver, "CC" sends a visible copy to others, and "BCC" sends a hidden copy that other receivers cannot see.

Search engines: a search engine like Google or Bing works in three steps. First, programs called crawlers visit billions of pages by following links. Second, the content is stored in a huge index, like the index at the back of a textbook that tells you which page mentions which word. Third, when you search, the engine ranks the matching pages by how relevant and trustworthy they seem. Tips: put words in quotes to search an exact phrase, use a minus sign to exclude a word, and type site:gov.bd to search only Bangladeshi government sites.

Other Internet services: besides the web and email, the Internet carries video streaming (YouTube), voice and video calls (VoIP, like WhatsApp calls), cloud storage (Google Drive), online banking and mobile financial services, e-commerce, social media, online games and FTP for transferring files. They all use the same basic Internet, but each has its own protocols.

Ways to connect: years ago people used dial-up over phone lines, which was very slow. Today we use broadband: cable, ADSL and especially fiber to the home. Mobile data (3G, 4G and 5G) connects phones through towers, and satellite internet reaches remote places like islands and hills. Remember that Wi-Fi is only the short wireless link between your device and your router. If the router's connection to the ISP is down, you can be connected to Wi-Fi and still have no Internet.

Intranet and extranet: an intranet is a private network inside an organization that uses the same web technology as the Internet, but only members can use it, like a company's internal portal for leave applications and notices. An extranet is part of an intranet that is opened, with a login, to selected outsiders like suppliers or partners.

Real-life example 1, ordering on Daraz: you type the address. DNS finds the server's IP address. Your browser opens an HTTPS connection and sends a GET request for the home page. The server builds a dynamic page with products picked for you, and your browser renders it. When you press "Place order", your browser sends a POST request with your order. The server saves it in a database, talks to a payment gateway if you pay online, and then sends you a confirmation by SMS and email. Dozens of packets went back and forth, all in a few seconds.

Real-life example 2, watching a live cricket match: when you stream a BPL match, the video is split into small chunks of a few seconds each. Streaming companies keep copies on content delivery network (CDN) servers close to you, maybe inside Bangladesh, so the data does not have to cross the ocean for every viewer. If your connection gets slow, the player automatically switches from 1080p to 480p so the match keeps playing. That short wait while chunks load is called buffering.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: do not say the Internet and the Web are the same. Do not think Wi-Fi is the Internet. Do not believe that HTTPS means a site is safe to trust. Do not mix up an IP address, which can change and is used for routing, with a MAC address, which is fixed to the network card. Exams love full forms: WWW, HTTP, HTTPS, URL, DNS, ISP, TCP/IP, SMTP, IMAP and FTP. They also ask you to label the parts of a URL, compare IPv4 and IPv6, explain how DNS works, and tell the difference between the Internet, an intranet and an extranet.

Quick recap: the Internet is a global network of networks that sends data in packets using TCP/IP. Devices are found by IP addresses, and DNS turns names into those addresses. The Web is one service on the Internet, made of pages built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, fetched by browsers using HTTP or HTTPS. Email, search engines and streaming are other services riding the same roads. Next, we will look at what all this data actually is and how organizations store it in databases.
key_points: The Internet is a global network of networks; the World Wide Web is just one service that runs on it.
Data travels in small packets; IP delivers them and TCP makes sure they all arrive in order.
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits (about 4.3 billion addresses); IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.
DNS works like a phonebook that turns domain names into IP addresses.
A URL has a protocol, a domain, a path and sometimes a query.
HTTP status codes: 200 OK, 301 moved, 404 not found, 500 server error.
HTTPS encrypts the connection, but it does not prove a website is honest.
Email uses SMTP to send and IMAP or POP3 to receive.
lessons.tip: Learn the full forms and the one-line job of each protocol together, like "DNS: Domain Name System, turns names into IP addresses". Making a small flash card for each one works really well for exams.
lessons.task: Open any website on your phone or computer and tap the address bar. Write down the full URL and label its protocol, domain, path and query. Then type a made-up page on the same site (like /abcxyz) and note the error message and status code you see.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly describes the Internet and the Web?
options: They are exactly the same thing
The Internet is the global network, and the Web is one service that runs on it
The Web is the hardware and the Internet is the pages
The Internet can only carry email
quiz.explain: The Internet is the infrastructure. The Web, email, video calls and games are services that use it.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns domain names into IP addresses
quiz.explain: DNS is like a phonebook for the Internet. It finds the IP address for a name like www.example.com.

quiz.q: How many bits long is an IPv4 address?
quiz.explain: IPv4 uses 32 bits, which allows about 4.3 billion addresses. IPv6 uses 128 bits.

quiz.q: What does the HTTP status code 404 mean?
quiz.explain: 404 means the server could not find the requested page. 200 means OK and 500 means a server error.

quiz.q: Which protocol is used to send email from your mail program to the mail server?
quiz.explain: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends email. IMAP or POP3 is used to receive it.

lessons.title: Data, Databases and Information Systems
lessons.content:
Picture the office of an old school. Shelves are packed with thick registers: admission books, fee books, result books, one for every year. Now the headmaster asks, "What was Rahim's math result in 2015, and has he paid all his fees?" Someone has to find two different registers, flip through hundreds of pages and hope nothing was written wrongly. With a database, the same answer takes one second. This lesson is about how computers store, organize and use data so we can get answers like that.

Data versus information: data means raw facts with no meaning on their own. "78", "85", "Rahim" and "2015" are data. Information is data that has been processed so it means something useful: "Rahim's average in 2015 was 81.5, so he passed with an A." When information is understood and used to make decisions, like "Rahim is good at math, so he should try the math olympiad", it becomes knowledge. A simple way to remember: data is the rice and lentils, information is the cooked khichuri.

The data processing cycle: turning data into information follows the same input-process-output idea you learned at the start of this course. First data is collected, for example marks from teachers. Then it is input into the computer. Then it is processed: sorted, added, averaged and compared. Then the result is output as a report or a screen. Finally, it is stored so it can be used again next time. Collection, input, processing, output and storage: five steps that happen in every system, from a school to a stock exchange.

Good information: information is only useful if it is accurate, timely, complete, relevant and easy to understand. A result sheet that comes out six months late is not timely. A bank statement that misses half your transactions is not complete. Computer people have a famous saying for this: "Garbage in, garbage out", or GIGO. If you type in wrong data, even the best computer will give you wrong answers.

Types of data: computers store many types of data. Numbers (like marks or prices), text (like names and addresses), dates and times, true/false values (like "fee paid: yes"), and multimedia such as photos, audio and video. Data can also be structured or unstructured. Structured data fits neatly into rows and columns, like a mark sheet. Unstructured data does not, like WhatsApp voice messages, photos or a long essay. Today most of the world's data is unstructured, which is one reason why big data and AI have become so important.

The data hierarchy: data is organized in levels, from small to big. A bit is a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte, which can store one character like "A". Characters together make a field, which is one piece of information such as a roll number or a name. A group of related fields makes a record, such as all the details of one student. Many records of the same kind make a file or table, such as all students of a school. A collection of related tables makes a database. So: bit, byte, field, record, table, database.

The trouble with plain files: before databases, each department kept its own files. The library kept student addresses, and the accounts office kept them again. This caused problems. Redundancy means the same data is stored many times, wasting space. Inconsistency happens when the address is changed in one file but not in the other, so nobody knows which is right. Searching across files is slow, it is hard to control who can see what, and two people cannot easily work on the same data at the same time.

Databases and DBMS: a database is an organized collection of related data, stored so it can be easily searched and updated. A Database Management System, or DBMS, is the software that creates the database, stores the data, answers questions about it and protects it. Popular DBMS software includes MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, Microsoft Access and SQLite. SQLite is tiny and lives inside millions of phone apps; the app you are using right now stores its lessons in an SQLite database.

Why a DBMS helps: a DBMS reduces redundancy because each fact is stored in one place. That also keeps data consistent. It provides security, so a teacher can enter marks but a student can only view them. It handles backup and recovery, so data survives a crash. It allows concurrent access, meaning many users at the same time, and it enforces integrity rules, such as "marks must be between 0 and 100".

Tables, rows and columns: most databases you will meet are relational databases, which store data in tables. Each column is a field, also called an attribute, like Roll, Name, Class and GPA. Each row is a record, also called a tuple, holding one student's values, like 101, Rahim, 10, 4.75. A second row might be 102, Karima, 10, 5.00. Every row in a table has the same columns, which makes searching and sorting easy.

Keys: a primary key is a field whose value is unique for every record, so it can identify that record exactly. A student ID or roll number works well. A name does not, because there can be two students called Rahim. In Bangladesh, an NID number is a good example of a unique key for citizens. A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. For example, a Results table can have a StudentID column that points to the Students table, which links each result to the right student. When a key is made of two or more fields together, like StudentID plus CourseCode, it is called a composite key.

Relationships: tables are connected by relationships. One-to-one: each person has exactly one NID, and each NID belongs to one person. One-to-many: one class has many students, but each student is in one class. Many-to-many: one student takes many courses, and each course has many students. A many-to-many relationship is stored using a third linking table, for example an Enrolment table with StudentID and CourseCode.

SQL, talking to a database: most relational databases understand SQL, the Structured Query Language. It reads almost like English. To find top students: SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE GPA > 4.5; To add a student: INSERT INTO Students VALUES (103, 'Tanvir', 10, 4.20); To change data you use UPDATE, and to remove it you use DELETE. You will learn SQL properly in the Database Management Systems course, but you can already see how simple the idea is.

Other kinds of databases: not all data fits nicely into tables. NoSQL databases store data in other shapes, like documents (MongoDB stores JSON-like documents), key-value pairs or graphs of connections. Social media sites use them for huge amounts of flexible data such as posts, comments and likes. Many databases now run in the cloud, so a company does not need to buy its own servers.

People around a database: a database administrator (DBA) designs, secures, backs up and tunes the database. Application developers write the programs, like websites and apps, that use the database. End users, like teachers, bank officers or customers, use those programs, often without knowing a database is behind them.

Information systems: an information system is a combination of hardware, software, data, procedures and people that work together to collect, process, store and share information. A transaction processing system (TPS) records everyday transactions, like each sale at a shop counter. A management information system (MIS) turns those records into regular reports for managers. A decision support system (DSS) helps answer "what if" questions, like "what if we cut prices by 10%?" Executive systems give top leaders a quick summary, and expert systems give advice using rules collected from human experts. You will meet these again in the MIS course.

Information systems in Bangladesh: the Election Commission's NID database stores data for over a hundred million citizens and is used by banks, mobile operators and passport offices to verify identity. The e-passport system, BRTA's vehicle registration, online university admission, the national birth registration system and hospital management systems are all information systems built on databases.

Bigger ideas: a data warehouse collects years of data from many systems into one place for analysis. Data mining searches that data for hidden patterns, like "customers who buy nappies often buy baby wipes too". Big data refers to data so large, fast or varied that ordinary tools cannot handle it, like all the posts on Facebook in one day.

Keeping data safe and correct: data is valuable, so it must be protected. Regular backups protect against crashes and ransomware. Access control makes sure people only see what they are allowed to see. Validation checks catch mistakes at input time, such as a phone number with only 9 digits. And privacy rules mean organizations should collect only the data they need and keep personal information safe.

Real-life example 1, a library system: a library database has a Books table (BookID, Title, Author), a Members table (MemberID, Name, Phone) and a Loans table (LoanID, BookID, MemberID, IssueDate, DueDate). When you borrow a book, the librarian scans your card and the book, and the system adds one row to Loans. The BookID and MemberID in that row are foreign keys. At the end of the day, one query lists every loan whose DueDate has passed, and the system sends SMS reminders. No register, no flipping pages.

Real-life example 2, a bKash transfer: when you send 500 taka to a friend, the system records a transaction with an ID, the time, the two account numbers and the amount. It must take 500 from your balance and add 500 to your friend's balance as one single unit called a transaction. If the power fails halfway, the database rolls everything back, so money is never taken from you without reaching your friend. This all-or-nothing rule is one of the most important ideas in databases.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: students often mix up data and information, so always give an example of each. Do not confuse the database (the data itself) with the DBMS (the software). Remember that a field is a column and a record is a row. Exams often ask you to define data, information and knowledge; write the data hierarchy; list the problems of the file system and the advantages of a DBMS; explain primary and foreign keys with an example; and describe types of information systems.

Quick recap: data is raw facts; information is processed, meaningful data. Data moves through collection, input, processing, output and storage, and is organized from bits up to databases. A DBMS stores data in tables of rows and columns, linked by primary and foreign keys, and we talk to it using SQL. Information systems combine people, procedures, data, software and hardware to help organizations work. Next, we will learn how to keep all these systems and data safe from attackers.
key_points: Data is raw facts; information is processed data that has meaning and is useful.
The data processing cycle: collection, input, processing, output and storage.
Data hierarchy: bit, byte, field, record, table (file), database.
File-based systems suffer from redundancy and inconsistency; a DBMS solves these problems.
In a table, columns are fields and rows are records.
A primary key uniquely identifies a record; a foreign key links to another table's primary key.
SQL is the language used to query relational databases.
Information systems (TPS, MIS, DSS) combine people, procedures, data, software and hardware.
lessons.tip: Whenever you study a database idea, imagine it using your own school or university: students, classes, courses and results. Building the example in your head makes keys and relationships easy to remember.
lessons.task: On paper, design a tiny database for your class with two tables: Students (Roll, Name, Phone) and Marks (Roll, Subject, Mark). Fill in 4 students and 8 marks. Mark the primary key in Students and the foreign key in Marks, then work out each student's average by hand.

quiz.q: Which of these is information rather than raw data?
options: Rahim's average mark is 81.5, so he passed
quiz.explain: Information is processed data with meaning. A single number or name on its own is just data.

quiz.q: Which field is the best primary key for a Students table?
quiz.explain: A primary key must be unique for every record. Two students can share a name, but each has their own ID.

quiz.q: A column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table is called a...
quiz.explain: A foreign key links records across tables, like StudentID in a Results table pointing to the Students table.

quiz.q: An address is stored in two departments' files but updated in only one. What problem is this?
quiz.explain: When copies of the same data disagree, the data becomes inconsistent. A DBMS avoids this by storing each fact once.

quiz.q: Which one of these is a DBMS?
quiz.explain: MySQL is database management software. The others are an image editor, a browser and a media player.

lessons.title: Computer Security: Staying Safe
lessons.content:
Every house has a lock on the door, and most people would never leave their wallet on a bench in a busy bazar. Yet many of us carry our photos, chats, bank details, bKash account and passwords in a phone with a four-digit PIN like 1234. Thieves have noticed. In this lesson you will learn what dangers exist in the digital world, how attackers think, and the simple habits that keep you, your data and your money safe.

What computer security means: computer security, also called cyber security, is the protection of computers, networks, programs and data from theft, damage and unauthorized access. It covers hardware, like stopping someone stealing a laptop, and software and data, like stopping someone reading your messages. Security is not one tool you install once. It is a mix of technology, rules and good habits.

The CIA triad: security experts describe their goals with three letters, CIA. Confidentiality means only the right people can see the data; your exam results should not be visible to the whole world. Integrity means data is not changed without permission; nobody should be able to secretly change your marks from 45 to 85, or your balance from 5000 to 50. Availability means the system works when you need it; a bank app that is down on payday is a security failure too.

Threat, vulnerability, risk: a vulnerability is a weakness, like an open window. A threat is something that could use that weakness, like a thief walking past. An attack is when the thief actually climbs in. Risk is how likely that is and how much damage it would do. Security work means finding open windows (vulnerabilities), closing the most dangerous ones first and watching for thieves.

Malware: malware is short for malicious software, meaning programs written to harm you. There are many kinds, and exams love to ask you to tell them apart, so let us meet them one by one.

Virus: a computer virus attaches itself to a normal file or program. When you run that file, the virus runs too, copies itself into other files and may delete or damage data. Like a flu virus, it needs a host and spreads through contact, such as sharing an infected pen drive. The key point: a virus needs a person to run the infected file.

Worm: a worm is a program that spreads by itself across networks without anyone opening a file. It finds a weakness in other computers and copies itself onto them, again and again. Because it does not need human help, a worm can spread around the world in hours. In 2017 the WannaCry attack used worm behaviour to spread to hundreds of thousands of computers in about 150 countries.

Trojan horse: in the old Greek story, soldiers hid inside a giant wooden horse given as a gift, and once inside the city they opened the gates. A Trojan horse in computing is a program that looks useful, like a free game, a cracked copy of paid software or a "battery saver" app, but secretly does something harmful, like stealing passwords or opening a back door for attackers. Unlike a virus, it does not copy itself; it tricks you into installing it.

Ransomware: ransomware locks your files by encrypting them and then demands money, usually in cryptocurrency, to unlock them. WannaCry was ransomware; it hit hospitals in the UK, forcing some to cancel appointments. Paying is risky, because there is no guarantee you will get your files back. The best protection is to keep backups, so you can restore your files without paying anyone.

More nasty software: spyware secretly watches what you do and sends it to someone else. A keylogger records every key you press, including passwords. Adware floods you with unwanted ads. A rootkit hides deep in the system so other malware cannot be found. A botnet is a large group of infected computers, called bots or zombies, controlled by one attacker and used together for spam or attacks.

Phishing and social engineering: often the easiest way to break into a system is to trick the person using it. This is called social engineering. Phishing means fake messages that pretend to come from a trusted source to steal your information. Smishing is phishing by SMS, and vishing is by voice call. A classic Bangladeshi example: "Your bKash account will be blocked. Call this number and tell us the OTP to keep it active." Remember: bKash, Nagad, banks and the government never ask for your PIN or OTP. Fake links also use names that look real, like bkash-offer-gift.xyz. Always check the exact address.

Other attacks: in a brute-force attack, a program tries millions of passwords until one works. In a man-in-the-middle attack, someone on the same public Wi-Fi secretly reads or changes your traffic. A denial-of-service (DoS) attack floods a website with fake requests so real users cannot get in; when a botnet does it from thousands of machines, it is called DDoS. SQL injection is when an attacker types special database commands into a website form to read or change data. And shoulder surfing is simply watching someone type their PIN.

Strong passwords: length matters more than fancy symbols. Let us do the math. A password of 8 small letters has 26^8 combinations, about 209 billion; a fast computer can try them all fairly quickly. A password of 12 small letters has 26^12, about 95 quadrillion (9.5 x 10^16), which is over 450,000 times more. A passphrase like "purple-tiger-rides-a-rickshaw" is long, easy for you to remember and very hard to guess. Never reuse the same password on different sites, because when one site is hacked, attackers try that password everywhere. A password manager can remember strong, different passwords for you.

Two-factor authentication: authentication means proving who you are. It can use something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (your phone or a security key) or something you are (fingerprint or face). Two-factor authentication (2FA) uses two of these together. Even if a thief steals your password, they still need the OTP code sent to your phone. Turn on 2FA for email, Facebook and banking.
