Also learn one more word: authorization is what you are allowed to do after you log in, like a student who can view marks but cannot edit them.

Encryption: encryption scrambles data so only someone with the right key can read it. Readable data is called plaintext and scrambled data is called ciphertext. One of the oldest methods is the Caesar cipher, which shifts each letter by a fixed number. With a shift of 3, A becomes D, B becomes E, and so on, so HELLO becomes KHOOR. Modern encryption uses complex math and very long keys. In symmetric encryption both sides use the same key. In asymmetric (public key) encryption there is a public key anyone can use to lock a message and a private key only the owner can use to unlock it. HTTPS, WhatsApp messages and bank apps all use encryption.

Tools that protect you: antivirus software scans files and stops known malware. A firewall works like a guard at a gate, checking network traffic and blocking what is not allowed. Updates and patches fix security holes that companies discover, so always update your phone, computer and apps. Backups save copies of your data; a well-known rule is 3-2-1: keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy kept somewhere else, like in the cloud.

Safe habits online: check that a website uses HTTPS and that the address is spelled correctly. Do not download cracked software or apps from unknown sources. Check what permissions an app asks for; a torch app does not need your contacts. Be careful on public Wi-Fi and avoid logging into your bank there. Lock your phone with a strong PIN or fingerprint, log out of shared computers, and do not plug unknown pen drives into your laptop.

Privacy and your digital footprint: everything you post, like, search and share leaves a trail called your digital footprint. Photos with your school uniform, home location or daily routine can help strangers find you. Turn off location sharing you do not need, keep your accounts private, and think before posting: once something is online, it can be copied forever. If you are bullied or threatened online, do not reply; take screenshots, block the person, tell a trusted adult and report it.

The law: in Bangladesh, as in most countries, hacking, online fraud, identity theft and cyberbullying are crimes under the country's cyber security laws. The police have cyber crime units where victims can report, and the national emergency number 999 can also help in serious cases. Organizations like the government's computer incident response team help protect important national systems.

Real-life example 1, the OTP scam: Shila gets a call: "I am calling from your mobile banking company. Someone sent 10,000 taka to your account by mistake. You will receive a code; please tell it to me so we can reverse it." The code is actually an OTP to reset her own account. If she shares it, the scammer takes control and empties her balance. What she should do: hang up, never share the OTP, check her real balance in the official app and call the official helpline number printed on the company's website.

Real-life example 2, the cracked game: Arif, a first-year student, downloads a cracked game from a random website. It contains a Trojan that installs ransomware. Two days before his project deadline, all his files are encrypted and a message demands money. Luckily, his teacher had told the class to keep their work in a cloud folder and on a pen drive. Arif wipes the laptop, reinstalls the system and gets his project back from the backup. He lost two days, not his whole semester.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: many students mix up virus, worm and Trojan. A virus needs a host file and a user to run it, a worm spreads by itself over networks, and a Trojan pretends to be useful. Another myth is that a padlock means a site is trustworthy; it only means the connection is encrypted. Antivirus alone is not enough without updates and good habits. Exams often ask you to explain the CIA triad, define and compare types of malware, explain phishing with an example, describe firewalls and encryption, and list ways to stay safe online.

Quick recap: security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability. Malware includes viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware and spyware, while social engineering tricks people instead of machines. Strong, long, unique passwords, two-factor authentication, encryption, firewalls, updates and backups are your shields. Most attacks still succeed because of human mistakes, so your habits are the strongest lock of all. In the final lesson, we will step back and look at how computers shape the whole of society.
key_points: Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability (the CIA triad).
A virus needs a host file and a user to run it; a worm spreads by itself; a Trojan pretends to be useful.
Ransomware encrypts your files and demands payment; backups are the best defence.
Phishing and social engineering trick people; never share your PIN or OTP with anyone.
Long passphrases beat short complex passwords, and passwords should never be reused.
Two-factor authentication adds a second proof, like an OTP, on top of a password.
Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext that only the key holder can read.
Firewalls, updates, antivirus and the 3-2-1 backup rule protect systems and data.
lessons.tip: For each type of malware, remember one short line: how it spreads and what it wants. Virus needs a host, worm spreads itself, Trojan is a disguise, ransomware wants money, spyware wants your secrets.
lessons.task: Check your own accounts today: turn on two-factor authentication for your email and Facebook, change any password you use on more than one site, and look at your phone's app permissions. Remove one permission that an app does not really need.

quiz.q: Which type of malware spreads across a network by itself, without the user opening any file?
quiz.explain: A worm copies itself to other computers over the network on its own. A virus needs a user to run an infected file.

quiz.q: An SMS says, "Your bKash account will be blocked, send us your OTP." What is this?
quiz.explain: It is a phishing message by SMS (smishing). Real companies never ask for your PIN or OTP.

quiz.q: In the CIA triad of security, what does "A" stand for?
quiz.explain: CIA stands for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability, meaning the system must work when users need it.

quiz.q: Using a Caesar cipher with a shift of 3, what does "CAT" become?
quiz.explain: Shift each letter forward by 3: C becomes F, A becomes D and T becomes W.

quiz.q: Which password is the strongest?
quiz.explain: Length makes passwords much harder to guess. A long passphrase is stronger than a short password, even with symbols.

lessons.title: Computers in Society: Uses, Ethics, Careers and the Future
lessons.content:
Think about your day so far. Your phone's alarm woke you up. Maybe you checked Facebook, paid for something with bKash, called a Pathao ride, or joined an online class. Even the rice you ate was probably sold through a supply chain tracked by computers. Computers are no longer just machines in a lab; they are part of almost everything we do. In this last lesson of the course, we will see how computers shape society, the good and the bad, the rules we should follow, the jobs they create and where they are heading next.

The big picture: computers have changed how we learn, work, shop, travel, get treated in hospitals and deal with the government. They do boring, repetitive work quickly and without getting tired, they let us talk to anyone in the world instantly, and they store and find information in seconds. But every powerful tool can also be misused, so a good computer scientist understands both sides.

Education: students now learn from videos, online courses and apps at any time and any place. Platforms like 10 Minute School teach millions of Bangladeshi students online. Teachers use projectors and slides, universities run their admission and course registration online, and SSC and HSC results are published on education board websites and by SMS. During the COVID-19 school closures, online classes kept learning going for many students.

Banking and money: computers made banking faster and available all day. ATMs let you withdraw cash at midnight, online banking lets you pay bills from home, and mobile financial services like bKash, Nagad and Rocket let even people without a bank account send and receive money with a basic phone. Shops now accept QR code payments. Behind every transaction there are databases, networks and security systems working together.

Health: hospitals use computers to keep patient records, book appointments and manage medicines. Machines like X-ray, CT scan and MRI rely on computers to create images of the inside of the body. Telemedicine lets a doctor in a city advise a patient in a village by video call. In Bangladesh, the government health helpline 16263 gives medical advice over the phone, backed by computer systems.

E-government in Bangladesh: many government services have moved online. You can apply for a birth registration, an NID correction or an e-passport (introduced in 2020) online. Union Digital Centres, started in 2010, bring services like land records, online applications and printing to villages across the country. The national helpline 333 answers questions about government services, and taxpayers can submit their income tax returns online. All of this reduces travel, time and paperwork for citizens.

Business and e-commerce: online shops like Daraz and Chaldal, food delivery apps like Foodpanda and thousands of small Facebook pages (often called f-commerce) let people buy and sell from home. Businesses use computers for accounts, stock, salaries and customer records. In Bangladesh's garment industry, designers use CAD (computer-aided design) software to make patterns, and factories use computers to plan production and track orders.

Transport and communication: ride-sharing apps like Pathao and Uber use GPS to match you with the nearest driver and calculate the fare. Bangladesh Railway sells train tickets online, and the Dhaka Metro Rail uses contactless MRT pass cards that you tap at the gate. Mobile phones, video calls and social media keep families connected even when one member works abroad.

Agriculture: farmers get weather forecasts and crop advice on their phones. The Krishi Call Centre, 16123, gives farmers expert advice by phone. Sensors can measure soil moisture so water is used only when needed, and market price apps help farmers know whether to sell today or wait.

Science, media and entertainment: supercomputers forecast cyclones days in advance, which has saved many lives in coastal Bangladesh. Scientists use computers to simulate medicines, space missions and climate. Films use computer animation and special effects, music is recorded and edited digitally, and games, streaming and online videos are a huge part of entertainment.

The positive side, in short: computers save time and money, improve accuracy, connect people, open up education and information to everyone, create new jobs and businesses, and help make better decisions using data. They also help people with disabilities, through screen readers for blind users and speech-to-text tools.

The negative side: too much screen time can cause eye strain, bad posture, neck pain and poor sleep. Games and social media can become addictive and reduce face-to-face time with family and friends. Privacy can be lost when personal data is collected and sold. Cybercrime, online fraud and cyberbullying are real dangers. Fake news and rumours spread fast on social media. Automation can replace some jobs. And old phones and computers become e-waste that contains harmful materials like lead and mercury.

The digital divide: not everyone has the same access to computers and the Internet. The gap between people who have access, devices and skills, and those who do not, is called the digital divide. In Bangladesh, a student in a big city may have fast Wi-Fi and a laptop, while a student in a remote char area may share one basic phone with the whole family. Cheaper smartphones, mobile internet, Union Digital Centres and school computer labs all help to close this gap.

Computer ethics: ethics means knowing what is right and wrong. In computing, that means not using computers to harm others, not reading other people's files or messages without permission, not stealing software, music or films, and not passing off someone else's work as your own. The Computer Ethics Institute published the "Ten Commandments of Computer Ethics" in 1992, with rules like "Thou shalt not use a computer to harm other people" and "Thou shalt not use other people's computer resources without authorization". The idea is simple: treat people online the way you would treat them face to face.

Intellectual property and piracy: software, books, music, films and designs are created by people who deserve credit and payment. Copyright protects their work. Copying paid software without a license is called software piracy, and it is illegal. Copying text or ideas without giving credit is called plagiarism, and universities treat it very seriously. If you cannot afford paid software, there are often free and open-source alternatives, like LibreOffice instead of Microsoft Office or GIMP instead of Photoshop.

Netiquette and green computing: netiquette means good manners online: be polite, do not type in ALL CAPS (it looks like shouting), do not spam, respect other people's privacy and check facts before sharing. Green computing means using computers in an environmentally friendly way: turn off devices when not in use, use power-saving modes, print only when needed and recycle old electronics properly instead of throwing them in the garbage.

Careers in computing: computer science opens many doors. Software engineers build apps and systems. Web and mobile developers make websites and phone apps. Data scientists find patterns in data. Network engineers keep networks running. Cyber security analysts defend against attackers. Database administrators look after data. UI/UX designers make software easy and pleasant to use. AI and machine learning engineers build smart systems. Game developers make games. There are also IT support specialists, teachers and researchers. Many Bangladeshis also work as freelancers for clients abroad; studies have found Bangladesh to be one of the world's largest suppliers of online freelance workers.

Skills you will need: more than any single language or tool, you need problem-solving skills, logical thinking and good math. Programming is a must for most roles. Communication in Bangla and English, teamwork, honesty and the habit of learning continuously matter just as much, because technology changes every few years and the people who keep learning keep growing. Start small: build tiny projects, join a programming club or contest, read other people's code, and share what you make. A portfolio of real work often impresses employers more than marks alone.

The future: artificial intelligence (AI) lets computers understand language, recognize images and help write and code. Cloud computing means using powerful computers and storage over the Internet instead of owning them. The Internet of Things (IoT) connects everyday objects, like fans, fridges, electricity meters and cars, to the Internet. Robotics brings computers into the physical world, from factory arms to delivery robots. 5G gives faster mobile internet, augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR) mix the digital and real worlds, blockchain keeps tamper-proof records, and quantum computing may one day solve problems that today's computers cannot. You will meet all of these later in your degree.

AI and jobs: AI will change many jobs. Some repetitive tasks, like typing data or answering simple questions, will be automated. But AI also creates new jobs and makes people more productive. The best plan is not to fear AI but to learn how it works and how to use it well. A person who understands both their subject and AI will be far more valuable than either alone.

Real-life example 1, a Union Digital Centre: Mitu lives in a village in Rangpur. Her family has no computer at home. She goes to the Union Digital Centre at the union parishad office, where an entrepreneur helps her apply online for a government scholarship, prints her birth certificate and downloads her land record for her father. In one visit she does work that used to need several trips to the district town. That is computers reducing the digital divide in real life.

Real-life example 2, a freelancer: Rakib learned graphic design and web design from free online courses using a second-hand laptop. Now he designs logos and websites for small businesses in other countries through online freelancing marketplaces. He talks to clients by email and video call, sends files through cloud storage, and his earnings come into his Bangladeshi bank account through international payment services. Computers turned his skills into a global job without leaving his hometown.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: in essay questions about the impact of computers, students often write only the good side. Always give both positive and negative impacts, with examples from Bangladesh. Know the definitions of digital divide, e-governance, computer ethics, software piracy, plagiarism, netiquette and green computing. Exams often ask for short notes on these terms, uses of computers in a given field like education, banking or health, and the careers available in computing.

Course recap: across these 25 lessons you learned what a computer is and where it came from, the types and parts of computer systems, how the CPU, memory and storage work, input and output devices, number systems and binary arithmetic, how text, pictures and sound are stored, logic gates, software and operating systems, programming languages and algorithms, files, networks, the Internet, databases, security and finally the role of computers in society. That is the whole map of computer science in miniature. Next, in Structured Programming, you will start writing real programs and give your own instructions to the machine.
key_points: Computers are used everywhere: education, banking, health, government, business, transport, agriculture and science.
Bangladesh's e-government services include online birth registration, e-passports, Union Digital Centres and helplines like 333.
Computers bring big benefits but also problems like eye strain, addiction, privacy loss, cybercrime, fake news and e-waste.
The digital divide is the gap between people who have access to computers and the Internet and those who do not.
Computer ethics means using computers honestly and without harming others; software piracy and plagiarism are wrong.
Computing careers include software engineering, data science, networking, cyber security, design and AI.
Future technologies include AI, cloud computing, IoT, robotics, 5G, AR/VR, blockchain and quantum computing.
Problem solving, programming, communication and lifelong learning matter more than any single tool.
lessons.tip: For essay questions on the impact of computers, use a simple frame: pick one field, then write how it worked before computers, how it works now, one good impact, one bad impact and one Bangladeshi example. It keeps your answer balanced and full of marks.
lessons.task: Make a list of every computer-based service you or your family used in the last week, such as bKash, an online class, a ride app or an online form. For each one, write one way it helped you and one risk it brings.

quiz.q: What does "digital divide" mean?
options: Splitting a hard disk into parts
The gap between people who have access to computers and the Internet and those who don't
quiz.explain: The digital divide is the difference in access to devices, the Internet and digital skills between groups of people.

quiz.q: What do Union Digital Centres in Bangladesh mainly do?
options: Give people in villages access to online government and other services
quiz.explain: Union Digital Centres help rural citizens with services like online applications, land records and printing documents.

quiz.q: Copying paid software without a license is called...
quiz.explain: Using or sharing paid software without a valid license is software piracy, which is illegal and unethical.

quiz.q: Which of these is a negative impact of computers?
options: E-waste and eye strain from too much screen time
quiz.explain: E-waste harms the environment and too much screen time harms health. The other options are benefits.

quiz.q: Which technology connects everyday objects like fans, meters and fridges to the Internet?
quiz.explain: The Internet of Things (IoT) links everyday objects to the Internet so they can send data and be controlled remotely.
